III

PREFACE 

THIS work represents the fruit of 34 years of teaching the Texas law of corporations plus an experience in practice largely devoted to the same subject. Its preparation has extended over a period of 12 years. Indeed some parts of it were started nearly 20 years ago. Every effort has been made to include every Texas decision, and although the work has extended over many years all cases have been brought to date.

Because many questions raised elsewhere in the law of private corporations have not been decided in Texas, these gaps in the Texas law have been filled by reference to the law of England and to American jurisdictions outside of Texas.

Wherever it seemed helpful, essential parts of Texas opinions nave been quoted verbatim, thus enabling the bar to have before them and to cite if necessary, the exact language of the courts. 

The Texas corporation statutes are quite fragmentary and some of them are outmoded, but since this is intended as a practical treatise on corporation law, designed to present the law of Texas as it is, no attempt has been made to point out needed amendments to Texas statutes nor has any effort been made to show how these obsolete statutes have been amended in other 

American jurisdictions.

However, many questions as yet undecided by the Texas courts are certain to arise in the future. These have been anticipated as far as possible and cases and other materials have been cited in an attempt to show what are regarded as the better holdings. 

It is hoped that this will afford Texas lawyers easy access to the best authorities on these questions involving the law of corporations.

In this discussion of the Texas law of corporations, court opinions have been frankly considered and where they seem to have

PREFACE 

deviated from the prevailing law in other jurisdictions or failed to recognize changed social and economic conditions, that fact has been pointed out. Suggestions are made for the improvement of our common law of private corporations. 

So much valuable assistance has been afforded the author from so many different sources and so many persons among my colleagues in the law school of the University of Texas, Texas practicing lawyers and judges, and my former pupils that an attempt to make a personal acknowledgement would be both inadequate and unjust. Some would be left out. Mr. C. B. Jeffrey, Mr. Andrew Fosler and Mr. Starling Thomas Morris, deserve special recognition, as does Mr. Searcy Johnson for his assistance on chapter one. Professor James William Moore, formerly of the 

Texas law faculty reviewed part of chapter 27. 

It is a pleasure to acknowledge the kindness of the hundreds of lawyers who over the long years encouraged my efforts. In this group Judge A. H. Carrigan of Wichita Falls deserves special mention.

The work is offered to the bench and bar of Texas in the hope that it may throw light in the dark corners of the corporation law of Texas and thus be a means of lessening the burden of our great profession.

IRA P. HILDEBRAND. 

AUSTIN, TEXAS, 

August, 1942.

§ 1. Introductory 

The age of the corporate mechanism is exceeded only by its importance to the progress of business as a factor in social development.

Concentration of wealth by pooling many individual fortunes while limiting the individual's liability has attracted industrial and financial brains and efforts that have resulted in making the United States of America the great industrial nation it is today. 

Only through the corporate organization could adequate capital have been attracted for the phenominal growth of American business. Only through the legal entity thus created could our great endowments for educational, medical and other social prerequisites have found adequate and extended sources of income to maintain the institutions for which such endowments were devised. 

The idea of a group of real persons associating together and forming thereby a distinct corporate existence is not of recent 

1 HILDEBRAND TEX.CORP.-1

birth. According to Gaius, corporate existence was known to 

Greek civilization long before Cicero orated in the Roman Senate.¹

Most legal writers say that these early ideas of corporate existence embodied in Roman law influenced to some degree the later English common law concepts of private corporations.* 

In earlier English history these corporations were primarily charitable, ecclesiastical, or municipal—private, with functions of a public character.³

By the end of the sixteenth century, trading companies acquiring monopolistic and governmental powers in their assigned territories made their appearance. American territory was assigned to some of these corporate organizations. It is from their character and operation that the people of the United States formed their ideas about the possibilities of the corporation as a legal entity. They saw that it enjoyed most of the legal privileges of the individual person, but escaped many of his liabilities. No one could shoot the legal entity that injured him. He could not even have the pleasure of giving a corporate organization a cauliflower ear, because the corporation had no ear.

These are only a few significant advantages to individuals in conducting business in that early day through the corporate organization. The so-called automatic corporation was known in 

England, but was recognized in the United States to a very limited extent. This type of corporation grew out of a position held, such as king, vicar, or archbishop. These automatic corporations were known as corporations per se and designated corporations "at common law." A court in this country once held that the Governor of a state is a corporation "at common law.” 4 

In another case the court held that the rector of an Episcopal

§ 2. Definitions 

A hole-proof definition of a corporation is impossible to give in a few words. Legal writers seldom accept each other's definitions. Professor Wormser has defined a corporation as follows: "A corporation aggregate is a collection of individuals united by authority of law, into one body, under a special denomination, with the capacity of continuous succession, and of acting in many respects as an individual." Professor Ballantine defines it as follows: "A corporation is an association of individuals, or sometimes of individuals and other corporations for some joint enterprise, invested by the law with capacity to sue and be sued, to make contracts, to take, hold, and convey property, and to do other acts like a single individual." Mr. Fletcher says: "A corporation is not only a mental conception. 

The only 'mental conception' involved in the idea of a corporation is found in the fact that the law, for purposes of its own, indulges in a benevolent fiction and endows the corporation with personality and treats it as a person for most purposes.' "9 Mr.

Taylor's definition is more comprehensive, and is the following: "The term corporation is used to denote what exists through the operation of rules of law as well as to denote physical existence and this indiscriminate use of the term has caused much confusion, but a double use of the term seems unavoidable in the present condition of legal terminology. A corporation considered as a legal institution is the sum of the legal relations resulting

Mr. Chief Justice Marshall, in the famous Dartmouth College case, gave the most frequently quoted definition of a corporation when he said: "A corporation is an artificial being, invisible, intangible, and existing only in contemplation of law. Being a mere creature of law, it possesses only those properties which the charter of its creation confers upon it, either expressly or as incidental to its very existence." Mr. Justice McKenan informs us that: "A corporation is a creature of the law, and none of its powers are original. They are precisely what the incorporating act has made them, and can only be exerted in the manner which that act authorizes. In other words, the State prescribes the purposes of a corporation and the means of executing those purposes. 

Purposes and means are within the State's control." 12 

The Texas courts have also defined a corporation. In the case of Houston National Exchange Bank v. Osceola Irrigating Co.,13 

the court laid down the general rule that a corporation is a legal entity or artificial person entirely distinct from its members or stockholders. It transacts its business by and through its officers or agents, and their acts are the acts of this legal entity or artificial person as distinguished from the acts of the persons who compose its membership. In Sayers v. Texas Land & Mortgage 

Co.14 Judge Gaines said that the creation of the corporation in question was by operation of law, and upon its formation it became an artificial being, distinct from its corporators. It remained for Mr. Justice Brown of the United States Supreme Court to take what seems to be a very common sense attitude in speaking of a corporation, when he stated: "A corporation is, after all, 10. But one idea seems common to all these attempts to say what a corporation is. All express the idea that it is a legal entity with an existence of its own separate and distinct from those who formed it and from those who finance it. 

Sometimes such 

Attempts at logical definitions profit little. attempts lead us mentally astray. Perhaps a common place illustration can best suggest this central idea of corporate existence which is expressed or implied in all attempts by legal writers to define a corporation. Corporate existence may well be compared to that of offspring. People associate to form a new being which shall carry on for them. The child is theirs, but is a separate and distinct existence. It's their creature, but has its own duties and liabilities.

Corporate existence is created through associations of persons petitioning the State for the privilege of creating a distinct legal representative to carry on business or what not, for those associated as creators. The corporation belongs to the associates who formed it, but it is not they nor are they the corporation any more than the offspring is the same being as its parents, or vice versa.

The corporation, however, cannot be created without the authority of the state; offsprings sometimes are, unfortunately.

The unlawful corporation is treated more harshly than the unlawful child, as is shown in the chapter on "Dissolution of Corporations" in this text. One reason for this difference is the attitude of the courts towards the corporation in its early existence. 

The corporation existed only in the imagination of the judges, but the unlawful child could be seen and even heard to cry.

Until the courts visualize a private corporation as a legal personality composed of live human beings existing in its own created right, their decisions will be conflicting and unsatisfactory. 

15. Hale v. Henkel, 26 S.Ct. 370, 201 

U.S. 43, 50 L.Ed. 652. 

See the same idea in Railway Co. v. 

Allerton, 85 U.S. 233, 18 Wall. 

233, 21 L.Ed. 902.

§ .3  

A corporation is in reality a collection of real persons formed into a separate and independent legal existence and may therefore be defined as follows: A private corporation is a collection of individuals amalgamated into a legal personality to whom a franchise has been granted to conduct a business or a non-profit activity with limited individual liability of its stockholders, unless some statutory liability is imposed on them by the state. where the corporation was organized. A corporation is no more fictitious in fact than a partnership, a law class, or the United States army or navy. It is less fictitious in law, as it is a legal person existing in its own right. In early common law the corporation existed only in contemplation of the law. For this reason, Blackstone and other authorities said that it could not be appointed executor or administrator for the simple reason that it could not take an oath. That sounds very technical today. But when that view prevailed, learned men were still spending years debating "How many angels could dance on the point of a cambric needle." Today, statutes in practically all states authorize certain corporations to act as executors or administrators of estates.16 All judges now realize that a corporation can act only vicariously, and, therefore, hold that a corporation can make an affidavit or take an oath by and through one of its agents.¹7 

§ 3. Corporations Distinguished from Other Types of Organiza tions

shows that the transfer of the stock will not affect the existence of the corporation as such. In a partnership the delectus personarum is very important. It is sometimes said to be the characteristic feature of a partnership. A partnership's existence is dependent upon the contractual association of its constituents. 

The death of a single partner will dissolve the partnership.36 

Likewise bankruptcy, or changing personnel through sale of an interest, will dissolve the firm.37 

Perhaps the most attractive and useful characteristic of a corporation is that it limits the liability of the shareholders. Except when otherwise provided by statute, shareholders in a corporation are liable for the debts of the corporation only to the extent of their respective subscriptions to the capital. The shareholders may lose what they invest in the corporation, but they will not be individually liable if the assets of the corporation are insufficient to pay its liabilities. Corporate liabilities are not personal debts of the persons making up the corporate entity. Stockholders' individual liability for corporate debts when the stock is fully paid must be imposed by a statute, where the corporation was organized if personal liability exists.38

courts have consistently held that a partner is individually liable for all the firm debts,41 as well as for the torts of a partner or servant of the firm.42 In Texas it is also held that a partnership creditor may sue one partner without joining the other copartners.43 Of course, the partners are liable for all debts created by the firm and their liability created before they form a corporation is not destroyed by the formation of a corporation and the conveyance of all the property to the corporation.44 

There are other differences between a corporation and a partnership. A corporation cannot be created by agreement as can a partnership. The corporation can only be created by or under legislative enactment. The corporation is not the only type of business association created under or by legislative enactment, such as a statutory joint-stock company. Partnerships may dissolve at any time they see fit, but a corporation cannot be dissolved by mere agreement of the stockholders. The approval and consent of the sovereign state is necessary for its dissolution.45 

If there is a partnership, there is mutual agency of the partners. 

It is said that each partner is both a principal and an agent; all the partners have a right to take part in the operation of the business. But in the corporation the business is conducted by the directors, or by agents appointed by the directors. An agreement by the stockholders to give sole management of the business to one person is illegal since the statute provides that the affairs of the corporation must be conducted by a "board of directors." 46

To the student of private corporations no historical incident is more interesting than that of the joint-stock company in England, and, especially, the English statutes with reference to companies with "transferable shares," finally culminating with their first really general incorporation statute in 1862. In fact, in England many judges thought that it was illegal at common law to form a company with "transferable shares."

It was so held in 1837 in the case of Blundell v. Windsor, 8 Simon 601.

So many frauds were perpetrated by such companies during the latter part of the seventeenth and the early part of the eighteenth centuries that in 1719 Parliament passed the celebrated Bubble Act, which made companies with "transferable shares" illegal. (6 Geo. 1, Chap. 18, Sec. 18); 

R. v. Dodd, 3 B. & C. 639; Josephs v. 

Pebur, 9 East 516; The King v. 

Webb, 14 East 406. The background of the Bubble Act is thus described by Mr. Napier in A Century of Law 

Reform, pages 382 and 383: "But later cases seem to have proceeded upon the principle that a company with freely transferable shares is not at common law an illegal association or a nuisance, although it was, of course, impossible for the Court to give effect to any provision in the deed of settlement of such a company limiting the liability of the shareholder to the amount unpaid on his shares or otherwise. Walburn v.

Act, which remained in force rather over 100 years, and must have retarded the development of joint-stock trading. The history of the Bubble

Except in so far as statutes have provided otherwise, jointstock companies are in general subject to the same principles of law as govern the common law partnership.51 Joint-stock companies may be formed by mere agreement of the associates. A joint-stock company with transferable shares was valid at common law in America.52 The joint-stock company, like the partnership, may be dissolved at any time without the consent of the state, except where a statute has changed the rule.53 But unlike the partnership, and resembling the corporation, the withdrawal of a member, by death, bankruptcy, or sale of his interest, does not per se work a dissolution of the joint-stock company.54 

Like the corporation, the affairs of the joint-stock company are conducted by a board of directors or trustees; the shareholders themselves are not agents of the joint-stock company merely because of their status as stockholders.55 Unless the statute so provides the joint-stock company cannot acquire and convey property in its common name. The public, to use a modern promoter's expression, was so much on the feed, that 

1000 subscriptions were paid the same morning, with which the promoter disappeared in the afternoon."

At common law the joint-stock the members as individuals.56 company could not sue or be sued in its common name; it could only be sued in the name of the associates, and at common law all were necessary parties to the action.57 But today the jointstock company, by statutory provision in most states, can sue and be sued in the common name.58 Ownership in the modern jointstock company is represented by shares of stock, which are freely assignable or transferable, as are corporate stocks, but this feature alone does not make it a corporation.59 As one leading authority has stated: "It seems impossible to say of joint-stock companies and associations existing or formed under statutes any more than this: If enough corporate attributes exist, and if nothing repels it, they are corporations. If essential attributes are lacking, or the implication is repelled otherwise, they are not corporations. Each one, of the particular class to which it belongs, must be judged by these attributes given by and found in the varying statutes of the different states." 60

Massachusetts, prohibiting corporations from dealing in real property, this type of organization reached its fullest development and most extensive use in that state; but has been adopted for use in many other states. The chief advantages of such organizations, from the standpoint of those desirous of combining their wealth for business purposes, are that until recently, they were, in most states, free from regulation, enjoyed freedom from corporation taxation, and its members enjoyed the freedom from personal liability that is imposed upon partners. This type of organization is nothing more than an attempt to use the old common law trust for the purpose of carrying on business enterprise." 1 The business trust is created, not like the ordinary common law trust by a testator or donor for the benefit of some third party, but by the beneficiaries themselves. In general these trusts or associations are organized for the purpose of carrying on a business for profit. While in many respects they resemble corporations, it seems that there should be no great difficulty in distinguishing the two, for the business trust is usually created or organized under the common law and not by statute, though business trusts have been recognized by statute in at least two jurisdictions.63 Business trusts most nearly resemble corporations in that they carry on business with a concentration of management in trustees, resembling directors, have transferable shares of beneficial interest similar to corporate stock, and enjoy continuity of the business for the term for which the trust is created.64

Whether there is or is not a business trust is determined primarily by the question of control. "If the declaration of trust confers absolute and uncontrolled power upon the trustees with respect to the management of the property given them and the beneficiaries have only the rights that are implied because they are fundamental to the trust relation, viz.: to call upon the trustees to account, to have them removed for misconduct or neglect, to receive the income while the trust lasts, and their share of the corpus or of the conversion thereof upon its termination, then plainly, the arrangement is a pure trust and the shareholders are not primarily liable to the creditors." 65 If by the declaration of trust the shareholders reserve the actual or potential power, as a practical matter, to control the trustees in conducting the business of the organization, it is a partnership. But, on the other hand, if the trustees are the principals and not subject, as a practical matter, to the actual or potential control of the shareholders, the organization is a pure trust, and not a partnership.6 

In Texas the law was certainly unsettled for some time. In the case of Fisheries Co. v. McCoy,67 the Fourth Court of Civil

Court in 1925 apparently sounded the death knell of the Massachusetts Trust in Texas. Under the declaration of trust in that case the title to all of the property was vested in certain named trustees and their successors for the benefit of the certificate holders. The stockholders had the right to examine the books of the business, receive dividends, and upon dissolution of the company to have a division of the principal and profits. The trust declaration also stated that stockholders were not to be personally liable for debts of the company and the trustees were to incorporate this provision into all contracts. Schmitt sued 

Thompson, a shareholder, on an obligation created by the trustees, who, known to the plaintiff, had exceeded their authority in creating the obligation. The court held defendant liable as a partner. It seems there is no reason of public policy that would require the investors in such an association to be personally liable, and generally in other jurisdictions such an arrangement would be held to be a Massachusetts trust, and the shareholders not personally liable." The court said that the Legislature has provided statutory methods of avoiding personal liability, corporation and limited partnership, and those methods are exclusive.72

§ 4  § 4. Consequences of the Separate Corporate Entity 

It is generally well established that a corporation is a legal entity, separate and distinct from its individual members or shareholders, with rights, liabilities and attributes of its own in no manner dependent upon, connected with, or similar to the rights of the stockholders." The corporation and its officers are not the same personality." This recognition or existence of the corporate entity distinct from the shareholders makes possible several of the other attributes of the corporation, e. g., transfer of shares and change in membership without change in the corporation," the right to sue and be sued in the corporate name, and the right and capacity to own and hold property in the corporate name in its own individuality.80

The sale of the stock of the corporation does not affect the rights and obligations of the company. Therefore, when the 

State of Texas agreed to give 3,000,000 acres of public domain for building the capitol of Texas, and the tracts patented to the contractor contained 60,000 excessive acres, the State could recover this excess even though some of the shareholders had sold their stock to innocent purchasers after the patents were issued and before the State instituted a suit to recover the excess.81 

Even though the shareholders sell land to their own corporation, if the latter does not pay the purchase price, materialmen making improvements on the land at the instance of the vendee cannot fix a lien against the property superior to the vendor's lien for unpaid purchase price.82 As the officers of the company and the corporation are separate personalities, limitation on a claim against the corporation is not suspended by reason of Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 5537, during the period the officers of the corporation are absent from the state.83 As a general rule, though one man acquires all the stock of a corporation, the legal entity is yet intact; he and the corporation are not one and the same personality, but are distinct legal entities.84 And this seems to be true even where the owner of all the stock is another corporation or several corporations.85 However, there are a few cases

§ 5. Disregarding the Corporate Entity 

Texas, consistent with the fundamental theory of corporations, follows the general rule acceptable today that a corporation is a legal entity or artificial person entirely distinct from its members or stockholders, and that its acts, through its officers or agents, are the acts of this legal entity as distinguished from the persons who compose its membership.20 This is true irrespective of the parties who own the stock,21 and applies even if part of the property is owned by another corporation.22 Nor is one corporation liable for the obligations of another corporation merely because the two corporations have the same president and attorney.23 

The terms "corporate fiction," "corporate entity," and "legal fiction" are used so frequently and interchangeably in the cases paid to it, it is not an abuse of discretion to sustain a challenge for cause to jurors related to stockholders of the bank within the third degree of consanguinity under statute defining a challenge for cause as an objection disqualifying the juror in the opinion of the court. that confusion often results. As was stated by Canfield 24 it is misleading to call the theory of corporate entity a fiction, for it is not an arbitrary assumption without regard to facts and does not involve a false deduction, as was true of early fictions used in the law.25 But whatever name may be given to this legal concept, as a practical matter a corporation is in reality an association of persons, and no judicial dictum or legislative enactment can alter this fact.26 The conception of corporate entity was given to this group of persons for a purpose, as a formula for working out the rights of real parties in interest, and for convenience in making contracts, in the acquisition of property, and to preserve limited liability of stockholders.28 Since a corporation is looked upon as a legal entity for a purpose, when that purpose is abused, a court is under no duty to continue to regard the corporate entity, and may consider the corporation as an aggregate of persons.29 27 As Professor Ballantine suggests,30 the problem of responsibility of acts of a corporation or stockholders is to be solved not by disregarding the corporate entity, but by a study of the just limitations on the exercise of the legal privileges of separate capacity.

Where a corporation is organized and used for legitimate business purposes, it will be looked to as a separate legal entity, 24. 17 Col.Law Rev. 129.

Lone Star Gas Co.,45 for determining when the subsidiary corporation is the agent of the holding company: "The cases are legion which deal with the relationship of two or more corporations from the standpoint of ownership of the capital stock in one by another, and from the standpoint of association together for the purpose of carrying on a single or common business enterprise. The rule is well settled that courts will look through the forms to the realities of the relationship between two or more corporations in order to determine whether each is a separate entity or corporation; or whether their commingled affairs are such as to constitute them one integrated and single business enterprise; or whether, through intercorporate set-up, affiliation, or stock ownership, the purpose is to control the subsidiary corporation or corporations so that they are used as the mere instrumentalities or agents of the owning corporation or corporations. In discussing the rule, it has been held that while 'ownership, alone, of capital stock in one corporation by another, does not create an identity of corporate interest or create the relation of principal and agent or representative between the two'; still it has been repeatedly held that such rule is not applicable 'where stock ownership has been resorted to, not for the purpose of participating in the affairs of a corporation in the normal and usual manner, but for the purpose of controlling a subsidiary company so that it may be used as a mere agency or instrumentality of the owning company or companies.' 46

Where the officers of the two corporations are the same and the officer of both the bank and the loan company looked after the notes of Mr. Davies who had loaned the loan company ten thousand dollars and took its note as evidence of the loan, secured by a deed of trust on property of the loan company, a mere notation, "Interest on Note," on a check of the loan company in paying the semi-annual interest was a sufficient acknowledgment of the debt. Such acknowledgment was sufficient to prevent the note being barred within four years of the original date. Though the renewal was not recorded, a subsequent mortgage by the loan company in favor of the bank would not have priority over the Davies' lien. To claim the corporate entity is acting separately here would be unjust. For notice of the extension agreement to the officers of the loan company will be likewise notice to the officers of the bank. Therefore, the court held that the bank's lien on the same property that had been mortgaged to Davies was secondary to his lien.51 Fundamentally, this action by the court is to prevent using the legal fiction of corporate entity for fraudulent ends. But as Professor Warren said many times before his classes at the Harvard Law School every "legal right" has an ending. 

The privilege of incorporating a business is granted for lawful purposes.64 When the promoters attempt to effectuate an unconscionable result by means of the franchise to carry on a lawful business, the courts will disregard the legal entity and determine the rights of both parties just as though no attempt had been made to incorporate. When this should be done is a question of fact and common sense. The court must weigh the facts and consequences in each case carefully, and common sense and justice must determine his decision.65

The question of disregarding the corporate fiction often arises where parent and subsidiary corporations are concerned. As a general rule, the bare fact of a holding company and a subsidiary, will not create liability in the parent corporation for the contracts of its "off-spring." There must be additional circumstances showing fraud, or agency in which the holding company has reaped benefits." To treat them as one, it must be shown that they are the business conduits of each other.

Texas decisions are consistent, with but very few exceptions, with the majority and favored rule,68 and continue to look on a corporation as a separate entity though it is practically a branch of the parent organization and organized for the purpose of better effectuating the work of the parent organization.69 

However, where one corporation is but a mere automaton for the other, used for the purpose of securing indirectly what could not be done directly, then equity will disregard the corporate entity and consider the two corporations as the same.70 

As to a parent corporation proving its claims against an insolvent subsidiary in competition with its creditors, a Texas case has held that where a parent company caused debts to be incurred by the subsidiary, the former still owes these debts which caused depletion of the security of bondholders by lessening the assets of the subsidiary corporation, and this parent corporation cannot in equity share equally with the other creditors of the subsidiary corporation in the distribution of the assets, until it has made amends for its own wrongs or discharged its own obligation to the corporation."

The same general rules should be applied in regard to the matter of enemy corporations. The mere fact alone that the corporation is owned principally or entirely by aliens should not cause its corporate entity to be disregarded in time of war. Something more should be required. As has often been said, when the courts disregard the fictitious character of the corporation, "this result has been reached by saying that the corporation has been the 'alter ego,' 'simulacrum,' 'nominal identity' or 'instrumentality,' (or agent) of the shareholders. These terms are not, of course, self-defining.” 73

If the courts would cease using a dead language and talk in Twentieth Century English, apply common sense to each case that comes before them, and quit trying to harmonize their conclusion with rules of law governing relationships that are not similar to the corporate set-up, less time would be consumed, the conclusions reached less nebulous, and their decisions would effect justice with clarity.74

Texas courts make no distinction as far as venue is concerned between domestic and foreign corporations.83 

For purposes of determining jurisdiction of Federal courts of suits by and against corporations, all the stockholders are conclusively presumed to be citizens of the state where the corporation was created,84 or that the corporation is a citizen of the state of its creation. 

Similar corporations with same directors may exist in several states, but the same corporation can not exist in several states, or several states can not unite in giving a charter to a corporation. It is considered a separate corporation in each state. This is because one state can not make a law that will affect another state. A law of one state can not aid in creating a corporation in another state.85

Care should be taken to distinguish between a license and a charter. An act merely recognizing a foreign corporation and allowing it to do business in the state, is a mere license and not a charter, and does not change the character of the corporation as a foreign corporation.86

The general rule is that where a constitution or statute grants a right, requires a duty or imposes a liability, upon any person, citizen or resident, it applies to a corporation as well as to a natural person, if it is within the reason and purpose of the provision.90 By express statutory provision, the word "person" in some states is made to include corporation.91 Under various acts of Congress and the 14th Amendment, the word "person" as used therein has been held to include corporation.⁹2

8. Classification of Corporations 

Corporations have been classified in as many different ways as there have been treatises on the subject. The most discussed classifications are reviewed here.

Sole and Aggregate.-It should be clearly understood that corporation sole does not refer to a corporation in which one party owns all the stock, for any corporation may have all its stock owned by one man and still retain its original character 4 as long as it carries on its proper and designated business. Corporation sole has been referred to as "one person to whom belongs legal perpetuity which is denied to a natural person." Perhaps the best example of a corporation sole known to us today is that of a Catholic priest, bishop, or archbishop.5 

A corporation aggregate is one composed of more than one member. Practically all corporations in the United States are of this nature.

Eleemosynary and Civil Corporations.-Corporations are often referred to as charitable corporations as contrasted to those operated for private gain or profit. Under this division come sanitariums open to all classes, and where profits are turned back if any are earned; and also the organization known as the 

Daughters of the Republic of Texas, an educational corporation."

These classifications are in most instances overlapping, for the last referred to corporation is classed as a private corporation as well as an eleemosynary one. 

Public and Private Corporations.-Texas statutes classify corporations as public and private. A public corporation is one which has for its object the government of a portion of the state.⁹ Private corporations are of three kinds: Religious, for charity or benevolence, and for profit.

Public corporations are looked on as subdivisions of the State to carry on business of the State and are subject to governmental control. Hence, their charter can be amended or changed by the legislature as it sees fit; while that of the private corporation can be changed only with the consent of the members who compose it. Private corporations are contractual in origin; public corporations are not. 

Public corporations as a rule are not liable for negligence or torts of their officers. The only exception to this rule is in the case of counties, cities and towns, and then only in a limited sense, and in regard to matters involving exercise of ministerial acts and not governmental functions.10 

Public corporations are usually political in nature. But public corporations, like public banks or State universities and colleges, do not have to be political. Their entire interests are the government's, and that makes them public corporate entities.¹¹

Quasi-Public Corporations.-Quasi-public corporation is also referred to as a public service corporation. It is inherently a private corporation, one formed for personal gain and profit, but because it exercises one of the functions of government and receives in turn special advantages or privileges, it is termed a quasi-public corporation.

As is shown in the text, the first general incorporation statute was finally passed in Texas in 1874. Up to that time while Texas was a part of the State of Coahuila and Texas, an independent republic and a State of the United States, the legislature created many private corporations by special acts. 

The first corporation created while 

Texas was part of the State of Coa huila and Texas was on the second day of October, 1830. The name of this corporation was "The Coahuila 

Manufacturing Company." Some of the provisions of the act creating this corporation are very interesting.

It provided that the "active capital shall not exceed the sum of one million of dollars, divided into two thousand shares, of five hundred dollars each." "At all the elections or meetings of the shareholders each shall be entitled to one vote; provided, that no individual shall have more than fifty votes, whatever be the number of his shares."

It was also provided that after the establishment of the company "no member shall acquire by purchase more than one share in addition to that which he holds, nor shall a shareholder sell except to a person having one share only or to one who previously had none. The purchaser shall be a Mexican by birth. * "The president and each director shall own at least one share each, and shall furthermore be citizens of the state of Coahuila and Texas."

About the most interesting provision was the one that required a bond of the agents of the company to guarantee the faithful discharge of their duties, and the stockholders "who voted for the persons appointed to the aforementioned stations (agents) shall be responsible, should the concerns of the company suffer in consequence of failing to require adequate bonds and security." It was further provided that obligations of the company "shall be binding against the capital stock and property of the company." The act also provided that the company shall never 54

The first company that was incorporated after Texas became the Republic of Texas was created by a special act approved December 16, 1836, entitled "The Texas Rail Road 

Navigation, and Banking Company."

The act provided that the company may have continual succession and power to do and perform all things which are necessary and common for companies of a similar nature, not contrary to the provisions of this charter or to the constitution of this republic. The company was given power to establish internal navigation, railroads and "banking privileges." Its capital stock was five million dollars. It could not charge more than ten per cent interest per annum. The act also provided that when a bank was established, said company shall pay over to the treasurer of Texas a bonus, in gold or silver, the sum of twenty-five thousand dollars, and also two and onehalf per cent per annum upon the net profits arising from the tolls, fees, and charges and the gov- ernment or republic of Texas shall have a free privilege of transporting all soldiers * and munitions of war, and also all transports and ships of war, free of tolls or other charges.

The act also provided that the company would continue for forty-nine years with the privilege of renewing the charter "for a like period, by paying to the government five hundred thousand dollars in gold or silver, and by further paying thereafter of five per cent per annum, upon the net profits arising upon all tolls, fees, and charges of said works. It was also provided that the capital stock may be increased to ten millions of dollars "by paying over to the government or State of Texas a further bonus of one hundred thousand dollars; provided, in no instance shall said company discount more than three dollars to one upon the capital paid in." It also provided that "all the chartered property of said company" shall be responsible for the obligations of the company. The company was given authority to establish as many branch banks "as they may think the necessities of the community require."

In a recent Texas case cited in the preceding note Justice Critz defined private and public corporations as follows: "This contention is based on the further contention that the special act purporting to create the incorporated 'Navarro Community Foundation' is void, because in contravention of Section 

I of Article XII of our State Constitution. Such constitutional provision provides: 'No private corporation shall be created except by general laws.' The constitutional provision next succeeding the one just quoted, Section 2 of Article XII, provides: 'General laws shall be enacted providing for the creation of private corporations.

Within the meaning of the above constitutional provisions, corporations are, divided into two classes, public corporations and private corporations. A corporation is public if it is created for public purposes only. 

In other words, a public corporation is one 'connected with the administration of the government, and the interests and franchises of which are the exclusive property and domain of the government itself.' A private corporation is any corporation not classed as public. Stated in another way, a private corporation is one created for private, as distinguished from purely public, purposes. A corporation is deemed private, though created for the administration of a public charity, where the endowments thereof have been received from individuals."

The first general incorporation statute was passed by the Twelfth Leg islature, December 2, 1871. Gen eral Laws of the Twelfth Legisla ture, Second Session, p. 68, Vol. III, 

Gammels' Laws of Texas, p. 68.

This statute did not contain an enacting clause, and for that reason was considered ineffective. The Thirteenth Legislature on April 23, 1873, passed "An act amendatory and sup plemental to 'An Act concerning Pri vate Corporations', approved December 2, 1871." General Laws of the 

Thirteenth Legislature, p. 42, Vol.

VII, Gammels' Laws of Texas, p. 

494. This act attempted to supply the enacting clause of section one of the act passed December 2, 1871, validate charters that had been approved under that act and repeal sections thirty-one and thirty-two of the original act. But as it did not re-enact the other provisions of the original act of December 2, 1871, it too was not considered effective to validate the original act. Therefore, it remained for the Fourteenth Legislature to pass our first valid general incorporation statute on April 

23, 1874. Laws of Fourteenth Legis- 

lature begun and held at Austin 

January 13, 1874, p. 120, Vol. VIII, Gammels' Laws of Texas, p. 122.

The original Act and the one finally passed as a valid statute in 1874 did not provide that all of the stock must be subscribed by the "three voluntary associates" who organized the com pany. By Sec. 14 of the Act of 1874 

it was provided that, "Whenever the full amount of the capital stock of a corporation having a capital stock shall not have been already subscribed in good faith, (before the charter is filed with the Secretary of State) the directors or trustees named in the charter, or a majority of them, may, within three months after the filing of the charter, cause books to be opened for receiving subscriptions to the capital stock of the corporation which books may be kept open till the whole amount of capital stock is subscribed." This part of the original statute shows that the Legislature left it optional with the promoters as to whether they would subscribe for some of the stock before the charter is applied for. It goes without saying that the

Legislature realized that three persons could not be "associated" in the formation of a corporation for profit unless each had a financial interest in the business of the association. If two of the promoters signed the charter as a mere formality and had no financial interest in the corporation to be organized where such corporation was for profit and never intended to purchase any stock after the books were opened for subscrip- 58

Ch. 

§ 22  

dates the statute 12 requiring the filing of the charter with the Secretary of State and its acceptance by him,13 before corporate existence begins. Nor is the provision 14 allowing the Secretary of State to demand further evidence than that specifically pre- * * tions, and especially where it was understood that such "signers" of the charter would not be made directors of the company and would have nothing to do with the business operations of the corporation, no one could contend with any show of reason that those two persons and the other one who subscribed for some of the stock of the company "were associated" in the conduct of a business for profit. Other provisions of the original Act show that there must be more than one subscriber to the stock of the corporation. For instance Subd. 8 of Sec. 11provides that "by a vote of its stockholders" the company may increase its directors "to be not less than three nor more than thirteen." By Sec. 12 it is provided that, "Any corporation may increase its capital stock by a vote of its stockholders." Sec. 

25 provides that, "The board of directors of any corporation may require the subscribers to the capital stock of the corporation to pay the amount by them respectively subscribed." In other words, the entire

Act shows that the Legislature intended group action and not that one person has the consent of the sovereign to organize a corporation, or even to purchase all the stock of the company after it is organized by three or more voluntary associates.

In National Bank v. Texas Invest ment Company, 12 S.W. 101, 74 Tex. 

421, the Supreme Court of Texas said before our statute was amended so that all of the stock must be subscribed and fifty per cent paid in before the charter is approved by the 

Secretary of State that "we find no provision in the law making the existence of the corporation depend upon the subscription to its stock or the payment therefor. On the contrary it is expressly provided that the existence of the corporation shall date from the filing of the charter in the office of the Secretary of 

State." However, in the next paragraph the Court also said: "It may be doubted whether the plaintiff is in a position to question the existence of the corporation if in fact it did not legally exist. Its allegations show that in discounting the note sued on it relied upon the representation that it was a corporation with a paid up capital of $100,000.00."

The conclusion of the court is correct since the corporate existence dated from the filing of the charter and the managers were then directed to open books for subscription of the company's stock within three months.

If the Court had referred to other parts of the original general incorporation act and followed the authorities discussed farther on in this chapter it would have concluded that the company was not fully organized until it opened books and had bona fide subscriptions for all of its stock.

§ 23  

ed by them.20 The general rule is that the charter is deemed to have been accepted when the proposed corporation has organized and met the terms of the statutes. The case of Quinlan v. Houston & T. C. Ry. Co.21 held that the organization of the corporation would have effected an acceptance of the charter as offered in the special act of 1866; that a charter is a contract and requires an acceptance, and that organization, at least to the extent required by the statutes, would be sufficient evidence of acceptance; that if no time is fixed for acceptance, it must be within a reasonable time. Davis v. Allison,22 in 1919, held substantially the same, when a bank attempted to accept the offer of a charter under a special act passed before the adoption of the Constitution of 1876, which prohibited the organization of such banks. The court held in this case that such a corporation was illegal and non-existent, despite the fact that its attempted organization was after the 1904 amendment which authorized incorporation of such banks under the general law. 

The promoters attempted to organize the bank under the old Act. The court held that its stock subscriptions were unenforceable. It follows also that although the charter is a contract, the statutes making the offer to the promoters may be repealed at any time prior to the acceptance of the charter, and the offer must be accepted or rejected as made without conditions being attached or modifications included.

Where the incorporation is by special act, the act is looked upon as an offer, necessitating acceptance.23 Where general incorporation statutes have been enacted, they are standing offers to the public, and, therefore, the state has given its consent in advance to all those who comply with the statutes to incorporate for a purpose authorized by the statutes; hence the

§ 26. Purposes of Incorporation 

The requirement 44 that the charter must contain the purpose for which the corporation is formed is based on the mandate of the constitution.45 Judge Hawkins in a dissenting opinion states: "The statutory requirement that the 'purpose' of the corporation shall be stated in its charter was intended for the protection of the incorporators and stockholders, and the public, in order that they may be advised as to the character of its corporate activities, and to enable the state, through its proper officers, to collect proper filing fees and franchise taxes, and to supervise and control the use and to punish the non-use of the franchise to do." 46 Or as was said in St. Regis Candies, Inc. v. Hovas: 47 "the 'voluntary associates' are required to select and publicly name that part of the field which shall encompass corporate activity. The main purpose here is to protect the 'public', first, against too great a delegation and any usurpation of powand, secondly, by affording the means whereby the right to a claimed power or rightful use of an admitted power may be tested." The Board must call such hearing to consider rate changes at the request of a company writing title insurance, or if the Board thinks that a change in rates may be proper. Any company or other person interested, feeling injured by any action of the Board with regard to rates, shall have the right to file a suit in the District Court of Travis County, within thirty days after the Board has made such order, to review the action, in which suit the Court may enter a judgment correcting the Board's order and fixing such rates as may be proper, or affirming the action of the Board. Sec. 5. Any foreign or domestic corporation issuing any form of policy or underwriting contracts or charging any premium rates to the public on either owners' or mortgagees' certificates or underwriting contracts on Texas properties other than forms and rates prescribed by the Board of Insurance Commissioners, hereunder, shall forfeit its right to do business in Texas; but this shall not be construed as intended to require the charge made by one title insurance company, qualified to do business under this Act and doing a general title insurance business for the public in this State, for reinsuring or underwriting all or any part of the business of another such company, to be the same as the charge to the public. 

Sec. 6. All corporations, domestic and foreign, writing title or mortgagee policies or underwriting contracts must at all times, have and keep on deposit with the State Treasury or such other depository as may be named by such corporation and approved by the Board of Insurance Commissioners, either cash or first mortgage notes or such other securities as are now admissible for investment by life insurance companies under the laws of this State, to an amount equal to one-fourth of the authorized capital of such corporation; provided however that such deposit shall in no event exceed the sum of $100,000.00. 

Sec. 7. The general laws applicable to paying of filing fees and franchise taxes of corporations having a capital stock are hereby made applicable to corporations coming under the provisions of this Act. Domestic corporations operating under this law shall not be required to pay premium taxes. 

Sec. 8. The charter of corporations incorporated hereunder, and the amendments thereto, shall be filed with the Board of Insurance Commissioners, which said Board shall collect from the said companies filing fees and franchise taxes required under the law.

Sec. 9. The Board of Insurance Commissioners after having satisfied itself by such investigation as it may deem proper with reference to the payment of capital stock and the value of the 88

assets offered in payment thereof (the expense of which examination shall be borne by the company), shall issue to such company a certificate of authority to transact the characters of business provided for herein, which said certificate shall expire on the first of June next succeeding. Thereafter on or before the first of June and after the filing of the annual report herein required of each company, the said Board, upon being satisfied that the laws applicable to such companies have been complied with, shall issue a certificate of authority to said company to conduct such business until June 1st of the ensuing year.

No company domestic or foreign shall transact business under this Act unless it shall hold a valid certificate of authority. 

Sec. 10. Every company doing a title insurance business under the provisions of this Act shall set aside annually as a reserve 5% of its gross premiums so collected, before any dividends are paid, the totals of such reserve shall never be required to exceed a total reserve of $100,000.00. Such reserve must be maintained separately and apart from the capital of the company and shall be invested in such securities as are admissible for investment by life insurance companies under the laws of this State. Funds accumulated under this provision shall never be used for the payment of any obligation other than those connected with title insurance, and, in the event of the insolvency of a company, the fund, hereby provided shall be used to protect title insurance policy holders even though there be no accrued title insurance claims and even though there be unpaid obligations of other sorts. 

Sec. 11. No company operating under the provisions of this 

Act shall issue any policy of title insurance involving a contingent liability on said policy of more than fifty per cent of the capital stock and surplus of the company, unless the excess shall be simultaneously reinsured in some other responsible company qualified to do business in Texas. Such company may reinsure any or all of its business provided the reinsuring company shall be qualified to do business in Texas and the reinsuring contract shall be first approved by the said Board. 89

Sec. 12. The capital stock of every company operating under the provisions of this Act must be maintained intact over and above all of its outstanding liabilities, except contingent liabilities on policies of title insurance, and if such company shall permit the impairment of its capital stock, it shall not transact any further business of any sort until such time as it shall have made good its impairment and received permission of the Board of Insurance Commissioners to resume operations. 

If such impairment shall be permitted to remain for a period of time up to six months, said Board of Insurance Commissioners shall immediately require the reinsurance of the outstanding policy or policies of any such concern and a liquidation of its assets and the winding up of its business. 

Sec. 13. If any company operating under the provisions of this law shall engage in the characters of business described in subdivisions (2) and (3) in the first section hereof in such manner as might bring it within the provision of any other regulatory statute now or hereafter to be in force within the State of Texas, all examination and regulation shall be exercised by the Board of Insurance Commissioners rather than any other State agency which may be named in such other laws, so long as such corporation engages in the title guaranty or insurance business.

Sec. 14. Every company, domestic and/or foreign, operating under the provisions of this Act shall, upon or before the first of March each year, file with the Board of Insurance Commissioners a verified statement, in such form as the Board may require, setting forth the statement of the business done by it during the preceding year, and the condition of its affairs as of December 31st preceding. It shall be the duty of the Board of 

Insurance Commissioners, biennially or oftener, if it shall be deemed advisable, in person or through a duly appointed representative, to make a thorough examination of the company's books and affairs and the transactions in which it is engaged at the expense of said company, for which purpose the said Board, or its representative, shall have access to the books and records of the said company and shall have the right to interrogate 90

and require answer under oath from any officer, agent or employee of the said company concerning any matters pertaining to the business thereof.

Sec. 15. Corporations chartered or operating under the provisions of this Act may use in their corporate name the words "Title and Trust Company," but they shall not use the word "Trust" alone, and where the word "Trust" appears, then in letter-heads and literature used by them they shall print the words, "Without Banking Privileges."

Sec. 16. Any foreign corporations desiring to transact the character of business provided for in this Act in this State shall make an application for permit or certificate of authority to the Board of Insurance Commissioners in such form as the Board shall prescribe and shall submit a financial statement showing its condition in such form as the Board shall prescribe. 

Sec. 17. No such foreign corporation shall be permitted to do business in this State unless it shall show from its financial statement, and such other examination as the Board may desire to make, an unimpaired capital of at least One Hundred 

Thousand Dollars. 

Sec. 18. Each such foreign corporation engaged in doing or desiring to do business in this State shall file with the Board of Insurance Commissioners an irrevocable power of attorney, duly executed, constituting and appointing the Life Insurance Commissioner and his successors in office, or any officer or Board which may hereafter be clothed with the powers and duties now devolving upon said Commissioner, its duly authorized agent and attorney in fact for the purpose of accepting service for it or being served with citation in any suit brought against it in any court of this State, by any person, or by or to or for the use of the State of Texas, and consenting that the service of any civil process upon him as its attorney for such purpose in any suit or proceeding shall be taken and held to be valid, waiving all claim and right to object to such service, and such appointment, agency and power of attorney shall, by its terms and recitals, provide that it shall continue and remain in force and effect so long as such company continues to do business in 91

this State or to collect premiums of insurance from citizens of this State, and so long as it shall have outstanding policies in this State, and until all claims of every character held by the citizens of this State, or by the State of Texas, against such company, shall have been settled. Said power of attorney shall be signed by the President or a Vice-President and the Secretary of such company, whose signature shall be attested by the seal of the company; and said officer signing the same acknowledges its execution before an officer authorized by the Laws of this State to take acknowledgments. The said power of attorney shall be embodied in, and approved by, a resolution of the Board of Directors of such company, and a copy of such resolution duly certified to by the proper officer of said company, shall be filed with the said power of attorney in the office of the Commissioner, and shall be recorded by him in a book kept for that purpose, there to remain a permanent record of the said department.

Sec. 19. Whenever the said Commissioner shall accept service or to be served with citation in any suit pending against any title insurance company in this State, he shall immediately enclose the copy of the citation served upon him, or a substantial copy thereof, in a letter properly addressed to the general manager or general agent of the company against whom such service is had, if it shall have a general manager or general agent within this State, and if not, then to the home office of the company, and shall forward the same by registered mail, postage prepaid. No judgment by default shall be taken in any such cause until after the expiration of at least ten days after the general agent or general manager of such company, or the company at its home office as the case may be, shall have received such copy of such citation; and the presumption shall obtain, until rebutted, that such notice was received by such agent or company in due course of mail after being deposited in the mail in Austin.

Sec. 20. If any corporation, domestic or foreign, while holding a certificate of authority to transact business in this State, shall fail or refuse to comply with any of the provisions or re- 92

quirements of this Act, the Board of Insurance Commissioners, upon ascertaining this fact, shall notify such company by actual notice in writing delivered to an executive officer of such company, of his intention to revoke its certificate of authority to transact business in this State at the expiration of thirty days after the mailing of such registered letter, or the date upon which such actual notice is served. If such provisions or requirements are not fully complied with upon the expiration of said thirty days, it shall be the duty of said Board to revoke the certificate of authority of such company. In case of such revocation, such company shall not be entitled to receive another certificate of authority for a period of one year, and until it shall have fully and in good faith complied with all such provisions and requirements of this Act. Any company feeling itself aggrieved by the action of the Board in revoking its certificate of authority to do business in this State may bring suit against it in Travis County to annul and vacate the order revoking such certificate. 

Sec. 21. No commissions, rebates, discounts, or other device shall be paid, allowed or permitted by any company, domestic or foreign, doing the business provided for in this Act, relating to title policies or underwriting contracts; provided this shall not prevent any title company from appointing as its representative in any county any person, firm or corporation owning and operating an abstract plant in such county and making such arrangements for division of premiums as may be ap proved by the Board of Insurance Commissioners. 

Sec. 22. But Article 1304 10 says that the charter must state the "purpose" for which it is to be formed, using the term in the singular, which raises the question as to whether a corporation may be formed for one or for several purposes. The first case to pass upon this question was Ramsey v. Tod,¹¹ where a writ of mandamus to compel the Secretary of State to file a charter was sought by persons attempting to incorporate an organization in whose charter there were two distinct purposes. One was the "purchase and sale of goods, wares, merchandise and agricultural and farm products," and the other was the "accumulation and loan of money in carrying out said purpose.” 

These two purposes were provided for under separate subdivisions in the statute. The Secretary of State refused to file the the subdivision in question being omitted, and no other section being inserted under which the corporation in question could have been legally chartered. If the act of March 27, 1885, was in effect when the charter was granted, there was no authority for its incorporation. The act, however, did not go into effect until 90 days after adjournment, which took place on March 31, 1885. The charter was dated June 27th, the ninetieth day after adjournment. The law did not take effect until after the expiration of 90 days from adjournment, and the 90 days did not expire until the close of the 27th day of June. The charter was therefore properly granted." In this case the court approved the purpose clause of the charter although two distinct purposes were authorized. Under the later Texas cases discussed in this chapter such charter would not be authorized.

The court held that Section 6 of the 1879 Act 12 provided that the "purpose of the business be stated," using the term "purpose" in the singular and that this tends to show that the intention of the Legislature was to allow only one purpose. 

Also the court argues that there is no explanation why the Legislature put all the different purposes into separate subdivisions of the statute, if it did not contemplate authorizing incorporation for only one of them. Further, the court pointed out that some of the subdivisions cover a certain purpose in general, as a class, and in another subdivision will be found a specific case out of this general class, and that this fact also shows that the Legislature contemplated incorporation for only one purpose. 

Therefore, the court held that in view of these facts, the evident intention of the Legislature must have been to authorize the creation of corporations only under one subdivision. 

The court further intimated that if one subdivision names two or more purposes, a corporation may be chartered for all of these purposes. This statement is dictum as the specific holding of the court was that a corporation could be incorporated for only the purposes in one subdivision and not for two purposes set out in different subdivisions. 

From this case, discussed above, it would seem that a corporation can be created for two or more purposes so long as these purposes are authorized under the same subdivision of the statute, but if two purposes are set out in different subdivisions, the two purposes can not be combined in the charter. One court of civil appeals in 1904 followed the dictum of the Ramsey-Tod case 13 and held that all of the purposes set forth in one subdivision of Article 1302, R. S., 1925, even though the subdivision includes two businesses may be included in the charter, but this doctrine was later modified and partially overruled in 1910 by

the Supreme Court of Texas in the case of Johnston v. Townsend 14 which has become the leading case in Texas upon this question and also the settled law. 

In this case a mandamus was sought to compel the Secretary of State to file a charter which set out the purpose of the organization to be, "the transaction of a manufacturing and mining business and the purchase and sale of goods, wares and merchandise used for such business." The Secretary refused to file this charter, contending that the charter included two separate purposes "manufacturing and mining." The corporators contended that the purpose as stated is authorized under Subdivision 14, Art. 642, R. S., 1895, which reads, "Transaction of any manufacturing or mining business," because both are mentioned in one subdivision of the statute. The attorney for the corporation relied on the authority of the Ramsey-Tod case, referred to above. But the court refused to follow the language of Ramsey v. Tod, saying that authorization by the Statutes, is for a business,15 and under Subdivision 14, R. S., 1895,16 a business could be either manufacturing or mining, but not both. The court stated frankly that the above statement in the Ramsey-Tod case was dictum, as the point actually decided in that case was that the purposes of two or more subdivisions can not be combined in the charter. There is no further controversy on that issue in 

Texas today. The Johnson-Townsend case limits the dictum of 

Ramsey v. Tod so that if two businesses are provided for in the same subdivision of the statute, a charter which includes both businesses will not be approved unless the charter shows clearly that one business is strictly ancillary or subsidiary to the principal business specified in the charter. On this question Judge 

Williams said: "It must be remembered, as was pointed out in Ramsey v. 

Tod, that another provision requires that the charter state 'the purpose' of the incorporation. It is also to be noted that that for which an incorporation is authorized by subdivision 14 is 

16. Now Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 

1302, subd. 34. 

14. 124 S.W. 417, 103 Tex. 122. 

15. Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1304, subd. 3. 102

the transaction of 'a business'-not of two or more businesses. 

Either mining or manufacturing may be a business by itself. 

The two may be wholly distinct from and unrelated to each other. A charter authorizing both, without restriction, would contain a statement not of the purpose, but of the purposes, and would empower the corporation to transact, not a business, but businesses. Instances of this are a business of mining for gold and another of manufacturing cottons, of mining for coal and of manufacturing shoes. "Regardless of the use of alternative language in subdivision 14, we think the character of the statutory provisions is such as to exclude the construction that the transaction of two distinct businesses of mining and manufacturing are here provided for. On the other hand, there may be a business consisting of both manufacturing and mining, in which the operations are so related to each other as to constitute an entirety. The products of the mine may be sold in their crude state, or may be manufactured into many different articles and these may be sold or devoted to their various uses. This might justly be treated as the transaction of a manufacturing and mining business and come within the language of the statute. We do not think that the use of the conjunction 'or' was intended to prevent an incorporation for that or any other one business, although it consists partly of mining and partly of manufacturing. "If other subdivisions are examined, it would be found that in some of them the general character of the purpose which may be promoted by a corporation is expressed by words closely related in meaning, but used disjunctively, in order, apparently to describe fully the kind of undertaking meant, rather than to require a critical distinguishing of them in the drawing of charters. In the second subdivision we have authority for incorporating 'any undertaking' which is 'benevolent, charitable, educational or missionary.' Was it meant that there should be a severe discrimination between several kinds of undertakings described by these different words; that the missionary undertaking should not be incorporated if it should be also a benevolent or an educational undertaking, or that the benevolent un- 103

one. dertaking should not include the charitable, or the missionary? 

While we do not intend, by pursuing this line of reasoning at length through the various subdivisions, to decide questions not before us, we think we risk nothing in saying that words indicative of the kind and character of a business meant are sometimes used disjunctively in the statutes to include a business or undertaking which is described or defined by one or all of such words; and that this is true of subdivision 14. To further illustrate from the second subdivision, a missionary undertaking is also a benevolent one and usually, if not always, an educational An educational one need not be either benevolent, charitable, or missionary, but it may possess all those qualities. Evidently an incorporation is allowed by this subdivision for any undertaking that comes within the meaning of all or either of these words. It does not follow that several undertakings which in their natures are separate and distinct may be included as one. So, we think, ‘a business' may properly be incorporated as a manufacturing and mining business, but two businesses, one of manufacturing and the other of mining, cannot be made one, because the statute does not so provide. The legislative intention that the business should be a unit is further shown by the fact that in subdivision 14 there is no general authority for the purchase and sale of goods, but only an authority for the purchase and sale of those 'used for such business.'"

It is evident from these quotations from the Johnson-Townsend case that under subdivision 14 (now 66) a corporation for the purpose of "mining and manufacturing" is not authorized by the statute as two separate businesses could be conducted under such a charter; that when the purposes are stated in such broad terms their meaning is too indefinite, as it might be construed as authorizing two distinct businesses. Therefore, the court held that the Secretary of State had the right to refuse to file this charter until the doubt is removed by specifying in the charter that one business is ancillary to the other. 

It is therefore evident that the purposes for which a corporation may be created were considerably restricted by the Johnson v. Townsend case; and now a corporation, as concisely stated 104

by a later court,17 is "limited to one business, which could consist of one or more of the purposes specified in any one subdivision of the statute, but not for two or more purposes designated in two or more subdivisions, unless expressly authorized by statute." A corporation cannot be chartered for a purpose not authorized by the statutes, yet in the preparation of the charter of a corporation it is not necessary to incorporate for all of the purposes set out in one subdivision of the statute, as the charter may specify as the objects of the incorporation more limited purposes than those set out in the statute."  § 27. Fees 

The fee for filing charters for corporations for profit organized under the Texas general incorporation statute is fifty dollars, with ten dollars additional for each ten thousand dollars of capital stock in excess of ten thousand dollars. The maximum fee chargeable is two thousand five hundred dollars.46 

Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 3914 as amended in 1931 provides: "Upon filing each charter, amendment or supplement thereto, of a private corporation created for any other purpose intended for mutual profit or benefit, a filing fee of Fifty ($50.00) Dollars, provided that if the authorized capital stock of said corporation shall exceed Ten Thousand ($10,000.00) Dollars it shall be required to pay an additional fee of Ten ($10.00) Dollars for each additional Ten Thousand ($10,000.00) Dollars of its authorized capital stock or fractional part thereof after the first.” 

For religious and educational corporations a filing fee of ten dollars only is charged. Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 3914, as amended in 1931 provides: "Upon filing each charter, amend ment or supplement thereto of a corporation for the support of public worship, any benevolent, charitable, educational, missionary, literary or scientific undertaking, the maintenance of a library, the promotion of a public cemetery not for profit and the encouragement of agriculture and horticulture, to aid its members in producing and marketing agricultural products, or for acquiring, raising, breeding, fattening or marketing live stock, a filing fee of Ten ($10.00) Dollars, and for filing the semiannual financial statement of such agricultural products or live stock corporation, Ten ($10.00) Dollars, which shall include the annual license fee."

The following corporations are charged a filing fee of two hundred dollars provided their authorized capital stock does not exceed one hundred thousand dollars. But if the capital stock exceeds that amount an additional fee of fifty cents for each $1,- 000.00 in excess of the above amount is charged. Vernon's Ann.

§ 28. When Corporate Existence Begins 

A corporation comes into existence as such as soon as the charter is "filed in the office of the Secretary of State," and not before such acceptance.49 In National Bank of Jefferson v. 

Texas Investment Company 50 it was said: "It follows, we think, that when the company filed its articles of incorporation with the Secretary of State, it became a corporation in law, and that
