For this purpose, all mandatory conditions precedent prescribed by the Statutes must be substantially complied with before a de jure corporation is formed.51

No one can be forced to become a stockholder in a private corporation without his consent.52 The essentials of a de jure corporation are (1) a valid law under which the company may be incorporated, (2) a substantial compliance with all mandatory conditions precedent to the birth of the corporation. Therefore, in Texas when all conditions precedent to the filing of a charter in the office of the Secretary of State have been substantially performed and the charter is so filed, a de jure corporation is organized provided there is a law under which the state has authorized the formation of the corporation. It is, therefore, evident that before a de jure corporation is organized a charter must be prepared in accordance with the Texas statute.53 If the charter, although prepared in due form, is never submitted to the Secretary of State for his approval neither a de facto nor a de jure corporation is organized.54 Those things that the statutes specify must be performed after the birth of the corporation are conditions subsequent. Failure to perform these conditions subsequent cannot be taken advantage of collaterally by persons dealing with the corporation or those who have claims against the company. Failure to perform conditions subsequent can be urged successfully by no one collateral-

Those conditions that must be performed before the birth of the corporation are conditions precedent. For instance, Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1308, provides that before the charter can be filed by the Secretary of State the full amount of its authorized capital stock must be subscribed and 50% thereof paid. As this fact must be shown before the corporation becomes a reality, it is clearly a condition precedent, which must be substantially complied with before the associates can claim to be a corporation.55 On the other hand, Vernon's Ann.Civ.

St. art. 1339 provides that the stockholders have two years after the date of the filing of the charter to pay the balance of their unpaid subscriptions to the original capital stock of the company. As this may be done after the company comes into existence it is evidently a condition subsequent.56 

Under the provision of all general incorporation statutes the courts have held that some of the provisions are mandatory and others merely directory. As we have seen above, before a de jure corporation can be formed all mandatory conditions precedent of the statute must be substantially complied with. Very often it is difficult to determine whether the provision of the statute is mandatory or merely directory. According to the test usually applied by the courts the provision is mandatory if it affects the interests of the public who may have dealings with the company. On the other hand, if it affects the rights of the stockholders only, it is directory merely.57 The Texas courts have not decided in many cases what sections of our general incorporation statutes are mandatory and what parts are merely directory. However, it is self-evident that the public has an interest in knowing the name of the corporation, the

amount of its capital stock, the name of its directors and their addresses for the first year and all other facts that must appear in the charter of a Texas corporation by the statute under which it is chartered. For this reason, if any of the above provisions of our statute are not complied with substantially, the company is not a de jure corporation.

If the provision of the incorporation statute is directory, and not mandatory, failure to comply with it does not affect the legal status of the corporation. If all other conditions precedent of the incorporation statute have been substantially complied with the corporation is de jure. In the case of Butler Paper 

Co. v. Cleveland 58 the statute of Illinois provided that notice of the meeting of the subscribers to elect directors shall be given "by depositing in the post-office, properly addressed to each subscriber, at least ten days before the time fixed, (for the meeting) a written or printed notice, stating the object, time and place of such meeting." The subscribers held a meeting without the written notice being given. The suit was by a creditor under an Illinois statute, which made the directors and agents of a corporation which was not de jure, liable for the debts of the pretended corporation. The court held that the directors were not liable under the statute since the statute was directory merely as it affected the subscribers as to the internal organization of the company and not the public. The consequences of the failure to comply with directory provisions are stated as follows: "The statute prescribes a certain course to be pursued in organizing a corporation in this State. It does not necessarily follow, however, that any departure from that course will prevent a corporation from becoming one de jure. Whether or not such departure will have that effect depends upon the nature of the provision which is violated. If it is a mandatory provision, a failure to substantially comply with its terms will prevent the corporation from becoming one de jure; but if the provision is merely directory, then a departure therefrom will not have that consequence." 

58. 77 N.E. 99, 220 Ill. 128, 110 Am.

The court in the above opinion states the test for determining whether the provision of the statute is mandatory or direc tory as follows: "This case is distinguishable from Loverin v. 

McLaughlin, 44 N.E. 99, 161 Ill. 417, which is relied upon by appellant, in that notice of the first meeting of subscribers is not intended for the benefit of the public, as no publicity of such meeting is required, but is merely for the benefit of the subscribers, while in the Loverin case the provision which was not complied with was that requiring the certificate of complete organization issued by the Secretary of State to be filed and recorded in the office of the recorder of deeds of the county in which the principal office of the corporation is located, and a compliance with the statute in that regard was essential because the provision was one for the benefit of the public, and could not be waived." 59 Applying the above test to conditions precedent to the existence of Texas corporations under Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. arts. 1302 to 1314, it seems evident that all of the provisions of the Texas statute are mandatory rather than directory, since the public is interested in knowing the name of the corporation, its purpose, the amount of its capital stock, that two of the incorporators are citizens of Texas, etc.⁰ By Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1304 subd. 5 it is provided that the charter must set forth, "The number of directors, and the names and residences of those who are the appointees for the first year."

In the opinion the court said: "Whether the record of the original might have accomplished the same purposes of publicity as would such verified copy is a question upon which opinions may differ. * If two opinions may be held as to the superior advantage of one method over another, the question was one for the resolution of the Legislature, and not by the courts." This seems too strict a construction of the statute. Surely the statute was substantially complied with. Those articles of the Texas statutes which provide that certain things must be done after the charter is approved by the Secretary of State are conditions subsequent to the existence of the corporation and failure to satisfy these provisions cannot be urged in a collateral suit or controversy, but only by the state in a direct action to forfeit the charter of the corporation.84 

One of the most pronounced of these conditions is found in Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1338, which provides that the balance of the capital stock must be paid in within two years after the approval of the charter by the Secretary of State. and

Under the California statute, filing the charter in the county where the corporation transacts its principal business is a condition subsequent and not precedent to the birth of the corporation. Therefore, failure to comply with this condition may be urged as grounds for forfeiting the charter by the state in a direct suit for that purpose but not by other parties in a collateral proceeding.85 But under the early general incorporation act of California of 1850, it was provided that the charter must be filed "in the office of the clerk of the county in which the business of the company shall be carried on, and a duplicate thereof in the office of the Secretary of State * when the certificate shall be filed as aforesaid," the persons executing the same shall be a body politic. Under this statute the courts of California held that as the birth of the company dated from the filing of the charter in the county where the company did business, the filing of a “duplicate thereof" with the Secretary of State was a condition subsequent. The court, therefore, held that failure to file the duplicate in the office of the Secretary of State could be urged only by the state in a direct proceeding to forfeit the charter of the corporation, and that no collateral attack upon the legal existence of the corporation would be permitted.86 In the opinion the court said: "The existence

But there is a broad and obvious distinction between such acts as are declared to be necessary steps in the process of incorporation, and such as are required of the individuals seeking to become incorporated, but which are not made prerequisites to the assumption of corporate powers. In respect to the former, any material omission will be fatal to the existence of the corporation, and may be taken advantage of, collaterally, in any form in which the fact of incorporation can properly be called in question. In respect to the latter, the corporation is responsible only to the government, and in a direct proceeding to forfeit its charter. The right of the plaintiff to be considered a corporation, and to exercise corporate powers, depends upon the fact of the performance of the particular acts named in the statute as essential to its corporate existence. 

If the duplicate has not been filed, the assumption of corporate powers amounts simply to a usurpation of the sovereign rights of the State, the remedy for which rests with the State alone."

§ 29. Corporate Name 

A name of some kind is essential to the existence of a corporation, but insofar as there are no restrictions in the charter, the corporation may adopt any name that it sees fit, provided the name selected is not the same as or so similar to that of another business conducted in the same field of operation that the public may be deceived or the original user may be deprived of the good will of his business.98 A corporation may have several names for different purposes. Its name cannot be legally changed without amending its charter. In Robinson v. First National Bank 99 there was some testimony that the stockholders of the Saxon Mercantile Company, a Texas corporation, took the goods of the company to Oklahoma and carried on the business as a partnership under the name of Saxon, Pierce & Co. The bank contended that it could recover against the former stockholders as partners under the new name. On this issue the Supreme Court said: "If, as there was testimony to show, the name of Saxon, Pierce & Co. was adopted as a new name for the corporation in the name of the Saxon Mercantile Company, and if the understanding between the parties 98. The policy of the Secretary of State has been that, if there has existed a delinquency in the payment of the franchise tax for a period of six months or longer, and the corporation has had notice that its tax is delinquent, and if the promoters of the corporation that is being organized desire to use this name, it will be given to them. In view of the holding of the Supreme 

Court in Federal Crude Oil Company v. Yount-Lee Oil Com pany this practice should be discontinued, otherwise two corporations may be doing business under the same name. In that case the Supreme Court of Texas held that the corporation could pay the back franchise taxes and penalties and be reinstated any time before the Attorney General brought suit to forfeit the charter of the company. The name of the corporation does not have to be very similar for a court of equity to enjoin the use of the name. For example, in Hughes et al. v. Howe Grain &

Mercantile Company,10 under the peculiar facts in that case the court granted relief. The Howe Grain & Mercantile Company was generally known as the Howe Grain Company, the name adopted by the corporate defendant. The defendant, Hughes, had been the manager of the Howe Grain & Mercantile Company for a period of about twenty years, and he was generally known "as the corporation". Some of the business was done in his name, and the mail of the two corporations was continually getting mixed.

In Brooks v. Heartfield," the defendant was enjoined from the use of the name "Brooks Supply Co." where the plaintiff used the name "Brooks Supply". In many states statutes have been enacted by which a corporation is prohibited from the selection of a name similar to that of an existing corporation. In a recent case the plaintiff was incorporated in 1896 under the name "Lawyer's Title Insurance Company." In 1925 the defendant was incorporated under the name "Lawyer's Title Insurance Corporation." In 1922 the plaintiff made a "working agreement" with two other companies and thereafter the public usually referred to the associated companies as "the District Title Company" and the plaintiff never acquired a reputation under its corporate name. The court held that the plaintiff lost its right to the exclusive use of its corporate name by associating with the other two corporations and conducting its business under a conglomerate name. For that reason the injunction was denied.15 Where the use of the plaintiff's name amounts to unfair competition, all courts will restrain the imitation of the plaintiff's corporate name by the defendant.16

As we have seen from the previous discussion in this section, the courts base the right of the plaintiff to enjoin the use of its name by a competitor in business more on their right and duty to prevent the deception of the public in the sale of its goods or securities than on the mere similarity of the names of the competitors. However, in a fairly recent case the Supreme Court of 

Michigan held that a corporation that had virtually ceased to do business and was in the process of dissolution could not prevent a newly formed corporation from the use of its name. The decision was based partly on a statute which prohibited the use of to be the name of the corporation, we see no reason why the law should not protect the corporation in the use of that name, upon the same principles, and to the same extent that individuals are protected in the use of trade-marks." Whatever may have been the ancient rule, it is now clearly established that the two products need not be competitive. 'It was at first a debatable point whether a merchant's good will, indicated by his mark, could extend beyond such goods as he sold. How could he lose bargains which he had no means to fill? What harm did it do a chewing gum maker to have an ironmonger use his trade-mark?' 'However,' said Learned Hand, J., in expressing the modern attitude, 'it has of recent years been recognized that a merchant may have a sufficient economic interest in the use of his mark outside the field of his own exploitation to justify interposition by a court. His mark is his authentic seal; by it he vouches for the goods which bear it; it carries his name for good or ill. If another uses it, he borrows the owner's reputation, whose quality no longer lies within his own control. This is an injury, even though the borrower does not tarnish it, or divert any sales by its use; for a reputation, like a face, is the symbol of its possessor and creator, and another can use it only as a mask. And so it has come to be recognized that, unless the borrower's use is so foreign to the owner's as to insure against any identification of the two, it is unlawful.' Yale

§ 30. May One Person-Even a Corporation-Subscribe Initially for All of the Stock of a Corporation Organized under the General Incorporation Statutes of Texas? 

Early in August, 1940, the Secretary of the State of Texas addressed to the Attorney General of the State the following inquiry: 

"Article 1305 [Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1305] provides that 

Texas charters must be subscribed by three or more persons, two of whom must be citizens of this State, but we are unable to find where there is any Statute requiring three stockholders of a corporation when the charter is granted. A charter has been presented to this office in which an out of state resident owns all of the capital stock but two Texas citizens subscribed to the charter as incorporators and acknowledged their signatures before a notary. "This department would respectfully request an opinion as to whether the Texas Statutes and the decisions of the courts require that at the time of incorporation at least two Texas citizens must own some portion of the capital stock." 

In response to that inquiry the Attorney General, on August 

16, 1940, transmitted to the Secretary of State an opinion, the pertinent part of which follows: 

"Art. 1305, [Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1305] provides in effect that an application for a charter must be signed or subscribed to by three or more persons, two of whom must be citizens of this State; however, the statute does not specify that 

33. Vernon's Ann.Pen.Code art. 1069 provides: "The preceding article shall in no way apply to any corporation duly organized under the laws of this State or to any corporation organized under the laws of any other 

State and lawfully doing business in this State." This applies to Vernon's 

Ann.Pen.Code arts. 1067 and 1068. 

Vernon's Ann. Civ.St. art. 5927 pro vides: "The three preceding articles 

(Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. arts. 5924, 5925, 5926) shall not apply to any domestic or foreign corporation lawfully doing business in this State." 140

each signer must own or have subscribed for any number of shares of stock. Construing the above mentioned statutes together, we are of the opinion that said statutes do not require that at least two Texas citizens who are required to acknowledge and subscribe to charter as provided by Art. 1305, must own any portion of the capital stock of said corporation. Therefore, your question is respectfully answered in the negative."

Thus the Secretary of State is advised to approve a charter, applied for under the general incorporation statute of Texas, when "an out of state resident subscribes for all of the capital stock" of the company and the two Texas citizens who sign the charter do not subscribe for any of the company's stock. Acting on this advice, on October 9, 1940, the Secretary of State approved and filed a charter for a Texas corporation signed by two citizens of Texas and one citizen of California, none of whom subscribed for one dollar of the stock of the company. The capital stock of the company was ten thousand dollars, and in the words of the affidavit attached to the charter "the full amount of the authorized capital stock of said corporation has been subscribed by the American Box Corporation organized and existing under the law of the State of Delaware, having its principal office at 904 Market Street, Wilmington, Delaware.' 

The Attorney General's opinion cites only two authorities in support of this position. A passage from the first edition of 

Fletcher's Cyclopedia on Corporations 34 is quoted, the pertinent part of which follows: "In some states, the general laws authorizing the formation of corporations expressly provide that the corporators shall be subscribers for a certain number of shares of stock in the corporation, but unless it is expressly so required by the statute, the incorporators need not be subscribers for stock in the proposed corporation.' 

The question propounded to the Attorney General was not only whether the incorporators need be subscribers of stock, but the important inquiry was whether a charter should be ap-

The Supreme Court of Texas may possibly hold that the three incorporators who sign the charter need not subscribe for stock so long as at least three persons subscribe for all of the authorized stock of the company. However, that is not very probable. That question is discussed in a subsequent part of this article. Furthermore, the passage quoted from the first edition of Fletcher has been revised in the permanent edition so that the principle is now stated that, “It is not essential to a corporation that the incorporators be financially interested therein, except under statutes so requiring expressly or by implication." It is thus recognized that a statute may "by implication" require that some of those who apply for the charter must subscribe for part or, as in Texas at the present time, all of the stock of the new corporation.

In American Ball Bearing Co. v. 

Adams, D.C.Ohio, 222 F. 967, the company was organized under the Ohio statute which provided that, "Any number of persons, not less than five, desiring to become incorporated, shall subscribe and acknowledge articles of incorporation." This and other provisions of the Ohio statute show that in that state the corporation was not completely organized when the articles of incorporation were filed. Three corporations, the American Ball Bearing Company, the Peerless Motor Car Company, and the Packard Motor Car Company, de cided to form a corporation under the Ohio law. They induced five of their attorneys to subscribe for one share each of the stock of the Kardo Company, and one of these attorneys subscribed for 995 shares as trustee for the American Ball Bearing Company. The federal district court held that the Ohio statute "contemplates that the action prescribed shall be taken by five natural persons having an actual and real interest, at least to the extent of one share of the capital stock, in the assets and in the welfare of the corporation, and it would be a reproach upon the law for the courts to put their stamp of approval upon so palpable an evasion of the law of Ohio as this record discloses." The Circuit Court of Appeals reversed the decision of the district court for the reason that, "There is no requirement in the law * that the incorporators of an

Ohio corporation must have any financial interest or benefit of any kind in the incorporation sought. In some jurisdictions, incorporators are directly held to be mere instruments 144

as to how many persons, under the applicable statute, must subscribe for the stock of the proposed corporation. of the law for purposes of preliminary organization." This case shows clearly that the Circuit Court was of the opinion that under the plain terms of the Ohio statute "the incorporators" had authority to form a "preliminary organization" merely and that such organization was authorized to sell stock and completely organize the company after the required amount of stock had been sold. It does not decide that the required amount of stock may be taken by a single stockholder. It follows the other cases discussed in the preceding part of this note, decided in jurisdictions where the statute does not provide how much stock must be subscribed before the charter is filed with the designated officer. Other cases that throw some light on the question under consideration will be discussed briefly.

In Aspen Water & Light Co. v. 

City of Aspen, 37 P. 728, 5 Colo.App. 

12, the court held that the Aspen 

Water & Light Company could not recover for breach of an alleged contract it made with the City of Aspen to install a water and light plant since the promoters of the purported corporation merely prepared and filed the charter of the company with the proper officer but did not sell or issue any of the stock of the company. 

The court said that the company came into existence when its charter was filed with authority to complete its organization, but since that was never done it was not competent to contract. "In some states the general incorporation act provides that upon the filing of the certificate the persons who sign it, and their successors, shall become a body corporate, and be invested with certain powers. But even in a case like that the authorities hold that it only thereby becomes a quasi corporation, invested possibly with certain powers for certain limited purposes. In reality it becomes a corporation only in name. It is universally agreed that a corporation cannot exist without stockholders or members." This case shows that in Colorado the statute created a corporation with limited capacity when the charter was filed but until its stock is sold to bona fide shareholders it had no other contractual capacity. Nothing was 145 In the syllabus of that case it is said: "No company exists within the meaning of the statute, until the requisite stock has been subscribed and paid in, and the directors chosen."

In Sterne v. Fletcher American

The Wisconsin statute provided that before the required amount of stock was subscribed the corporation was prohibited from "the transaction of business with any others than its members."

As the statute did not provide that some or all of the stock must be subscribed before the charter is filed the court held that "When the certificate specified is issued, the corporation would seem to be perfected, and possess all the powers of a corporation. There seems to be no provisions in the statutes of this state requiring any part of the capital stock to be paid in or subscribed as a condition precedent upon which the corporation is authorized to transact business. most of the states their incorporation acts provide for the subscription and payment of a certain proportion of the capital stock as a condition to the right of the corporation to transact business. When such is the case, incorporators who proceed to incur debts in the name of the corporation before such funds are provided, have been held liable for such debts." It is evident from this statement in the new edition that the quotation from Fletcher's recent text that the term "incorporators" in the old edition was intended to mean "subscribers to the stock of the company." It is clear from the revised text that Mr. Fletcher was of the opinion that a statute providing that three or more persons may associate themselves together to form a corporation is not complied with unless at least that number of persons, "inceptively or in operation" subscribe for some of the stock of the corporation. The fact is that when text writers and judges use the term "incorporators" they usually mean "subscribers" to the stock of the corporation. For instance, Professor Stevens in his recent text on Corporations says: "General corporation laws usually require a certain minimum number of incorporators. In the great majority of American jurisdictions, these general acts offer incorporation to three or more persons." 43 Later, when referring to the holding of the

House of Lords in the celebrated case of Salomon v. Salomon & 

Co.,44 the same author states: "It was said that, since the statute permitted a member to hold a single share, it really sanctioned a scheme by which all the shares, except those necessary to qualify the incorporators, are owned by a single individual. 

Furthermore, there is no requirement in the statutes that the number of shareholders shall never be less than the minimum number of persons required for incorporation." 

These quotations show clearly that Professor Stevens concluded from the authorities that when the statute provides that, "Private corporations may be created by the voluntary association of three or more persons" 45 the number of "incorporators" specified in the statute must subscribe for some stock in the company.

The best discussion of this question is found in Machen's text on the Modern Law of Corporations.46 His views are more pronounced and definite than those of Professor Stevens. He shows that if one person should undertake to incorporate by signing 43.

He assumes that where the statute provides that the charter must be "signed by three or more persons" those who sign must subscribe at least one share of stock. In Section 1084 of his text he says: "But suppose one incorporator associates with himself a number of 'dummies' or persons having a merely nominal interest in the company, sufficient to make up the minimum required by the act. 

For example, suppose the capital of the projected corporation is to be divided into a thousand shares, and suppose one man subscribes the incorporation paper for nine hundred and ninety-four shares, while six of his clerks or servants subscribe for one share each. Is the company validly incorporated under a statute requiring the incorporation paper to be signed by seven individuals." He then shows that even though the required number of persons sign the charter, and all of them subscribe for one share each except the one who is mainly interested in the financial success of the company who subscribes for most of the stock, there is a square conflict in the authorities as to the due incorporation of such a company. That conflict is discussed in succeeding paragraphs. Mr. Machen quotes from the opinion of Lord Halsbury in the Salomon case 47 to show that the House of Lords would not have upheld the incorporation of the company involved in that case if all of the seven parties who signed the charter had not each subscribed for some of the stock of the proposed corporation.48

Every corporation lawyer knows that many schemes for the "evasion" of the statutes requiring three or more persons to subscribe initially for some of the stock of the company have been devised, and that our courts have too often upheld these pretenses at compliance with the statutes. A consideration of some of them is worthwhile. 

The leading case on this question is Salomon v. Salomon & 

Co.,50 involving a corporation organized in 1892 under the English Companies Act of 1862. Aron Salomon, while solvent, organized the company and had 20,001 shares out of a total of 20,007 shares issued to himself in return for his mercantile business, which he transferred to the corporation. His wife and five children each subscribed for one share. The Companies 

Act provided that "any seven or more persons, associated for a lawful purpose may form a company

No subscriber shall take less than one share." The trial judge (Vaughan Williams) was forced to admit that the statute was technically complied with, but he determined that, as the facts showed such a glaring attempt to evade the real purpose of the statute in attempting to form a "one-man corporation," the company was Salomon's agent and decreed that the company was entitled to be indemnified by Salomon. Upon appeal the Court of Appeals held that the corporation was Salomon's trustee "a trustee improperly brought into existence by him to enable him to do what the statute prohibits," and that under the English law the cestui que trust must indemnify the trustee.51 When the case finally reached the House of Lords it was decided that the English Companies Act was strictly complied with, and therefore, Salomon was not liable for the debts of the company.

American courts have declined to acquiesce. In Dixie Coal Mining & Manufacturing Co. v. Williams 54 one Ross organized a mining company. He subscribed for all the stock except that "enough other persons were put down" for sufficient shares to comply formally with the Alabama statute, but such other persons did not "actually pay anything into the corporation." The plaintiff sued the corporation and Ross for damages caused by the death of her husband, alleged to have been suffered in the course of employment by the two defendants. In holding Ross liable, the court said: "Our judgment is that the court correctly found that the Dixie Company Corporation was a mere simulacrum, formed in the image of a corporation, the only possible effect of which, whatever the purpose, was to mislead persons dealing with it away from any idea that the personal responsibility of appellant (Ross) was involved. 

The court will not permit a person, acting under the guise of a corporation formed for that purpose, to evade his individual responsibility." Other courts in America have taken the same view.55 In all these cases the stockholders were personally liable, although in most of them there had been a formal compliance with the incorporating statutes.

 § 31. The Texas Law 

The first valid general incorporation statute was passed by the 

Fourteenth Legislature of Texas on the 23rd of April, 1874.57

Section 4 provided that, "Private corporations may be created by the voluntary association of three or more persons, for the purpose and in the manner mentioned in the following sections of this article." 58 Section 10 of the original act provided that, "The existence of the corporation shall date from the filing of the charter in the office of the Secretary of State." Section 14 provided that, "Whenever the full amount of the capital stock of a corporation having a capital stock shall not have been already subscribed in good faith, the directors or trustees named in the charter * may within three months after the filing of the charter, cause books to be opened for receiving subscriptions to the capital stock of the corporation which books may be kept open till the whole amount of capital stock is subscribed." The act did not provide that a certain amount of the stock must be subscribed before the charter is approved by the Secretary of State. The reason for the omission of that provision in the original general act was that up to that time charters were granted by special act of the legislatures, and those acts in most instances provided that certain persons are hereby created a corporation and that the persons

named in the act are authorized to "open books for subscriptions to the capital stock of the company." 59

Usually the special act fixed the amount of the capital stock, and the persons put in command of the corporation were given a specified time in which to sell the stock of the company. At the time of the adoption of the act in 1874 only a few of the states had enacted general incorporation acts and in most instances such acts did not require that any part of the stock be subscribed before the charter is approved by the proper officer. 

Hence, under the original Texas Act, the three persons who signed the charter and subsequently opened books for subscriptions were "associated" together in the formation of the corporation if they subscribed for some of the stock after the books were opened for that purpose. As the statute provided that "the existence of the corporation dated from the filing of the charter in the office of the Secretary of State," the birth of the company was complete when the charter was filed in that office, and failure to subscribe for stock after the books were opened would be the breach of a condition subsequent and only the state could complain of that irregularity. That exact question did not arise in the courts of Texas under the original wording of the statute. 

There is a dictum by the Supreme Court of Texas in a case that has been cited very often to the effect that under the original statute there is "no provision in the law making the existence of the corporation dependent upon the subscription to its stock or the payment therefor. On the contrary, it is expressly provided that the existence of the corporation shall date from

the filing of the charter in the office of the Secretary of State." 60 

No other conclusion could have been reached by the court since the statute specifically provided that the corporation's birth should date from the filing of the charter by the proper officer, and the statute did not provide that some of the stock must be subscribed before the charter is filed. The National Bank-Texas 

Investment case may be cited for the rule that, until that statute was amended, subscriptions to the stock of a proposed corporation were not necessary to corporate existence and were not required before the approval of a charter. That question evidently is foreign to the inquiry as to whether under the present Texas statute one person can subscribe for all of the stock of the company before its charter is filed. 

In the National Bank-Texas Investment case the bank sued the Texas Investment Company on a $10,000 note originally executed by the corporation to certain payees for the price of cattle purchased by the company. The payees for a valuable consideration indorsed the note to the plaintiff bank. As the assets of the defendant corporation were not sufficient to pay all of its debts, the bank made the stockholders of the corporation parties to the suit and contended that they were liable as partners for the debts of the Texas Investment Company since it was alleged that the stock of the company had never been subscribed. 

The plaintiff also alleged that if it were mistaken in its contention that the Texas Investment Company was a partnership, the stockholders of the corporation were individually liable for the damages that the bank sustained in giving credit to the corporation for the reason that the stockholders defrauded the bank by representing that the capital stock of the company was $100,- 

000 and that it was fully paid.

On this issue the court said: "If the capital stock of the corporation was not paid, and if the directors held out to the world that it was operating upon a full paid capital stock of $100,- 000.00, and if plaintiff relied upon such representation when it 

60. National Bank v. Texas Invest ment Co., 12 S.W. 101, 74 Tex. 421. 158

purchased the note of the corporation, then it may be that the directors rendered themselves liable to respond in damages for any loss that was thereby occasioned. But if so, they were liable in action of deceit sounding purely in damages-that is to say, not in an action for breach of a contract, but in an action for fraudulent representations by which the plaintiff was induced to make the contract. This was a distinct cause of action. 

* * In so far as recovery was sought for the alleged fraud of the directors of the old corporation in representing that its capital had been previously paid, we think that the petition was subject to exception for multifariousness." 61 

On another issue the court said: "It may be doubted whether the plaintiff is in a position to question the existence of the corporation if in fact it did not legally exist. Its allegations show that, in discounting the note sued on, it relied upon the representation that it was a corporation with a paid up capital of $100,000.00."

In view of these two statements of the court it is evident that the court did not consider it necessary to cite and discuss all of the relevant provisions of the original statute and determine whether the "three voluntary associates" under the old statute before its change in 1907 must subscribe for some of the stock of the company before the charter was approved or after the books were opened for subscriptions within three months after the birth of the corporation. In 1874 the general incorporation statutes were patterned after the special incorporation acts of the different states and these latter acts almost universally created the corporation and empowered the directors subsequently to sell the authorized stock of the company. In view of this fact, and especially since practically every case in the Anglo-American jurisdictions involved merely the construction of a special act, no author should say that the incorporators of a company

The Texas statute, as it exists today, is a piecemeal job consisting of the original act and several amendments approved since its passage in 1874. For this reason a modern general incorporation statute should be passed in Texas patterned after those that have been adopted in recent years in a dozen or more of the American states. But it should be abundantly clear that the Texas statute in its present form contemplates group action as the only permissible activity of a corporation. Professor Fuller has written in a recent article: "One accustomed to accept language at its face value would be at a loss to find authority for the creation or existence of such a corporation (one-man corporation) in enabling legislation. With rare exception the one-man corporation has not been expressly authorized under the general incorporation statutes, and if the language of the statutes is to be given its fair import, none would seem even to be contemplated.62 

An examination of the Texas incorporation statute reveals all the internal evidences mentioned by Professor Fuller, that group activity was contemplated, with only a single possible exception. 

Directors of Texas corporations are not, except in a few instances, required to be shareholders. The other features mentioned by Professor Fuller are present.

The statute was amended in 1897 and 1901 so as to require the promoters "to subscribe at least fifty per cent and pay in at least ten per cent of its authorized capital" before the Secretary of State was compelled to file the charter.63

A correct definition of the noun “association” or the infinitive "to associate," should reveal the exact meaning of the above article. Many words have different meanings under varying circumstances; to determine the meaning of the term "to associate," its setting must be ascertained. If for instance the question before the court is to determine with whom A "associates" socially, an investigation that reveals the persons with whom A usually commingles in a social way would answer the question. 

Again, if the question is to determine whether A had two other "associates" when he organized a religious corporation possibly the statute was complied with if the facts show that A, B and C prepared the charter in accordance with the Texas law, designated themselves as directors of the company and then took an active part in the religious affairs of the corporation even though A, B and C did not contribute one dollar to the support of the church. Under the Texas statute religious corporations may be incorporated "without capital stock." But what is the meaning of three associates in the above statute when they organize a "private corporation for profit"? Are three persons "associates" where only one is financially interested in the success of the corporation and the other two sign the charter and affidavit as a mere formality, do not jeopardize one dollar of their private fortunes in the enterprise, are never elected directors of the company and have nothing to do with the conduct of the business owned by the corporation? Fortunately we are not left to conjecture or surmise as to the meaning of the above statute. No Texas court has yet been asked to define its meaning. The reason for this dearth of authority in Texas is that until the above charter was presented to the Secretary of State for his approval every lawyer in Texas, and practically every lawyer where Anglo-American law prevails, understood that each one of the three "voluntary associates" must subscribe for some of the stock of the corporation.

However, the courts of last resort of two states of the American union have determined the meaning of statutes almost identical with Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1303.

The capital stock of the company was twenty thousand dollars and in the charter it was stated that, "the places of business were Nashua in New Hampshire, and East Brookfield in Massachusetts." Un- der this state of things, the defendant bought goods of the plaintiffs for his own sole benefit, adopting the name of the apparent 165

corporation, which had no real existence, and which represented nobody but himself." 

In Louisville Banking Co. v. Eisenman 69 the company was regularly organized under the Kentucky statute which provided: "Any number of persons may associate themselves together and become incorporated for the transaction of any lawful business." 

The plaintiff sought to hold the defendant liable for the debts of the company for the reason that he purchased all the stock of the corporation. In defining the meaning of the word "associate" the court said: "It is, we think, manifest the Legislature never intended to permit one person to conduct his ordinary business in the name of a corporation, so as to exempt him from personal liability, or his property not embraced by or used in his corporate business from the payment of a debt for no other reason than its being a debt of the corporation. The purpose of the statute was to enable two or more persons possessed of capital or skill to associate themselves in business, and to limit their liability as against the improvident acts of each other, or the act of the corporation, in the event of pecuniary loss in the legitimate and proper conduct of its business. It invites the investment of the capital stock of one to be placed in the same business with the skill of another, or a combination of capital that encourages trade, the burden of which mere individual enterprise would be unwilling to assume, and it could not have been the legislative intent that any one man could form a corporation of which he is the creature and sole stockholder, so as to limit his liability for debts contracted, and from which he has derived the benefit, to the extent only of what he might designate his corporate estate. 

There is no such being in this State as a sole corporation, and certainly none such allowed to be created by the statute. There is a difference between the attempt to create one person a corporation under this statute, and the purchase, in good faith, of all the stock after the corporation had been created. The meaning of the term "associate" as defined in the above opinions seems conclusive. No doubt these opinions will be followed in Texas. In the chapter on Stockholder's meeting it is shown that one shareholder cannot hold a meeting of the stockholders. In the case of St. Regis Candies, Inc. v. Ho- 

71 the court held that the directors for the first year must be elected by the "voluntary associates" who organize the company. In that case the court said: "The 'voluntary associates' in the beginning must select those officers (directors named in Art. 1304 [Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1304])-the manner of their selection being in no wise regulated in the statute." Did the legislature intend to authorize the formation of a corporation by a person who could never hold a stockholders' meeting until he sold some of his stock? Is it reasonable to assume that the legislators would enact a statute which authorized two promoters, who signed the charter as a formality and who understood that the owner of the stock would never permit them to serve as directors, agent or officers of the company, to vote for the election of the first board of directors, but not for subsequent directors, unless they could persuade the real owner of the business to sell them some of his stock? The answer must be that no legislature, by providing that three associates may form a corporation, ever intended to authorize the formation of a one-man corporation for profit where the statute provides that three "associates" may form such a corporation.

Under the present ruling of the Secretary of State, adopted after receiving the above opinion from the Attorney General, not only is a natural person permitted to organize a one-man corporation, but an existing corporation is permitted initially to subscribe for all the stock of the new company so long as two citizens sign the charter as a mere formality.

From the foregoing authorities the conclusion seems inevitable that under the first general incorporation statute passed in Texas in 1874 subscriptions to the capital stock were conditions subsequent to the existence of the corporation. Under such laws the corporation could carry on its business for several years and incur obligations before its stock was subscribed or paid for. The result was that creditors dealt with the corporations in the belief that the stock was subscribed and fully paid. But very often only a small part of the stock was subscribed, and when the sheriff levied the creditor's execution on the company's property, he found nothing but an empty bag. As stated in the case of National Bank v. Texas Investment Company, ,75 the remedy of the creditors was an action of deceit against those stockholders or officers who made the false representations. But how many of the contract creditors could prove that they knew the amount of the capital stock of the corporation and would swear that when they gave credit to the company they relied on the fact that all the capital stock had been subscribed, and not on the net assets owned by the corporation at that time? Tort creditors could not recover in an action of deceit, since evidently they could not prove that they relied on the company's capital stock being fully paid." The contains even a hint that in Texas or anywhere else can one person subscribe for all the stock of a new corporation. Every case cited by the author is discussed in its appropriate place in this text. All the rest of the quotation from Texas Jurisprudence deals with the power of the owner of all of the stock of the company to conduct the affairs of the corporation and his liability for the obligations of the corporation if the facts are sufficient to induce the court to disregard the corporate fiction. Those matters are discussed in other parts of this text.

That was definitely the reason why our legislature amended the statute so as to provide that subscriptions for all of the stock and the payment of fifty per cent thereof were conditions precedent to the existence of the corporation. If under our present laws a foreign corporation, or one person, can subscribe initially for all the stock of the newly formed corporation, the first bill passed by the next legislature should be one providing that each of the three persons who sign the charter must subscribe for a certain per cent of the stock of the company. If, on the other hand, it is thought that the one-man corporation should be encouraged, the legislature of Texas should face the problem frankly and pass statutes similar to those adopted in Michigan and Iowa providing for the formation of a corporation by a single person." The language quoted above from the present Texas statutory requirements for organizing corporations in this State should also be so changed as not to imply, as they now do, a group or collection of persons associating themselves for profit to act as a legal entity in performing legal transactions.

 § 32. Extension, Revival and Amendment of Charters 

In Texas railroad corporations are not incorporated under the general incorporation statute. In 1876 a special statute was passed providing for the incorporation of such companies. That statute with its amendments is now published as Title 112, arts. 

6259-6274 of Vernon's Ann.Civ.Statutes. Articles 6267 and 6268 provide for the renewal of expired railroad charters by a vote of three-fourths of the stockholders. The resolution must be "certified to by the president of the company". The renewal of the railroad corporation dates from the filing and recording of the resolution and certificate in the office of the Secretary of State. 

The above articles apply only to railroad companies. 

Until 1937 there was no provision in Texas authorizing the renewal of the charter of all corporations incorporated under the general incorporation statute. Before that time the only provision on that subject was article 1315 of Vernon's Annotated Civil Statutes. It provided that "Corporations created for the support of benevolent, charitable, educational or missionary undertakings, the support of any literary or scientific undertaking, the maintenance of a library, or the promotion of painting, music or other fine arts, whose charter has expired by limitation, may revive such charter with all the privileges and immunities and rights of property, real and personal, exercised and held by it at the date of the expiration of its said charter, by filing, with the consent of a majority of its stockholders, a new charter under the provisions of this chapter." Why the Legislature was averse to the renewal of all corporations whose charters had expired by limitation, no one can now determine. At the Regular Session of the 45th Legislature article 1315 (a), Vernon's Ann.Civ. Statutes was enacted. It provided: "Subject to a finding by the 

Secretary of State as hereinafter provided, any private corporation organized or incorporated for any purpose or purposes authorized under this Title, at any time within ten (10) years prior to the expiration of its charter, or any extension thereof, may extend such charter and the corporate existence of such corporation for an additional period of not to exceed fifty (50) years from the expiration date of the original charter, or any exten- 173

§ Ch. 2 

sion thereof, with all the privileges, powers, immunities, right of succession by its corporate name, and rights of property, real and personal, exercised and held by it at such expiration date, to the same intents and purposes as upon original incorporation. 

The manner of extending any such charter shall be by a resolution in writing, adopted at any annual or special meeting of stockholders called for that purpose by stockholders holding a majority of the shares of capital stock of such corporation then outstanding, such resolution to specify the period of time for which the charter is extended, and a copy of such resolution, duly certified by the secretary of the corporation, under the corporate seal, shall be filed and recorded in the office of the Secretary of State. Upon the adoption of such resolution and the filing of a certified copy thereof with the Secretary of State, together with payment of the filing fee herein prescribed, the charter and corporate existence of such corporation may be extended for the additional period of time recited in such resolution. The filing fee to be paid for any such extension of a charter shall be such fee as said corporation would be required under the Statutes of Texas to pay in the event it was then applying for a new charter instead of extending its then existing charter. "Such extensions, however, may be made only in instances where the Secretary of State shall have found, after proper investigation, that such corporation is solvent and its capital unimpaired."

At the First Called Session of the same Legislature article 

1315 (b), Vernon's Ann. Civ. Statutes was enacted. It provides: "The provisions of Article 1315 (a) shall extend to and include all private corporations incorporated under the general laws of Texas. The period of ten (10) years prior to the expiration of the charter or any extension thereof referred to in Article 1315 (a) shall include the period of time during which such corporation may have continued its existence under the provisions of Article 1389 of the Revised Civil Statutes of 1925.” 

The effect of articles 1315(a) and 1315 (b) is to permit all corporations incorporated under the Texas general incorporation statutes to renew their charters any time within ten years prior 174

Ch. § 32 

to the expiration of their charters or the three years of existence permitted under article 1389, Vernon's Ann.Civ.Statutes after the expiration of the time provided for in their original charters or "any extension thereof". However, in the case of

Flowers v. Pecos River Ry. Co.78 the Supreme Court of Texas held that these articles do not repeal the renewal provision of statutes that apply "to a particular type of corporation with regard to which particular or specific legislation has been" enacted. 

In other words, the Court held that the two articles passed in 1937 apply to corporations organized under the general incorporation statutes but not to corporations organized under specific statutes such as railroads which are specifically provided for in the articles referred to in the first paragraph in this section. In this recent case the Court also held that the renewal of a charter is tantamount to the filing of a new charter. However, the Court intimated that there is a difference between the renewal of a charter and an amendment of a charter. In the Flowers-Pecos 

River case, referred to in the last note, Justice Critz said: "The 

Railroad contends that the case of St. Louis S. W. R. Co. of Texas v. Tod, 64 S.W. 778, 94 Tex. 632, is decisive authority in its favor of its contention that it is only liable for the fee of $200 tendered by it in this instance. We shall not extend this opinion by attempting a complete analysis of the Tod opinion. It is sufficient to say that it deals with an amendment to a railroad corporate charter. It does not deal with what amounts to a new charter, as does this case."

As was shown in the preceding paragraphs a very limited number of the corporations organized under the general incorporation statutes could renew their charters under article 1315 of Vernon's Ann. Civ.Statutes where their charters had expired by limitation. However, as those corporations are chartered under the general laws of Texas it seems evident that they may now renew their charters either under article 1315, or under articles 

1315(a) and 1315 (b) of Vernon's Ann.Civ.Statutes. The period

Under the reserved power our general statute fixing the maximum membership fee that can be charged by building and loan associations not in excess of two per cent of each $100 share of stock is constitutional although the defendant corporation made a contract to last for ten years for a larger fee before the statute was passed. The charter of a Texas corporation incorporated under the general law consists of the constitution and statutes that are passed concerning corporations.88 The same is true with reference to the premiums that title insurance companies can charge. Their "business is affected by public interest," and, therefore, the Legislature of Texas can prescribe the rates that must be charged by such companies. Since the reserved power of the state cannot be contracted away, a ten year's contract made before the rates were prescribed by the Texas Legislature may become illegal by the statute. Such a statute is constitutional.89

51. Introductory 

The powers of a corporation are its legal rights to perform functions and to transact business. In dealing with the powers of corporations, it is intended in this chapter to deal with the validity or invalidity of some particular transaction proposed or entered into by the corporation after the charter has been granted. 

§ 52. Source of Powers-In general 

1 2 The express powers of a corporation are derived from the purpose clause of its charter and the statute by which it was created or the general incorporation statute under which it was incorporated. Corporations chartered under general statutes do not have the same inherent powers as an individual.³ This distinction was aptly drawn in Rue v. Missouri Pacific Ry. Co.,* where the court said: "Natural persons may make any contract or perform any act not prohibited by law, while artificial persons (corporations) can do only those things which, by express grant or necessary implication, they are authorized or 

1. North Side R. Co. v. Worthing ton, 30 S.W. 1055, 88 Tex. 562, 53 

Am.St.Rep. 778. 

2. Chapter 2 herein. 

3. Lyons-Thomas Hardware Co. v. 

Perry Stove Mfg. Co., 24 S.W. 16, 86 Tex. 143, 22 L.R.A. 802. 

Rue v. Missouri Pac. Ry. Co., 8 S.W. 

533, 74 Tex. 474, 15 Am.St. Rep. 852. 

4. 8 S.W. 533, 74 Tex. 474, 15 Am. 

St.Rep. 852. 181

§ Ch. 3 

empowered to do by the laws of the state under which their charters were obtained.”

The present Constitution 5 of Texas gives to the legislature the power of passing general laws governing the formation and functions of private corporations. Subject to the limitations in the Constitution of the United States and that of our own State, the statutes passed by our Legislature constitute the index to the powers with which a private corporation is endowed. Even the name of a corporation puts the third party on notice that the powers of the corporation are limited to transactions reasonably necessary to conduct the business indicated by its name."

In view of what has been said, a corporation, even though acting with the consent of all its members or stockholders, cannot enlarge the powers conferred upon it by its charter. Even though the statute authorizes each corporation to make bylaws, by its terms the by-laws are limited to the control of its officers and agents and to the management of its business,⁹ and cannot extend or enlarge the powers of the corporation conferred by the statutes. 

§ 53. Express Prohibitions and Limitations 

The Texas statutory law has placed certain express prohibitions and limitations on the powers to be exercised by private corporations organized under the Texas statutes.

Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1349 provides: "No corporation, domestic or foreign, doing business in this State, shall employ or use its stock, means, assets or other property, directly or indirectly for any purpose whatever other than to accomplish the legitimate business of its creation, or those purposes otherwise permitted by law; provided that nothing in this article shall be held to inhibit corporations from contributing to any bona fide association, incorporated or unincorporated, organized for and actively engaged for one year prior to such contribution in purely religious, charitable or eleemosynary activities, nor to local, district, or statewide commercial or industrial clubs or associations or other civic enterprises or organizations not in any manner not to any extent directly or indirectly engaged in furthering the cause of any political party, or aiding in the election or defeat of any candidate for office, or aiding in defraying the expenses of any candidate for office, or defraying or aiding in defraying the expenses of any political campaign, or political headquarters, or aiding or assisting the success or defeat of any question to be voted upon by the qualified voters of this State or any subdivision thereof." 

Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1348, provides: "No corporation, domestic or foreign, doing business in this State shall create any indebtedness whatever except for money paid, labor done which is reasonably worth at least the sum at which it was taken by the corporation, or property actually received reasonably worth at least the sum at which it was taken by the corporation."

Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1353 provides: "No corporation shall issue any stock whatever, except for money paid, labor done which is reasonably worth at least the sum at which it was taken by the corporation, or property actually received reasonably worth at least the sum at which it was taken by the company. Any corporation which violates any provision of this article shall, on proof thereof in any court of competent jurisdiction, forfeit its charter, permit or license, as the case may be, and all rights and franchises which it holds under, from, or by virtue of the laws of this State."

§ 54. Power of Business Corporations to Contribute to Charity 

In general, according to the old authorities, a corporation did not have implied power to make donations or contributions to charitable, religious, or civic enterprises where the benefits accruing to it from such contributions would be shared in common by the rest of the community." 18 This rule of law is slowly, but surely, crumbling. The hesitancy on the part of the courts to give corporations more latitude in making donations is due to the fact that they fear that the directors may squander the assets of the corporation by contributing to campaign funds and enterprises that have only a remote bearing on the business of the company.32

As we have seen in the preceding section the courts hesitated for a long time to permit private business corporations to give to charitable activities as freely as its individual competistock subscribed for and receive profits therefrom, yet that did not prevent the subscription from being "a contribution." And in the Adams case a mercantile corporation was permitted to subscribe for stock in a "warehouse" for the storage of cotton. 

In the Anderson case in 8 S.W.2d 

704 the court said: "Since the chief purpose which prompted the building of a hotel was the upbuilding of the business interests of the citizens, the undertaking was no less a civic enterprise by reason of the fact that as a secondary consideration the subscribers for stock contemplated some possible return therefrom out of the profits arising from the operations of the hotel." The court held that the subscription did not create a prohibited indebtedness within the meaning of Vernon's Ann. Civ.St. art. 1348. 

In the Adams case the court said: "Appellee corporation was formed and chartered 'for the purpose of buying and selling goods, wares, and merchandise of every description, by wholesale and retail.' It is obvious that under this purpose clause in its charter appellee was not authorized to engage in a cotton warehouse business, and, if the evidence in this case had disclosed that in subscribing for stock in the proposed warehouse corporation appellee thereby sought to enter and pursue the warehouse business, the act would have been beyond its corporate objects, and its obligation to appropriate its corporate funds in payment of the stock would have been void and unenforceable. 

But the evidence disclosed no such purpose. On the contrary, it was shown that it subscribed for the stock, not for the purpose of engaging in the warehouse business, but in order to aid other members of the public in securing the establishment of a much coveted public warehouse in the town of Devine, for the bene fit of the public generally, and of appellee and others doing business in the community. The establishment of the warehouse was looked upon as a greatly needed civic enterprise and improvement, and appellee, along with others in the community, subscribed for stock in the proposed corporation in order to secure that improvement, and not to engage in the warehouse business. It now seems to be settled that a corporation, chartered for a particular purpose, may properly subscribe for stock in civic enterprises of this character, regardless of the fact that such enterprise is foreign to the purpose of such corporation, and the latter's obligation to pay its subscription will be enforced as any other obligation."

In view of this statement by the court, if the Adams Company had subscribed for a majority of the stock of the warehouse company, that fact may have shown that the "sub- 198

A large majority of the stockholders sustained a recommendation on the part of the directors that (1) 1050 pounds be given to the officers of the company "for the loss of their employment" and that (2) 1500 pounds be given to the directors for past services. The court held that as the corporation was no longer a going concern the directors and a majority of the stockholders could not give away the assets of the company since those assets belonged to the stockholders in proportion to the stock owned by each shareholder. The attorney general has ruled that Texas corporations have no authority: 

1st. To contribute to a State Com mercial Organization. 

2nd. That while they have authority to contribute to local commercial organizations, yet they do not have authority to contribute to a local commercial organization which in turn makes contribution to a state commercial organization, for the reason, of course, that they would be doing indirectly that which they have no authority to do directly. 

3rd. That corporations may contribute to local commercial organizations so long as these local commercial organizations confine their activities to local affairs. 

4th. Corporations may contribute to purely religious, charitable and eleemosynary institutions, regardless of the extent of the activities of the latter, where such institutions are bona fide and have been in operation one year prior to the contribution.

Price's Patent Candle Company 45 which held that the directors of a corporation have authority to make a gift of a week's wages to its faithful employees especially during "very good years," Lord Bowen said: "The Master of the Rolls there held that the company might lawfully expend a week's wages as gratuities for their servants; because that sort of liberal dealing with servants eases the friction between masters and servants, and is, in the end, a benefit to the company. It is not charity sitting at the board of directors, because as it seems to me charity has no business to sit at boards of directors qua charity. There is, however, a kind of charitable dealing which is for the interest of those who practise it, and to that extent and in that garb (I admit not a very philanthropic garb) charity may sit at the board, but for no other purpose."

One question suggested in the Hutton case has not been decided by the courts have the directors of a business corporation authority to pay employees for loss of their jobs regardless of the reason why the servant was let out of the employment of the corporation, as, for instance decrease of business or the consolidation with another company. The question arose in a proceeding before the Interstate Commerce Commission to approve a lease in a railroad reorganization hearing. The Interstate Commerce Act, as amended in 1933, provides that if the Commission finds that the lease will promote the public interest, it may approve the lease upon such terms and conditions as it shall find to be just and reasonable." 46 

44. This practice has brought millions of dollars of new business to some of the American insurance companies, as for instance to the insurance companies that paid losses for which they were not liable after the 

San Francisco earth quake and the floods in recent years in Corpus 

Christi and San Antonio, Texas.

Many policy holders in companies refusing the loss immediately switched over to the insurance companies who had waived their defense and accepted a burden for which they were not legally responsible. Just another method of purchasing good will, which is the basis of much of our modern advertising.

The testimony showed that the consolidation would save the roads $100,000 a year. A majority of the Commissioners, one 

Commissioner dissenting, held that under the above statute the Commission could approve the consolidation "on condition" that an allowance be made to dismissed employees who were unable to find other employment.47 It would seem that Congress, in passing the above statute, must have intended to confer power on the Commission to approve a consolidation under just and reasonable conditions that had a direct bearing in determining whether the consolidation would "promote the public interest," and not incidental questions resulting from the consolidation. The Commission's decision seems doubtful in view of some decision by the Supreme Court of the United States.48 

It is reasonable to say that the directors of a going concern have authority to give a small present to a faithful employee when he quits the company's service, but an altogether different question where they vote to give a sizable amount to one they reluctantly discharged when the business no longer needed the services of the employee and he did not have a contract for a definite term. 

§ 57. 

Housing Facilities for Employees 

Under many circumstances it is necessary for a corporation to furnish housing facilities for some or all of its employees. 

Many of the Texas oil companies in developing new oil fields and establishing new manufacturing plants remote from a city have never hesitated to purchase land and build cottages for their employees. They never fail to install water and light systems and contribute to the community churches and schools. 

A construction company employed to build a dam at a remote 

47. Chicago, Rock I. & Gulf Ry.

Trustees Lease, I. C. C., Div. 4, Finance Docket No. 11847, Oct. 

1938. 29, 48. New York Central Securities Corp. v. United States, 53 S.Ct.

Atlantic Coast Line R. Co. v. United

location and a cement company owning six hundred and forty acres of proven territory ten miles north of San Antonio have furnished housing facilities for their employees. If these companies did not possess that implied authority under the above circumstances, their operations could not be made successful. 

The same thing is doubly true in the case of lumber manufacturing corporations. They must construct their saw mills in the remote districts in southeast Texas. When the timber is exhausted within ten miles of the saw mill the mill and all out houses, including the temporary dwellings of the employees, must be removed to a new location. Evidently under those circumstances outside capital could not be induced to build the facilities necessary to carry on the business of the corporation. 

On the other hand, if the plant is built near an established city, and the existence of the plant is not temporary, outside capital will seize upon the opportunity to build all houses necessary to care for the needs of the employees, and the city will gladly extend its water and light facilities for the use of the new inhabitants. At the first opportunity the city will extend its limits so as to include the new territory. Several illustrations of the truth of this statement could be given from actual situations that have arisen in Texas. One will suffice. In the case of the New Braunfels Cotton Mill company the manufacturing plant was established in the edge of a thriving town sufficiently large to furnish most of the common labor needed by the plant. 

Under those circumstances the corporation should not have implied authority to buy property and virtually establish a city with water, light and sewage. On the other hand, it is necessary for the two rock quarries five miles south of New Braunfels to build housing facilities for their employees-not as necessary now in the day of the automobile as a quarter of a century ago; but still, fairly necessary for some of the employees. 

The best considered case on this question makes the above distinction. In People ex rel. Maloney v. Pullman Palace Car

In the Pullman case the court said: "Manifestly the acts of the corporation which have resulted in the creation of this town or city and its acts in connection with the streets, alleys, dwellings, tenements, school, church and business houses, water system, sewerage, heat, etc., which the plea admits it was performing at the time of the filing of the information, can not be regarded as the exercise of powers expressly given. Can they be justified as the proper exercise of powers incidental to the express powers possessed by the corporation, or by the provision in the sixth clause of the charter that it may be lawful for the corporation to acquire and told such real estate as may be deemed necessary for the successful prosecution of its business? The declaration of the sixth clause is not that the company may acquire and hold such real estate as it or its directory may deem necessary, but such as may deemed necessary to the successful prosecution of its business. The true meaning of this clause is not that the company or its governing body is vested with unlimited and unbridled power to acquire and hold such real estate as it may deem necessary, but be with power to purchase and hold only such real estate as, under the rules of law, may be deemed necessary for the successful prosecution of its busi

"The averment of the plea the corporation was obliged to construct such houses and tenements is but the statement of a conclusion, and we find the facts pleaded do not justify such a deduction. No reason existed, nor do we find in the pleas even a suggestion that there was reason or ground, for the apprehension that individual enterprise and private capital would not at once, after the purpose and intention of the corporation became known, provide all necessary dwellings and tenements for the accommodation of the workmen, or that the wants of the community composed of such workmen would not at once be met by the location in its midst of schools, churches, dry goods and grocery stores, meat markets, etc., or that the necessary streets, alleys, and public ways would not be provided without any intervention whatever on the part of the corporation.
