51 other hand, an intermediate court in New York held that a large manufacturing piano corporation had implied authority to furnish housing facilities to its employees where it located its plant near the city of New York.5 In this case the plans were formulated by a partnership. The partners bought 400 acres and then formed the corporation. That fact influenced the attitude of the court, as the judges realized what a disappointment it would have been to force the corporation to sell all of its land except what it needed for its manufacturing plant and permit outside capital to reap the gains due directly to the establishment of a permanent manufacturing center by the corporation. 

But that is part of the price the partners must pay for the privilege of carrying on their business with limited personal liability for the debts of the corporation. In the opinion the court said: "The transfer of their factory (from New York City) to the Astoria site (in Long Island City) was a reasonable exercise of a conceded discretionary power which cannot be criticised or questioned here. As, however, it involved also the transfer of ing religious instruction. It is idle to argue it became in any sense necessary or directly appropriate to the accomplishment of the lawful and chartered purposes or objects of the corporation it should engage its efforts or capital in the construction of dwellings, tenement houses, store houses, streets, alleys, theaters, hotel, churches, school-houses, water-works, a system of sewers, etc. Workmen, if they have families, must have homes, or if unmarried must be accommodated with boarding and places of lodging. Homes, groceries, vegetables, bread, meat, clothing, furniture, light, heat, water, school books, medicine, the services of physicians, dentists and other professional men, and many other things, become necessary to the health, comfort, or convenience of such workmen and their families; but the right and power to supply such wants had, in this instance, so far as the pleas show, no direct relation or connection with the successful prosecution of the specific object of the appellee corporation. The relation was but remote, indirect and mediate,-not direct and immediate. Implied power can not be invoked to authorize a corporation to engage in collateral enterprises but remotely connected with the specific purposes it was created to accomplish. A power which a corporation may exercise by implication must be bounded by the purposes of the corporate existence and the terms and intention of the charter, and acts which tend only remotely and by indirection to promote its interests and chartered objects can not be justified by implication of law, but are ultra vires."

a large number of operatives, whose well-being was essential to the proper and efficient performance of their work, and thus to the success of the corporation, a close and practical business relation subsisted between the provision made by the defendants for their employees and the object for which the corporation was organized. The district was sparsely settled, and it was desirable that the men should live within easy reach of their work. It was also desirable-it may, I think, be said to have been necessary to the success of the scheme that some provision should be made for the moral as well as the material needs of this new and isolated community, thus brought, by the exigencies of their employment, into a measure of social dependence upon their employer. It was also a part of the scheme, by this segregation of their employees and surrounding them with healthful influences, to remove or at least minimize the temptation to participate in unreasonable strikes and agitations. The scheme must be taken as a whole, and from that point of view every part of it was directly related to the legitimate objects of the corporation. "Indirect Benefits. In a few cases even less direct benefits to employees have been drawn into question and sustained as properly given by the corporation. Most of the cases have involved the right of the corporation to deduct expenditures for such purposes as an ordinary and necessary business expense in computing net income for federal income tax purposes. While these cases may be doubtful under more recent decisions as interpretations of the federal tax statutes, they probably remain unscathed in so far as they also bear upon the issue of ultra vires."

In this case the court said: "We see corporations pensioning old and infirm employees, establishing benefits for the sick and disabled, permitting regular vacations with continuing pay, aiding in sickness, and doing many humane and praiseworthy acts which formerly might have been questioned as not fairly within the powers or duties of the corporation. These acts are not to be defended on the ground of gratuity or charity, but they enter into the relation of the employer and employee, become as it were a part of the inducement for the employee to enter the employment and serve faithfully for the wage agreed upon, and become a part of the terms of employment. The considerate employer, who treats his employees well, is thus able to secure better service, and upon more satisfactory terms, than the unwilling, illiberal employer. A corporation with 13,280 employees is called upon to exercise great care in selecting and managing them, so as to receive the best service. Upon their loyalty and efficiency much of its success must depend. 

The employment, training, disciplining, and managing of such a force, and obtaining from it the best results, is an important part of the relator's business. It is well within the corporate power to assume, as it has done, the care and treatment of such of its employees as are afflicted with tuberculosis; and, unless it is shown to be wasteful of the company's money and unproductive of beneficial results, the practice may stand as well within the scope of its business." Pensions to Employees and Their Families 

Three principal forms of pensions to employees and their families have become fairly common during the past few years, in addition to reliefs granted to employees under state or federal statutes. In the first place, quite often the directors will pass a resolution providing that when an employee quits the company's service or dies, a pure donation may be made to the employee or his family for past services. Obviously, if this promise is made for the first time when the servant quits, there is no consideration for the promise.59 The motive for the promise is gratitude for past services, and motive should not be confused or substituted for consideration. If the facts show that when the promised gift of the pension was made, the promisor reasonably expected his promise "to induce action or forbearance of a definite

If the agreement is based on a valuable consideration it is enforceable as a valid contract. Therefore, if the employee agrees not to work for a competitor or makes any other detrimental promise in consideration of the corporation's promise to pay him a definite amount, the bilateral contract is based on a valuable consideration, as where the employee agrees to waive participation in the general pension plan of the corporation.62 

These agreements are upheld for the same reason that an agreement by A to give a church corporation $1,000 in consideration of the corporation agreeing to build a church according to certain plans and specifications, or an agreement by A to give the church $1,000 in consideration of B's agreement to give the church $500. § 62. 

Bonus to Executive Officers and Directors 

As we have seen in § 740 in the chapter on Election there is no inherent objection to the payment of a bonus to executive officers and directors of the corporations.81 The amount of the bonus to such officers should be provided for in the by-laws or by a vote of the stockholders. § 64. Express Powers

§ 65. Implied Powers-In General 

Whenever a corporation is created certain powers are implied because of the powers expressly granted.5 The difficulty arises in a particular case when we attempt to determine whether the power of a corporation to do an act can be implied or not. The question has given rise to much litigious controversy and to much conflict of decision. It is difficult to lay down a rule by which the question may be determined. In short, if the means be such as are usually resorted to and a direct method of accomplishing the purpose of the incorporation, they are within its powers; if they be unusual and tend in an indirect manner only to promote its interests, they are held to be ultra vires. 

A corporation, created der a statute which merely states the nature of the business and does not further define its powers, may exercise such powers as are reasonably necessary to accomplish the purpose of its creation; and it may be such as are usually incidental in practice to the prosecution of the business, and no more." " 9 un- "Corporations have an implied power to make such contracts as are usual and necessary for carrying into effect the purposes for which they were created. 

The power of a corporation, in respect to contracts and business dealings, extends not merely to those which are absolutely essential or indispensable to the performance of the specified acts authorized by its charter, but as well to those which, not being prohibited by statute or public policy, are designed and may be useful to promote the main enterprise. The choice of means which are reasonably promotive of the main purpose is with the corporation; and where different methods stand this test, judicial tribunals will not revise its discretion by holding that the one chosen was not indispensable, and that another might have been more wisely taken." 10 "It is our opinion that a corporation in the transaction of its business, the business for which it was organized, has the same latitude as the individual in the same character of business in those things that are essential to the successful operation of that particular business."'11

"Every corporation is created with certain express powers. 

Being endowed with these express powers, it has the implied power to do whatever is necessary or reasonably appropriate to their exercise. It has, in a word, the authority to do whatever will legitimately effect the express purposes of its creation."12 "Undoubtedly the main business of a corporation is to be confined to that class of operations which properly appertain to the general purposes for which its charter was granted. But it may also enter into contracts and engage in transactions which are incidental or auxiliary to its main business, or which may become necessary, expedient, or profitable in the care and management of the property which it is authorized to hold under the act by which it was created." 13 “To crystalize the rule, it may be said the implied powers of a corporation embrace those that are reasonably necessary, according to the usual methods of that particular business, to the successful prosecution of the specific business authorized, and is not limited to those things indispensably necessary to the business, provided always the benefits to be derived from the contract are direct, and not so indirect as to be remote." 14

This doctrine does not mean that a corporation in carrying out the purpose or purposes for which it was incorporated can utilize any power which might possibly under given circumstances be called into exercise to affectuate these objects, or that a corporation has the same inherent powers possessed by the individual. The meaning is rather that a corporation may use all such powers as a natural person, measured by the standard of a reasonable man, might properly and lawfully use in carrying on such a business under the same or similar circumstances,20 or that the corporation may exercise those powers that the individual usually and customarily adopts in the conduct of the same or similar business.

furtherance of that purpose. The problem is to determine just what powers may be utilized. How directly connected with the purpose of incorporation is the intended exercise of the power? 

Is it reasonably appropriate, usual or customary?

The legislature, from the very nature of things, has not attempted to give a detailed enumeration of the specific transactions 22 that a corporation can enter into. However, the proper procedure in determining whether a given transaction is within the corporate powers is to view, as a first step, the statutory enactments. If the statutes do not specifically determine the question, then it can only be upheld upon the ground that it is incidental to the carrying out of the purpose or purposes for which the corporation was formed. In order that the power may be implied, the act must tend directly and immediately, and not indirectly or remotely, to accomplish the object for which the corporation was created.23 "In short, if the means be such as are usually resorted to, and are a direct method of accomplishing the purpose of the incorporation, they are within the powers. If they be unusual, and tend in an indirect manner only to promote its interests, they are held to be ultra vires." 24 

An incidental or implied power exists only for the purpose of enabling a corporation to carry out the powers expressly granted to it; i. e., the powers necessary to accomplish the purpose of its existence, and can in no case be employed to enlarge the express powers, and thereby warrant it to devote its efforts and capital to other purposes than those its charter expressly authorizes, or to engage in collateral enterprises, not directly, but only remotely connected with its specific corporate purpose.25

§ Ch. 3 

The scope of corporate activity is constantly being expanded. 

At the present time the statutes authorize incorporation for more than one hundred purposes. Where the business is an old established one the best guide is to prove what business men, in the conduct of the same or a similar business, have usually regarded as reasonably necessary for the successful prosecution of such business. If the business for which the company was chartered is new and not the same or similar to other well established businesses, the court must exercise common sense and thereby determine what is reasonably necessary for the successful conduct of the business. The leading Texas case 26 has given us the following standard: "A limit must be laid down as to the implied powers of a corporation; and, with reference to a company chartered for a business purpose, we think the proper line of demarcation is between those powers which are reasonably necessary to the business, or which are usually incident to its prosecution, and those which are not." 

In the application of a rule so general in its terms, much leeway is given. Accordingly the courts have been actuated by strictly practical considerations in determining the ambit of corporate activity. The tendency of the recent cases has been to avoid, so far as possible, loss and injury to those acting on the faith of the powers that the corporation has assumed.28 This has been accomplished by a very liberal interpretation of the particular corporate power 29 or by holding that the corporation was

Usual or Customary Acts 

It is not necessary that the act be usual or customary if it meets the requirements stated in the preceding sections.44 However, the determining factor, in a number of Texas cases, in deciding whether the corporation possessed the asserted power was whether the transaction in question was usual in the operation of a business of that kind.45 This point is illustrated in 

North Side Ry. Co. v. Worthington,46 where Judge Gaines, in delivering the opinion for the Supreme Court, said: "If the means be such as are usually resorted to and a direct method of accomplishing the purpose of the incorporation, they are within its powers; if they be unusual and tend in an indirect manner only to promote its interest, they are held to be ultra vires." 

Recent decisions have stated that, "A corporation in the transaction of its business has the same latitude as the individual in the same character of business, in those things that are essential to the successful operation of that particular business." 47 

Thus, where it can be shown that individuals operating a given type of business customarily enter into such transactions, the corporation organized to carry on the same business may do like-

For instance, it is within the memory of the writer when only the manufacturer of fuel gas sold gas stoves and electric appliances. For this reason, the Texas 

Supreme Court in a recent decision properly held that a gas company had implied authority to sell such articles.50 But in recent years it has become customary for other companies and individuals to sell those articles. Formerly housewives had to be taught how to operate a gas stove. Now small children soon learn to cook on gas ovens. How long, therefore, will it be before the manufacturers of gas will cease to sell gas stoves and electric appliances? When they do, corporations of this kind will cease to have implied power to sell these articles. Where custom can be established, it should be proved just as any other question of fact and not left to the guess of the judges of the Supreme Court as is so often done.51 It is not customary for a corporation to agree to pay a commission for the sale of the personal stock of an officer or shareholder. Any Means Reasonably Appropriate 

Private corporations may exercise all the powers within the fair intent and purpose of their creation which are reasonably appropriate to give effect to the powers expressly granted, provided they do not violate the constitution, any statute, charter or the public policy of the state.59 The Texas courts have often actions called in question before the Shoe Company became indebted to plaintiff in error, we do not think it is in a favorable position to question the validity of these transactions. "We recognize as correct the doctrine announced in Reagan Bale Co. v. Heuermann, Tex.Civ.App., 149 S.

W. 228, to the effect that holders of preferred stock cannot assert a claim to the assets of a corporation superior to the rights of its creditors. However, that doctrine has no application here, because the fund in question (proceeds of policy) was never an asset of the corporation. The insurable interest in the life of Isaac 

Jolesch did not belong to the corporation, nor was the policy an item of property, but simply the evidence of a contract providing that, upon the death of Isaac Jolesch, the amount thereof ($50,000), when collected, should be paid to the Mercantile National Bank at Dallas, as trustee for the benefit of holders of the preferred stock; therefore, the fund belonged, not to the corporation, but to the named beneficiaries-that is, the bank as trustee for the holders of preferred stock."

It is self evident that if the charter gives a corporation express authority to carry on a certain business if a certificate of authority to conduct such business from an official is required under the local law, the corporation must obtain such certificate before it can lawfully conduct such business. The Court of Civil Appeals in construing such a charter said: "Appellant invokes the doctrine of ultra vires, and in support of its contention asserts that its charter did not authorize it to maintain an establishment for refrigerating turkeys, unless such establishment had been constructed by it. 

The language of its charter is, 'the construction and maintenance of establishments,' etc. It is true, that as a general rule 'and' does not mean 'or'. * "It is not necessary, however, to hold that 'and' means 'or' in the instant case; but if the meaning insisted upon by appellants be given, that is, that 'and' means 'adding to,' still we think the charter authorized appellant to maintain a refrigerating establishment not theretofore erected by it. That is to say, we think the language of the charter means that it may construct, and it may also maintain, such establishment, without both constructing and maintaining the same establishment. That 'and' was used in this sense in the charter is evident from the fact that the company was chartered for 'slaughtering, refrigerating, canning, curing, and packing meat;' that is to say, for doing each of these things, and not that before being authorized to pack meat it must first refrigerate, can, and cure it." 92

2 By legislative enactment, every private corporation is given the power "to enter into any obligation or contract essential to the transaction of its authorized business." § 75. Mode of Contracting and Conveying Real Estate 

17 The ancient rule was that a corporation could bind itself by contract only through the execution of an instrument in writing bearing the corporate seal.16 This doctrine has long since been repudiated, and today for most purposes a corporation may bind itself by a contract in any way that an individual can.18 

The essential difference between the contract of a corporation and that of an individual is that a corporation may act only by and through its agents. The authority given an agent may be by parol, in writing, or may be implied from circumstances. 19

31. Burnett v. Atteberry, 145 S.W. 

582, 105 Tex. 119; Allen v. Hall, Tex.Civ.App., 52 S.W.2d 661. In the

Burnett case Justice Dibrell said: 

"While the retention of the vendor's lien in the deed of conveyance retains in the vendor the superior title to the land conveyed it is not the retention of such an estate in the conveyed premises as requires a written release to make the title absolute in the vendee, but is such an estate only as remains in the vendor until payment of the purchase price. The payment of the purchase money, or its satisfaction under agreement by the acceptance of other security, divests the vendor of the estate in such property. This result arises from the discharge of the debt. Without the existence of the debt for the purchase money the retained estate has no foundation for its existence. The moment the debt is paid the lien is satisfied and the retained title or estate is released ipso facto. The function of the release is practically in such cases nothing more than the written evidence of the payment of the purchase money and the consequent discharge of the lien. It adds nothing to the purchaser's title. After the payment of the purchase money the vendor has no claim on the land whether he has or not executed a release. Beyond its effect to serve as notice and enduring evidence of the payment of the debt for the purchase money the release bears no legal import. So that when reduced to a proper analysis the question as to whether a release of the vendor's lien as applied to the facts of this case may be made by verbal agreement is wholly immaterial."

In 1939 Article 1322 was amended so as to read as follows: "Any corporation may convey lands by deed, sealed with the common seal of the corporation, and signed by the president or vice-president or presiding member or trustee of said corporation, or in common form without seal by its attorney in fact where the instrument constituting such attorney in fact is executed in said manner first mentioned. Such deed, when acknowledged by such officer or attorney in fact to be the act of the corporation, or proved in the manner prescribed for other conveyances of lands, may be recorded in like manner and with the same effect as other deeds."44 By a comparison of the original article with its amendment, it is evident that the only effect of the amendment is the addition of the words, "or vicepresident," to the original article. As the placing of the seal on a deed or a power of attorney to execute the deed is a mere formality that performs no useful purpose in this day and time, that part of this article should be repealed by the Texas Legislature. It has long been held that where an instrument purports upon its face to be under seal, and it appears to have

By virtue of the statute it is no longer necessary for individuals to use seals and no effect will be given them if they are used, and an ordinary written contract will not be raised to the dignity of a sealed instrument by placing a seal on it.

However, corporations are excepted, and, therefore, the common law rules still apply to them, and in those cases where at common law an instrument had to be under seal, it is still necessary for a corporation to use a seal. Therefore, a conveyance of real estate must be under seal. The failure to put a seal on an instrument conveying real estate does not vitiate the instrument entirely, but the instrument will operate as a conveyance of the equitable title and will be effective as a contract to convey where it is based on a valuable consideration. Texas also requires the signature of the grantor to the instrument, although at common law the seal alone was sufficient. The 

Supreme Court of Texas held that an instrument though signed by the proper officers of the corporation, but not under seal, was invalid and "insufficient to convey to the assignee any real estate owned by the corporation." 48 Where the clerk in record-

In 1858 the Texas Legislature passed a statute with reference to the seal, and ever since our statutes were first revised in 1879 the original Act was separated into two articles until the Revised Statutes of 1925 were adopted. The original Act provided: "Article 4487. No Private seal or scroll shall be necessary to the validity of any contract, bond or conveyance, whether respecting real or personal property, or any other instrument of writing, whether official, judicial or private, except such as are made by corporations, nor shall the addition or omission of a seal or scroll in any way affect the force and effect of the same. "Article 4488. Every contract in writing hereafter made shall be held to import a consideration in the same manner and as fully as sealed instruments have heretofore done." 50 When the statutes were revised in 1925 these articles were thrown together as Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 27 and several provisions of the old articles were omitted. Nothing is left of the original 

Act so far as private corporations are concerned except the provision that, "No private seal or scroll shall be required in this state on any written instrument except such as are made by corporations." Even before the original Act was passed in 1858 the Texas courts had minimized the importance of the seal.51

However, in the noted case of Sanger v. Warren,52 the Supreme 

Court of Texas held that the common law rules of sealed instruments were still operative in Texas as to all instruments that had to be under seal at common law, and that the Legislature had merely dispensed with the necessity of placing a seal on the instrument if executed by an individual. In that case the court held that at common law a freehold estate in land must be conveyed by deed, and therefore held that an undisclosed principal could not be held liable on a deed conveying real estate, as at common law only those whose names appear on the sealed instrument could sue or be sued on the same. According to the old common law a corporation had to use its seal in every transaction except minor ones such as the appointment of a cook or butler.54 But as time wore on the reason given for the old rule seemed so foolish that the courts held that a corporation must use its seal only in the execution of deeds and bonds. The usual reason given for the old rule was that the corporation could speak only by and through its seal, as it had no mind or body. It should have occurred to the old judges that as it had no mind or body it certainly had no hand with which to place the seal on the instrument. Under the doctrine of Sanger v. Warren 55 Texas corporations are still required to place the seal on deeds conveying real estate.56 If the vendee has paid a valuable consideration for the land, the equitable title will pass to the vendee even though the secretary fails to impress the corporate seal on the instrument; and, therefore, a subsequent purchaser from the corporation with notice of the outstanding equitable title will take subject to the equitable title of the first vendee.57

Until the statutes were revised in 1925 62 the statute always provided, "that every contract in writing hereafter made shall be held to import a consideration in the same manner and as fully as sealed instruments have heretofore done." If this statute had been literally construed any promise in writing would have been enforceable even though not based on consideration, as a sealed instrument at common law needed no consideration; but our courts have always held that a promise in writing is unenforceable, aside from the doctrine of promissory estoppel, unless based on a valuable consideration. If 

Article 2010, Subdivision 10, had also been omitted from the Revised Statutes of 1925, it would now be necessary for the plaintiff to allege and prove that the written instrument that he sues upon is based upon consideration. But as this article was brought forward in the Revised Statutes of 1925, the Commission of Appeals held that the omission of the above provision of the statute did not change the Texas law. Therefore, the burden of alleging and proving consideration where the plaintiff sues on a written instrument is not upon the plaintiff, but is a defensive matter that the defendant must allege under oath and prove.63

By a recent Act of the Texas Legislature, the use of the seal by the corporation has been largely minimized.64 This Act provides: "Every instrument of writing which is permitted or required by law to be recorded in the office of the clerk of the County Court, and which has been so recorded, after being proved or acknowledged in the manner provided by the laws of this State in force at the time of its registration, or at the time it was proved or acknowledged, or every instrument which 

62. Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 27. 

63. Wright v. Robert & St. John Mo. tor Co., 58 S.W.2d 67, 122 Tex. 278.

has been * actually recorded for a period of 10 years in the book used by said clerk for the recording of such instruments, whether executed, proved or acknowledged in such manner or not, shall be admitted as evidence in any suit in this State without the necessity of proving its execution, provided, no claim adverse or inconsistent to the one evidenced by such instrument shall have been asserted during that 10 years. 

And after such instrument shall have been actually recorded as herein provided for a period of 10 years, it shall be no objection to the admission of same, or a certified copy thereof, as evidence that it has not been signed by the proper officer of any corporation; or that the corporate seal of the corporation has not been impressed on such instrument; or that the record does not show such corporate seal. It is very seldom that the defect in a conveyance is discovered within ten years after the deed is executed, and since the Act makes the conveyance valid after the instrument has been recorded for ten years even though the corporate seal has not been impressed on the instrument, very few innocent parties will be injured hereafter because of the failure of the secretary to impress the seal of the corporation on the instrument. When the great majority of the people in England could neither read nor write there may have been some justification for the use of the seal; but in modern times, after the board of directors has resolved to sell the land and the president has signed the corporate name to the deed of conveyance, there is no necessity for requiring the secretary to perform the meaningless act of impressing the seal on the instrument. To meet present day needs, the Legislature should amend Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 27 so that the corporation will no longer be excepted from that article. The above statute which partly relieves our citizens from the hardships of the common law rule was upheld in a recent decision by the Commission of Appeals.65

Therefore, the contract was binding on the company.84 A corporation organized to buy and sell cattle has the power to guarantee payment of an indebtedness due a bank from a firm as part of the price of the cattle bought by the corporation from such firm.85 The main business of a banking corporation is to lend money. Where the bank lends a depositor money and agrees to pay it to the depositor's creditor instead of to the borrower, the bank is liable to the creditor and such arrangement and contract are not ultra vires on the part of the bank, and is not a guaranty contract; but the agreement on the part of the bank to pay the amount to the borrower's creditor is merely incidental to the contract by which the bank agreed to make the loan to the depositor.86 

In collecting obligations due it, a corporation may take property other than cash money in payment of the debt; and if there is a mortgage or other lien against the property, it may agree to assume the payment of the debt secured by the lien. 

This is a reasonable method used by the individual very often in collecting debts due him, and this right has been extended to corporations.87 One Court of Civil Appeals held that where a realty company sold land to a hotel company for some of the stock of the latter company, it has implied authority to endorse notes of the hotel company where that was necessary to protect the credit of the hotel company. This is an extreme extension of the implied powers of a realty company. As a general rule, even an individual would soon find himself in the bankruptcy court if he went surety or a guarantor for all of his debtors, 88

In the last cited case the Deaton Grocery Company agreed to guarantee the payment of Turner's debt to the International Harvester Company, if the latter company would renew and extend the time of payment of Turner's debt. The International Harvester Company accepted the offer of the Deaton Grocery Company, and before the extended obligation became due Turner was thereby enabled to pay several thousand dollars of his indebtedness to the Deaton Grocery Company. As the Deaton Grocery Company received no direct benefit from the contract itself, the court, however, held that it was not liable on its guaranty. In the opinion the court said: "So it is contended on behalf of appellee that appellant derived a benefit from the contract of guaranty, because the making of it prevented a collapse in Turner's business earlier than it did occur, thereby enabling appellant, in part, to collect what Turner was owing it. After careful consideration we have reached the conclusion that if it be conceded, which however was not shown, that Turner was insolvent at the time that the contract of guaranty was made, and that by reason of appellee's extension of time on its debt, appellant collected more from Turner than it otherwise would, still the contract of guaranty was ultra vires, and is not binding upon appellant. merit in appellee's contention that appellant is estopped from denying its liability. If the doctrine of estoppel can be invoked to defeat a plea of ultra vires, such doctrine has no application to this case. Appellee is not in the attitude of an innocent purchaser or holder without notice. At the time that the contract of guaranty was made, the law charged it with notice of the fact that the Deaton Grocery Company had no power to make that contract, and that, for that reason, the contract was null and void. The Deaton Grocery Company received nothing from appellee or any one else as a consideration for making the contract, and therefore is not now withholding from appellee or any one else anything received by it upon the contract. For these reasons the facts fall short of what is necessary to constitute an estoppel."

The holding of the Deaton Grocery case has recently been affirmed by the Supreme Court of Texas. In L. G. Balfour Co. v. 

Gossett 5 the defendant company was chartered to manufacture, buy and sell badges and jewelry. The Supreme Court held that the corporation did not have authority to guarantee the debt of its regional manager even though by doing so the company would receive an indirect benefit in that the manager would be able to sell more goods of the defendant by reason of his extended credit. The Court said: "According to the undisputed evidence, Balfour's interest in Jones' transactions with the Bank, here involved, were, at best, indirect and remote. It was not primarily responsible for Jones' debt, absent a guaranty, and the only interest it had in the matter was that if Jones' business should prosper and be properly financed, Jones might sell more of its goods. Any benefit Balfour could have hoped to gain from the Bank extending credit to Jones would have been one 'not immediately, but immediately by reaction, as it were, from the success of the (Jones) operations, thus encouraged'.

It is also the law that it is not ordinarily necessary for the conduct of a corporation's business that it lend its credit to another corporation, or to an individual. In this connection, it is the law of this state that, in the absence of ex-

In exercising its corporate powers, a corporation may foster its business by the usual means exercised by corporations of its character; but it cannot go beyond this." "

Where the corporation received a direct benefit from the contract itself, the courts of Texas will enforce the contract although it is ultra vires." Therefore, even though it is ultra vires for a manufacturing company to lend money, if it actually lends money to the defendant, the corporation may recover on the debt since the defendant received an actual benefit from the ultra vires contract itself. If the corporation is permitted under the facts of the case to escape liability on the plea of ultra vires, the sureties are liable if the contract is not illegal.⁹

Federal Glass & Paint Co.,28 where it was said: "It is the law that a corporation, unless its charter authorizes it to do so, may not enter into a partnership.

Some of the authorities refer to them as 'joint adventurers,' and the liability arising from such relationship as that of persons engaged in a joint enterprise.'" The rights of the parties engaged in such an enterprise (and those dealing with them as to past transactions) are settled on practically the same basis as if they had been partners. § 78. Trustee, Receiver, Executor, Administrator, Guardian or

Agent Private corporations may be created to act as trustee,35 receiver,36 executor,37 administrator,38 guardian 39 or agent.40 The constitutionality of such statutes has been upheld.11 Before the enactment of these statutes the power of a private corporation to act as a trustee was recognized in Bell County v. Alexander.42 

Chief Justice Wheeler said that public corporations had the same power to hold property in trust as private corporations and copied with approval the following from Judge Story's opinion in Vidal v. Girard Ex'rs.: 43 "Although it was, in early times, held that a corporation could not take and hold real or personal estate in trust, upon the ground that there was defect of one of the requisites to create a good trustee; viz., the want of confidence in the person; yet that doctrine has been long since exploded as unsound, and too artificial; and it is now held, that where the corporation has a legal capacity to take real or personal estate, it may take and hold it upon trust, in the same manner and to the same extent, as a private person may do. It is true that, if the trust be repugnant to, or inconsistent with the proper purposes for which the corporation was created, that may furnish a ground why it may not be compelled to execute it. But that will furnish no ground to declare the trust itself void, if otherwise unexceptionable, but it will simply require a new trustee to be substituted by the proper court possessing equity jurisdiction, to enforce and perfect the objects of the trust." But the courts which have most distinctly announced and upheld this doctrine have most definitely held to and rigidly enforced the collateral principle that a corporation cannot become such purchaser when it results in a fraud upon the rights of or injury or loss to the creditors of the corporation. * * The danger of fraud being perpetrated upon or of injury and loss resulting to creditors was one of the patent reasons moving the courts of England to establish and adhere to the rule that a corporation cannot become the purchaser of its own shares of stock. 

In view of the contrary doctrine obtaining in most of the courts of this country, the safety of the creditors of a corporation lies in the recognition and enforcement of the collateral principle above set forth. Were it not for the existence of this principle, creditors of corporations would occupy a most hazardous and perilous position." "Courts, we believe, should, however, be slow to approve a transaction which gives to one, who has received pay for his services in stock, if he finds the stock has little or no value, the right later to change his position from that of a stockholder to that of a mortgage creditor to the prejudice of ordinary creditors and other stockholders." 64

This rule is enforced, even though the rights of present creditors all arose subsequent to the purchase, if they did not have notice that the corporation was insolvent at the time.65 Where stockholders have been given the right to withdraw, they will not be allowed to do so if the rights of the creditors will be impaired, since this really amounts to a purchase by the corporation of its own stock.66

The American courts are in conflict upon the proper meaning to be given the word "insolvent," as used in this connection. 

Perhaps a majority of the courts regard the corporation as solvent and the purchase lawful if the assets exceed the liabilities, excluding the capital stock as a liability.67 Others, following what would seem to be the better rule, declare that the corporation is solvent only if it has a real surplus; i. e., if its assets exceed the sum of its liabilities including its capital stock.68 This latter view is the better rule since clear assets equal to the capital stock should always be kept intact for the creditors of the company. In some states the purchase is improper if at the time of the purchase the corporation is insolvent in the sense that it does not have assets equal to its liabilities without putting the amount of its capital stock on the liability side of the balance sheet, or if the purchase threatened its insolvency in the above sense.69

The Texas law on this point is uncertain. There are intimations in some of the Texas cases to the effect that the Texas courts follow the former view.70 It is generally held that

the proper time to gauge the solvency of a corporation for this purpose is at the instance when payment for the stock is to be made. Consequently, a corporation, solvent at the time of giving a note for stock, but insolvent at the maturity date of the note, must apply all of its assets to the satisfaction of non-stockholder creditors before any payment on the note may be made."¹

And it would seem equally clear that even though the corporation is solvent and has a surplus when the note matures, if the note is extended, and the company is not able to pay all of its obligations when the stockholder finally demands payment, he should not share pari passu with other creditors, but only secondary to the rights of other non-stockholder creditors. Even though when the corporation buys its own stock it is entirely solvent, a court of equity will imply a condition in law to the effect that the stockholder-creditor will not be allowed to take from the corporate assets until all other creditors are paid in full. Equity and fair dealings are the bases of conditions implied in law. It would be the height of injustice to permit a stockholder to take from that fund that should always be kept intact for creditors. Even though the company is solvent at the maturity of the note that was given to the shareholder for his stock, very often he is induced to extend the note because the company has no liquid assets and he is still willing to give further credit to the company. To say that in such case the stockholder-creditor should share equally with other creditors of the same class because the note was conditional on the company's being solvent when the note matured is begging the question. 

The question is, should a shareholder-creditor ever be allowed to injure outside creditors? The sales agreement did not contain an express condition. Therefore, the only question that could arise is whether the court will imply a condition in law or in hachie Grain & Implement Co., 35

fact. Justice demands that the corporation should keep the safety fund inviolate for outside creditors. The court should, therefore, imply a condition that a shareholder-creditor should not compete with outside creditors in the fund that the stockholders agreed to keep intact for creditors for their privilege to conduct a business without personal liability. This is the way the courts should look at this problem, even though the claims of the outside creditors arose after the stockholder resold his stock to the company, unless the stock purchased by the corporation has again been sold for par.72 If the stock is sold for less than par, the stockholder-creditor should be permitted to share pari passu with outside creditors only for the amount received by the corporation for the stock, even though the company agreed to give him above par for his stock, for, only to that extent, has the safety fund been replenished.73 If the note is actually in good faith paid, and the stockholder subsequently lends the money to the corporation, he thereby becomes an outside creditor, and if the company subsequently becomes insolvent he would share equally with such creditors. These rules do not apply where a stockholder, in good faith and at a time when the corporation appeared to be solvent, lends money to the corporation for the purpose of buying the stock of the managing stockholder who is mis-managing the business.74

is adopted, the courts hold that the corporation can redeem its stock "if solvent" at the redemption date; and many courts that adopt that position declare that the corporation "is solvent" if its assets equal or exceed its liabilities without putting the amount of the capital stock on the liability side of the ledger. 

Under such a rule the safety fund which should be kept sacred for creditors is dissipated. The same result is ultimately reached even if the court holds that the stock can be redeemed or repurchased only out of surplus, as the stock may never be resold and future dividends will be declared when the books show a surplus. This surplus is shown by placing on the liability side the original capital stock of $100,000 less treasury stock of $90,- 000. In other words, the corporation advertises that it has a capital stock of $100,000. Yet it declares a $2,000 dividend, if outside creditors have been paid and its assets amount to $12,- 000 where it has repurchased $90,000 of the original capital of $100,000. Should this be permitted? Did the Legislature intend to empower the company thus to absorb itself and thereby deceive the innocent creditors? When some of the arguments that are made in favor of the above rule are considered, one realizes how weak and inconsequential they are. For instance, in some of the cases including the Texas case of Sanger v. San Antonio

Hardware Co.,80 the judges give as a reason for the above rule that a corporation should be permitted to get rid of an objectionable stockholder. It has always seemed to the writer that the . corporation should not be permitted to purchase the stock of a shareholder merely because he is objectionable to some of the stockholders, but that they personally should buy the stock of the objectionable party if they believe his ownership of the stock is inimical to the best interest of the corporation. But as the above rule has been announced, in so many cases, it is now possibly too late for the courts to face about and thereby get on firmer ground.

It is often said that the directors have power to repurchase the stock of the corporation out of surplus. There can be no 

80. Tex.Civ.App., 151 S.W. 1104, 13 Tex.L.Rev. 442. writ of error refused. 284

surplus unless the corporation has some assets above all of its liabilities, including the amount of its capital stock. Many courts have given as a reason for the above rule that where there is a surplus on hand, it is discretionary with the directors as to whether they pay out this surplus in dividends or repurchase some of the stock of the corporation.81 If a dividend is declared out of surplus, all stockholders share equally in the distributed fund in proportion to the amount owned by each shareholder. 

However, if the directors elect to use the surplus in repurchasing the stock of some of the stockholders, and the company becomes insolvent soon thereafter, those who were fortunate enough to induce the directors to repurchase their stock may receive one hundred cents on the dollar of their invested capital, whereas the other stockholders may not receive one cent on the dollar. Even if the purpose clause in the charter gives the corporation authority "to sell goods, wares and merchandise" the members of the Texas Legislature surely never imagined that the directors would ever contend that the shares of stock of the corporation are either "goods, wares or merchandise." 

As the rule of law which enables the corporation to repurchase its own stock has occasioned such conflict in the authorities, as it is so difficult to determine the meaning of "insolvency" when a court decrees a "solvent corporation" can re-purchase its own stock, as it causes such confusion where there is a conflict between stockholder-creditors and outside creditors, as quite often it causes injustice to some shareholders, and especially as no one has ever advanced a compelling, or even a valid reason, for the rule, would it not be well for the Supreme Court of Texas to follow the suggestion of Judge Critz in the case of Woods v. Wichita Falls Building & Loan Ass'n 82 to its logical conclusion, and hold that a corporation can never repurchase its own stock? 

Would it not be wise for our Court to say that the only way a Texas corporation can reduce its stock is to comply with Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1332?

82. 96 S.W.2d 64, 128 Tex. 1.

never squarely decided the point, and is therefore free to follow the celebrated English case of Trevor v. Whitworth.83 That case holds that an English corporation does not have implied authority to repurchase its own stock. The court gave two reasons for its holding. They are so forcibly stated in the opinion that they are in part reproduced. They should be compared with the opinion of Justice Fly in the Sanger-San Antonio Hardware case: "The creditors of the company which is being wound up, who have a right to look to the paid-up capital as the fund out of which their debts are to be discharged, find coming into competition with them persons who, in respect only of their having been, and having ceased to be, shareholders in the company, claim that the company shall pay to them a part of that capital.

The capital may, no doubt, be diminished by expenditure upon and reasonably incidental to all the objects specified. A part of it may be lost in carrying on the business operations authorized. Of this all persons trusting the company are aware, and take the risk. But I think they have a right to rely, and were intended by the Legislature to have a right to rely, on the capital remaining undiminished by any expenditure outside these limits, or by the return of any part of it to the shareholders. 

If the claim under consideration can be supported, the result would seem to be this, that the whole of the shareholders, with the exception of those holding seven individual shares, might now be claiming payment of the sums paid upon their shares as against the creditors, who had a right to look to the moneys subscribed as the source out of which the company's liabilities to them were to be met. And the stringent precautions to prevent the reduction of the capital of a limited company, without due notice and judicial sanction, would be idle if the company might purchase its own shares wholesale, and so effect the desired result. I do not think it was disputed that a company could not enter upon such a transaction for the purpose of reducing its capital, but it was suggested that it might do so if that were not the object, but it was considered for some other reason desirable in the interest of the company to do so. To the 

83. L.R. 12 A.C. 409 (1887). 286

creditor, whose interests, I think, §§ 8 and 12 of the Companies Act were intended to protect, it makes no difference what the object of the purchase is. The result to him is the same. The shareholders receive back the money subscribed, and there passes into their pockets what before existed in the form of cash in the coffers of the company, or of buildings, machinery, or stock available to meet the demands of the creditors. "What was the reason which induced the company in the present case to purchase its shares? If it was that they might sell them again, this would be a trafficking in the shares, and clearly unauthorized. If it was to retain them, this would be to my mind an indirect method of reducing the capital of the company. * No doubt if certain shareholders are disposed to hamper the proceedings of the company, and are willing to sell their shares, they may be bought out; but this must be done by persons, existing shareholders or others, who can be induced to purchase the shares, and not out of the funds of the company. " 84 Two recent important cases have thrown some doubt on whether the law as stated by Judge Fly in the San Antonio 

Hardware-Sanger case is correct. In West Texas Utilities Co. v. 

Ellis, 85 the Supreme Court of Texas held that a contract to repurchase non-par stock is unenforceable. Vernon's Ann.Civ.

St. art. 1538a provides that: "Every such share shall be equal in all respects to every other such share, except that the charter or any amendment thereof may provide that such shares should be divided into different classes, the shares of each class to have such preferences, designations, rights, privileges and powers and be subject to such restrictions, limitations and qualifications as shall be stated in the charter or any amendment thereof." 

84. See, 43 Harv.L.Rev. 830; 29 

Col.L.Rev. 1152; 18 Harv.L.Rev. 

531; The Manor, 4 Br.R.C. 500; 

Cross v. Beguelin, 169 N.E. 378, 252 

N.Y. 262; Whaley v. King, 206 S.

259; Fuchs v. Meyer, 227 N.W. 265, 200 Wis. 103; Copper Belle Mining

85. 126 S.W.2d 13, 133 Tex. 104.

18 Tex.L.Rev. 67. 287

The Court held that in view of the above provisions of the "non-par" statute, the company could not repurchase part of the stock of any series. Whether the corporation could purchase all of the stock of a definite series was not determined by the 

Court. Judge Hickman stated: "To our minds the meaning of those provisions is clear. It is that a corporation may, by its charter or any amendment thereof, provide for the issuance of more than one class of non-par stock, but all shares of a given class must have the same preferences, designations, rights, privileges and powers and be subject to the same restrictions, limitations and qualifications as all other shares of the same class, and these rights, privileges, etc., shall be such as are stated in the charter or in an amendment thereof. All shares of the same class must be equal in all respects, and the rights and privileges attaching to each, as well as the restrictions and limitations, must appear in the charter or in an amendment thereof. The rights and privileges running with a share of stock are those and those only which the charter or some amendment thereof may attach to it."

The court stated definitely that all the rights of the owner of non-par stock must be "stated in the charter" of the company. 

On this point the Court said: "In providing for its issuance (nonpar stock) and sale the statutes have prescribed a method whereby a purchaser may know exactly what are his rights and privileges as owner." The court also held that no agent of a corporation could be given authority even by the directors to repurchase non-par stock unless such right was specifically stated in the charter since the owner of such stock has only such rights as are mentioned in the charter; that even the corporation has no power to repurchase its non-par stock where the company has issued two or more series of such stock. On this point the 

Court said: "He (the agent) was not impliedly or apparently authorized to change the law. The statutes point out to the purchaser the place to go to determine what rights and privileges attach to his stock, and leave no room for implications. 

If the charter does not grant the right to redeem (to repurchase), the agent has no authority to do so." The Court did not dis- 288

cuss whether the facts showed that the directors had given the agent authority to repurchase the stock of Mrs. Ellis. From the opinion of the Court of Civil Appeals, it seems evident that the directors had given the agent authority to repurchase the stock or ratified the contract of repurchase. But as the Supreme Court held that the corporation did not have such power unless the charter conferred such right on the owner of the stock, it was not necessary for the court to discuss the facts on this issue. 

If the Court properly construed the meaning of Vernon's Ann. 

Civ.St. art. 1538a the owner of non-par stock issued in series would not have the right to vote, receive dividends, to inspect the books of the company, to sell his stock to an outsider or any other right incident to the ownership of the stock, such as the pre-emptive right or the right to transfer his stock to the corporation in payment of a debt due by him to the corporation unless these rights were "stated in the charter" of the company. Surely the Legislature never intended such a result. The above statute in no way attempts to define the rights of the owner of non-par stock. It merely provides for a differentiation between the different series of the stock. It provides that where "the shares are divided into different classes, the shares of each class to have (shall have) such preferences, designations, rights, privileges and powers and be subject to such restrictions, limitations and qualifications (over the other classes) as shall be stated in the charter." Nowhere in the statute is it provided that the owner shall have only such "rights" as are "stated in the charter." Clearly the evident purpose of the statute is to force the lawyer to set forth clearly in the charter of the company the differences between "each class" of the non-par stock. The subject matter of the article is "different classes" and not "the rights of the owners of non-par stock."

The statute does not attempt to define all the incidents of ownership of non-par stock, but merely provides that if the stock is

tions" between the different series shall be stated in the charter. The New Jersey statute is very similar to the Texas statute. It was construed in the case of Lloyd v. Pennsylvania Electric Vehicle Co.89

The corporation organized under the New Jersey Act provided in its charter for the creation of preferred stock "the holders thereof to receive, and the company to pay, a fixed yearly dividend of 6 per cent before any dividends shall be set apart or paid on the general stock." Upon the dissolution of the corporation the preferred stockholders claimed that they were preferred not only as to dividends but also as to the par value of their stock. The statute provided that two or more classes of stock could be issued "with such designations, preferences, and voting powers, or restrictions or qualifications thereof, as shall be stated or expressed in the certificate of incorporation." The court held that the preferred stockholders were not preferred as to the assets on hand upon dissolution since all stockholders are presumed to be equal with the exception of the variations set forth in the charter. This significant statement is made in the opinion: "It is true, as was forcibly argued on behalf of the respondents, that it can hardly be that all of the rights of preferred stockholders need be set forth in the certificate of organization, but this fact does not require that we should hold that the certificate of organization cannot limit such rights."

This quotation properly construes the meaning of the above statute and should have been followed in the Ellis case. Not one authority is cited by the Texas Supreme Court for its holdstates, there is statutory authority for the allotment of shares in series, the permissible variations between the different series to be fixed in the articles or determined by the directors under authority contained in the articles. * Under these statutes, all shares of the same class must be identical, except that there may be variations between the different series of a class as to the following rights and preferences."

ing, and as it put such a peculiar and unnatural construction on the Texas statute, the Ellis case will not be followed in the other American jurisdictions having similar statutes. If the case is not overruled in the immediate future, the charter of every Texas corporation which provides for the issuance of two or more series of non-par stock should be amended since under the Ellis holding such stockholders have only those rights that are named or "stated in the charter." Obviously no Texas lawyer when he prepared the charter of such a corporation anticipated the holding of the Ellis case, and, therefore, did not devote three or four pages of the charter to a description of all the rights of the holders of non-par stock. Very few lawyers would attempt such a task. It would practically be impossible to prepare such a document without omitting some of the rights of the owner of such stock. 

The Court evidently overlooked Article 15387 of the Texas non-par statute, Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 15381. In specific and unambiguous terms that article shows clearly that the Legislature did not mean to provide by Article 1538a that all of the rights of the stockholder must be set out in the charter when the shares are divided into two or more series. That article provides: "The privileges and powers conferred by this chapter shall be deemed to be in addition to any and all powers and authority conferred by any other law or laws, and not in restriction or limitation of any of the powers now permitted to corporations of this State." 

The opinion of the Court of Civil Appeals is much better than that of the Supreme Court of Texas in the Ellis case unless the Supreme Court meant to decide only one question—that a Texas corporation does not have implied authority to purchase its own stock. That is the law in England, and the writer has always favored that holding. But the Ellis case does not discuss that rule of law and the opinion is based entirely on the meaning of Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1538a.

§ 80. Power to Take and Hold Stock on Other Corporations 

In the absence of express or implied authorization most courts hold that a corporation cannot subscribe to or purchase shares of stock in another corporation. The power will, however, be implied if such acquisition is a reasonable or necessary means of effectuating the corporate object.94 A mere benefit to the purchaser does not make the purchase lawful.95

There are several well defined exceptions to the rule that a corporation cannot purchase stock in other companies. The corporation may take all kinds of property, including stock, in satisfaction of a debt, or as collateral security for an existing debt. Similarly a corporation may take such stock in satisfaction of a disputed claim provided the transaction is bona fide.8 

A further exception exists in that a corporation may, with the consent of its stockholders, sell its entire property to another company and receive in payment stock of the latter company, when such sale is made for the purpose of winding up the corporate affairs. These exceptions are not all inclusive. 

§ 81. Lease 

Every private corporation is authorized to own such property as is necessary to effectuate the purposes for which it was incorporated.10 As an incident of ownership, a corporation may lease its property, if doing so will promote the corporate enterprise. § 82. Borrow Money and Give Security 

Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1321, provides: "Corporations may borrow money on the credit of the corporation and may execute bonds or promissory notes therefor and may pledge the property and income of the corporation." 

Power is given to mortgage the corporate property when required to accomplish the purposes for which the corporation was formed.23

These statutes confer broad borrowing powers on a private corporation. Formerly the power of a corporation to borrow money was limited to an amount not exceeding its authorized capital stock.24 Even then, notes given for a loan in excess of this amount were valid up to the amount of the indebtedness that did not exceed the "capital stock." 25 In order for a corporation to escape liability on notes executed by it, evidence must be given showing that they were not issued in the transaction of the corporation's authorized business.26 The execution of new notes for an existing indebtedness is not the creation of a new debt in violation of an agreement between the stockholders that

The right to mortgage the corporate assets includes also the giving of notes, secured by a mortgage for an existing debt.34 Thus a corporation may mortgage improvements placed at a mill site, that the corporation had leased, where the corporation retained the right to remove any improvements made.35

The same rule is applied to bonds as is applied to notes; namely, bonds can only be issued to carry out the purposes of incorporation.36 Thus a corporation may not issue bonds to secure money for the benefit of another corporation.37 While it is well established that a corporation should not issue stock except where it is sold for its par value,38 it has been held that corporate bonds may be sold for less than par.39 Judge Gaines in North Side Ry. Co. v. The decisions of the courts upon like provisions in the constitutions of other states have been such as in most cases to practically destroy its effect. It may be that it was not intended to prohibit corporations from selling their bonds below par, provided the transaction be made in good faith.

One method, frequently adopted by corporations, to effect the sale of their bonds is to secure the issue by a trust agreement wherein a trustee is named to represent the bondholders.52 A stipulation in such agreement is valid which provides that in the event of default the trustee is authorized, and upon request of the holders of the majority of the bonds, the trustee is under the duty to foreclose, but that no bondholder shall foreclose or enforce any right under the mortgage until the trustee or his successor should wrongfully refuse such request to foreclose.53 

In the case cited in the last note the court said: "In the absence of a refusal by the trustee to bring suit, and in the absence of fraud which is not charged, appellant, as a minority bondholder, had no standing in court, since the right to foreclose under the terms of the mortgage existed only in favor of the trustee. The right of a minority bondholder to foreclose under the facts alleged was withheld and denied by the provisions of the mortgage. It is well settled that those provisions conferred a valuable right on the majority bondholders which a minority bondholder in the absence of fraud could not destroy or impair by bringing suit." 54 However, before 1931, a provision giving the trustee exclusive right to enforce the security is illegal as such a provision is against public policy.55 By such a provision the jurisdiction of the court is not ousted, and an individual bondholder may bring suit to protect his rights.56 How-

the appellant are mostly cases where a corporation has contracted with parties on a valid consideration, and where a conveyance has been made, and then it is sought to raise the question as to the power of a corporation to take or convey title; and it has been held that in such cases of an executed contract, if the corporation has violated the statute, the party seeking to set up such violation would not be heard, and in such case none but the State would. That one who contracts with a corporation shall not, under such circumstances, be heard to raise the question, is, in substance, the principle decided.' And in the same case the learned judge states the rule applicable to cases like the one under consideration in the following language: 'In the case of a devise, however, the case is essentially different. 

The will does not take effect until the testator's death; and then, if his property is not legally devised or bequeathed, no title vests for a single moment in the devisee or legatee, but it vests instantly in the heir or next of kin; and the corporation claiming under the will asks the aid of the law to give the property to it, and in so doing it must show the authority it has to take. And if there were only a prohibition in words against holding the property, would the law not be doing a vain thing in handing it over to the corporation, which, by the very fact of holding, would render itself liable to have its charter forfeited on that account? Would not the prohibition against holding be properly and necessarily construed as a prohibition against taking also?' "Whether the distinction made by the courts between the effect of a purchase by and a devise to a corporation or person incapacitated to take the property be sound or not, it is well established by the authorities, and we think the rule as to devises is founded on sound principles. "If one dying testate devises to an alien lands which by the law of the State where it lies, the devisee cannot take under the will, the devise will be disregarded to that extent, and the property will go to the residuary legatee or next of kin who is capacitated to take it. (Hardy v. De Leon, 5 Texas 211; Orr v. 

Hodgson, 4 Wheat 453, 4 L.Ed. 613). This class of cases is 310

represented by Orr v. Hodgson, the leading case on the subject, which by analogy strongly supports the conclusion reached in this case. "Under the rule applied to purchase by an alien or corporation incapacitated to hold land, the vendor who has for a valuable consideration conveyed the property to such alien or corporation is estopped to deny the capacity of his vendee to take the title. The State alone can question such a title. But the doctrine of estoppel does not apply to a testator, and if the devisee named in a will has not the capacity to take the property the devise will be void and the law will vest the title in the heir." 

The reason for the difference between a conveyance inter vivos and a devise of land to a corporation stated in the House of Mercy-Davidson case is more legalistic than realistic. When the probate court is requested to probate the will, the legality of devises or bequests set out in the will, is not determined. The only question before the court is whether the will was properly executed by a competent person. Therefore, the devisee is not asking the affirmative assistance of the court as is so often stated by courts that follow the Texas holding on this rule of law. There is a conflict in the authorities. Some courts apply the same rule to devises as they do to conveyances inter vivos.80

that there is a very narrow difference, if there be any, between selecting this institution and selecting any other suitable trustee for the execution of the trusts committed to it, such a corporation as this being merely a technical and metaphysical entity through which the benefit of the trusts were to go to poor persons suffering from certain diseases; that the heirs could have no voice or interest in the matter, unless accidentally so through the innocent mistake of the testator, they having no lien on the estate of either a legal or moral kind; that there are no words in the charter of the corporation, or in the statute authorizing its organization, that forbid its holding more than the amount limited by the statute, nor any penalties attached whereby to punish any transgression of the limitation, the only punishment intended being the risk of a forfeiture of the bequests, or of the charter; that the limitation is chiefly directory and regulative, and, if impliedly prohibitory, incidentally and mildly so; that the charter is a contract between the corporation and the state in which no person is legally interested but the parties thereto, the same general rules of interpretation applying as in other contracts; that if the corporation fails to keep its side of the contract the state can take advantage of the default or not as it pleases; that the transgression may be so slight in its consequences that the state will forgive the offense, or forgive it because occasioned by some accident or error resulting while the corporation is acting in good faith, or the state may, acting through its prosecuting officers, punish the offense for the public good; that the state may by its legislature authorize the corporation to increase its capital before the act is done, or, if the increase be made without authority, may ratify the act afterward either by some legislative provision, or, as may be done between any other contracting parties, by its silence and any other acts indicating consent; that from the foregoing propositions it is clearly deducible that bequests like the present are voidable only, and may be avoided by the state alone, and are in no sense to be re garded as void; that a policy arose as to what better be done in the circumstances of each particular case, and that that policy belongs to the state and not to the court and is an executive and not a judicial right, for the court would decide the question in the case for all cases and all time, while the state may decide the question differently at different times according to its discretion and the public good. This right the state has never surrendered and the court can not take it from the state. But it would surely deprive the state of its privilege if the court fails to act upon these bequests as valid bequests until, in proper and independent proceedings, such bequests are declared to be void."

The Attorney General, or any district or county attorney, when either of them has reason to believe that any corporation is holding lands in violation of this law, shall institute suit in the name of the State of Texas, in Travis County, or in any county in Texas where such corporation may have an agent, or in any county where any part of the land may be situated, against such corporation, as if provided for the escheat of estates of deceased persons dying without devise thereof and having no heirs." 

Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1365, provides: "If it be determined upon the trial of said suit that lands are held contrary to this law, the court trying said cause shall enter judgment condemning such lands and ordering them to be sold as under execution, the proceeds of such sale to be first applied to the payment of costs of such suit, and the balance to be paid into the State Treasury subject to be paid to the stockholders, or persons entitled to receive the same as owners, upon proper proof made within twelve months from date of sale. If the legal representatives of such corporation fail to claim the said balance of money realized on sale of said land, then it shall escheat to the State and be applied to the available school fund. The court trying said cause shall allow the attorney representing the State a reasonable fee, to be taxed as cost in the suit. In no case shall the State be liable for costs or fees unless it is successful in said suit." 

In view of these articles, a stockholder may not have a receiver appointed because the corporation is holding land for which the state may institute forfeiture proceedings,81 as such action would not preclude the state from instituting forfeiture proceedings. Since the proceeds of the sale of the land is given to the stockholders, the penalty provided for by the statute is not onerous.

If a corporation is authorized to buy and sell land, its general manager has authority to make a contract for the sale of the land even though the title was conveyed to another as trustee for the corporation.82

Personal Property 

Every corporation has the capacity and power to take and hold personal property for the purposes consistent with the legitimate objects of its incorporation.83 This includes the acquisition of choses in action such as promissory notes, bills of exchange, and checks. A corporation may acquire patents 85 and contract rights 86 useful to the successful operation of its business. Even though the corporation intends to use the property in an ultra vires transaction, this may not be asserted as a defense in an action for the purchase price of the goods.87 A bank is empowered to take cattle to secure the payment of a debt due it.88 A cotton seed oil mill corporation may not buy baled cotton 89 or cotton seed 90 for speculation. A gin company may take cotton seed in payment of ginning charges.91 

Also, a gin company has the implied power to purchase planting seed to be sold to the farmers in that vicinity.92 An elevator company has authority to sell "seed wheat." 93 Since a country

In Hollis Cotton Oil, Light & Ice Co. v. Marrs & Lake,95 a corporation authorized to operate and maintain cotton seed oil mills and to sell cotton seed and any and all products and byproducts, was held to have the power to purchase four hundred bulls to be fattened on hulls for which no market could be found. The Court of Civil Appeals based their holding on Muñoz v. Brassel,⁹ saying: "In Munoz v. Brassel, 108 S.W. 417, by the Court of Civil Appeals for the Fourth District, writ denied, it was held that a corporation whose charter provided that its principal business 'shall be buying and selling liquors, etc., at wholesale and retail,' has implied power to sign a saloonkeeper's bond as surety, though no express or implied contract existed between them that he would purchase liquors of the corporation, since becoming surety for a possible customer is a proper and usual means of promoting its business.

Mitchell v. In holding the contract to be ultra vires, the court said: it may be that it could have effected a sale thereof in no other way than by doing the work specified in the contract. But this, we think, would not be a sufficient reason for holding its undertaking to do such work to be within its charter powers.

The testimony indicated that the work it undertook to do was worth about as much as the material it was to use in doing it. The work and material together was worth, according to the testimony of a witness, about $3,800. So, to 66 #
