support the contract as one the building stone company had power to make, it would be necessary to hold that its undertaking to do about $1,900 worth of work was an incident merely to the sale by it of about $1,900 worth of material. Such a holding, it seems to us, would not be reasonable. It would be only a little short of saying that the building stone company could bind itself to do any and everything which, directly or indirectly, would result in a sale of material it was authorized to deal in. 'It cannot be said,' the court remarked, in Safety 

Insulated Wire & Cable Co. v. Baltimore, C.C.A.Md., 74 F. 363, 372, 20 C.C.A. 453, 'that anything which will promote a demand for goods manufactured under the charter is within the incidental powers of the corporation. Were this true, a corporation organized for the business of quarrying rock could contract for the erection of a costly building, in the construction of which its rock would be used. A corporation organized for the manufacture of terra cotta pipes could contract for the sewerage of a large city.' Not only would such a view require us to ignore the general policy of the law (Ramsey v. Tod, 95 Tex. 614, 69 

S.W. 133, 93 Am.St.Rep. 875) forbidding the creation in this state of a corporation for more than one purpose, and forbidding the exercise by a corporation of other powers than those conferred upon it in its creation, but it also would require us to set at naught the right of the holders of the stock of the corporation to have the use of its capital limited to the purpose of its creation. It would have justified the building stone company had it ignored the protest made by one of its stockholders against its proceeding further with its undertaking to do the work specified in its contract, and it would have permitted the building stone company, in the face of such protest, to hazard its capital in an enterprise involving risks never contemplated by its stockholders, as, for instance, risks of liability for damages for personal injuries which might be suffered by its employes while engaged in the work, damages for faulty construction of or delay in the completion of the walls, etc., of the building. Such a view of the law clearly, we think, is not maintainable, and we hold that the undertaking of the building stone company was not incidental to the purpose of its incorporation as reasonably 317

§ Ch. 3 

necessary to enable it to accomplish that purpose. Safety Insulated Wire & Cable Co. v. Baltimore, C.C.A.Md., 74 F. 363, 367, 20 C.C.A. 453; Davis v. Old Colony R. Co., 131 Mass. 258, 41 

Am.Rep. 221; North Side R. Co. v. Worthington, 88 Tex. 562, 563, 30 S.W. 1055, 53 Am.St. 778." A corporation engaging in such an enterprise is inviting its own destruction for it jeopardizes a substantial amount of money in a transaction foreign to the purposes of its organization and from which the benefit to be derived is only incidental.

Upon principle the two cases are in conflict. The ratio between the money to be spent by the corporation and the value of the product to be utilized is more favorable to the corporation in the Building Stone case than in the Hollis Cotton Oil case. Normally, the hazards of erecting a foundation for such a building are not as great as buying cattle to be fed for the market. The Building Stone case is fortified by Bowman Lumber Co. v. Pierson,¹ where the Supreme Court held that a lumber company was not empowered to guarantee the performance of a building contract, although by doing so the company could sell the materials to be used in its erection. For these reasons, since the opinion of the Court of Civil Appeals in the Hollis Cotton Oil case was based on the Munoz decision, and the latter case was overruled by the Supreme Court of Texas in the Bowman Lumber case, the opinion in the Hollis Cotton Oil case no longer correctly states the law of Texas. §

Power to Dispose of Property Not Needed for Its Busi ness

A corporation has authority to dispose of surplus property that it owns. As we have seen in § 81 in this chapter a corporation can rent its surplus property especially if the surplus is occasioned by a dull season during some months of the year; and a corporation may lease part of its office building not needed for its present uses. But no rule of law must be bent too far or pressed to its brink. That is especially true of the point under consideration. In a fairly recent Missouri case it was held that a lumber company was authorized to make a contract to do work with dredges which it had no more use for and which it could not readily dispose of without serious loss.13 However, five years before the above decision, the Supreme Court of Minnesota held that an automobile finance corporation did not have authority to do construction work on a state road which required the use of more trucks than the company had retaken from vendees who failed to pay the purchase price, and more trained truck drivers than it had in its employment.¹4 

A corporation that has more land than it needs for its business, as where it has abandoned its old location for a new one, has authority to do what a reasonable prudent business man would do to dispose of the property. Therefore, if the land could

Any company that has implied authority to install plants reasonably necessary for the conduct of its business, such as electric, steam or water systems, is not limited to the installation of a plant that is adequate for present needs only, but may anticipate future expansion of the business and install machinery reasonably adequate to care for the future needs of the corporation's business. In the mean time the corporation has implied authority to sell its surplus products.16

It had been recorded for about a quarter of a century, and recites that it was executed by the officers of the company under its corporate seal. The officer who recorded the original could not transfer the seal to the record. The conclusion and attestation clause recite that the instrument is under seal of the corporation. The law required such instrument to be under seal, and it was contrary to the duty of the officer to take the acknowledgments of the officers of the company unless the corporate seal was affixed. It was contrary to the duty of the recording officer to record the instrument unless it was sealed. These things considered in connection with the fact that the stockholders of the corporation are making no objection to the validity of the deed, afford a strong presumption that the instrument was sealed. (Coffey v. 

Hendricks, 66 Tex. 676, 2 S.W. 47; 

Starkweather v. Martin, 28 Mich. 471.)"

Restrictions on Powers of Disposal in General 

At common law the power to dispose of property in general did not include the power to sell the corporate existence or franchise. "Nor will a judicial sale or sale under execution of the property of the corporation carry with it to the purchaser the right to be a corporate body." 52 The Texas statute conferring the power to "sell, mortgage or otherwise convey," confers the power to dispose of its franchises, and this includes the power to mortgage,53 but it cannot mortgage or sell its "franchise" to exist as a corporation. Thus a corporation to which a franchise has been given to construct water or gas pipes in the streets of a city and sell water or gas to the inhabitants of the city, may sell or mortgage such franchise, but its right to exist as a corporation cannot be mortgaged or sold. In other words, the corporation still exists as a person after all its property is sold under execution or a deed of trust.5 54

There have always existed certain restrictions on the power of corporations to dispose of their property. At common law, 50. Long Bell Lumber Co. v. Hamp ton, Tex.Civ.App., 20 S.W.2d 1081;

§ 91. Power to Practice Law or Medicine 

By statute in Texas a corporation is denied the right to practice law with few exceptions specifically set forth in the statute.“⁹ 

One of the Courts of Civil Appeals held that a corporation cannot practice law indirectly by employing lawyers to practice for it.70

That rule of law is sustained by the great weight of authority under statutes similar to Vernon's Ann.Pen.Code art. 430a.71

yers of its own selection, the insureds or assureds in policies issued in accordance with the terms of such policies."

§ 92. Capacity of a Corporation to Make Contracts While in Default of Payment of Franchise Tax 

The Texas statute providing for the payment of the annual franchise tax is a revenue statute and contracts made by a corporation while it is in default are not void, and may be enforced by the corporation after it has paid the back franchise taxes and all penalties and has, therefore, been reinstated by the Secretary of State." In the Ross Amigos Company case Justice Sharp said: "The Oil Company could have made valid contracts, because the law does not expressly declare that contracts made by a corporation whose right to do business has been forfeited are void. Nor does the law declare that the business transacted during the time of such forfeiture is void. It is undisputed that the Oil Company continued to do business in Texas as a chartered corporation. The only right or privilege taken away from such corporation by the forfeiture of its right to do business by the Secretary of State was its right to sue and defend in the courts of the State."

Where the Secretary of State has forfeited the corporation's right to do business for failure to pay its franchise tax, the

§ 93. Authority of Manufacturing Corporations to Purchase and Sell Goods of Others 

Has a manufacturing company authority to purchase and sell the goods produced by others even though the sale of the purchased goods will aid the manufacturer in disposing of its goods? 

The courts have answered this question in the negative, even though the purchased goods are practically the same or similar to those manufactured by the corporation. Therefore, the Ford 

Motor Car Company has no authority to purchase other makes of cars though the latter cars may enable the manufacturing company to dispose of its products. And Tiffany & Company cannot purchase a cheaper grade of merchandise to assist it in disposing of its high grade products.80 The most important exception to the above rule is corporations incorporated to manufacture gas. As we have seen in a previous section, they are authorized to buy from outside parties and sell gas stoves, water

It goes without saying that a manufacturing or processing corporation has authority to buy all the raw materials needed in its business, but the courts have held that it is ultra vires for such corporations, or a corporation that is a mere dealer in commercial commodities, to buy or sell materials used in their business by way "of dealing in futures.” 89

If the manufacturer or processor buys raw materials in January and expects to deliver them as parts of manufactured goods the next July or August, he wishes some kind of insurance that the price of the raw materials will not diminish in price to such an extent that he will lose on the manufactured products by the time they are ready for the market. The way the manufacturer protects himself is to enter into a "hedging" contract. 

That is he "sells" that amount of the raw materials used in the manufactured goods for August delivery. As he does not intend to deliver the goods, but balance accounts, on the delivery date at common law in Texas the contract would be illegal.⁹⁰

question now is-are such contracts ultra vires if entered into by a corporation that is (1) a dealer in raw materials, or (2) a manufacturer or processor. On this question the most recent book on corporation law prepared by two of our leading law professors says: "It is reasonably clear that if a corporation, whose purpose is not buying and selling commodities for profit but manufacturing or processing commodities, should engage in dealing in futures in such commodities, its action would be deemed ultra vires unless reasonably necessary or expedient to carry out its corporate purpose of manufacturing or processing. 

The question of present interest therefore seems to be whether 'hedging' by a manufacturing corporation can properly be brought within that qualification. The answer may depend upon what long-term experience shows as to the parallel between prices for the raw material involved and prices for the finished goods, involved; i. e., the reasonableness of the expectation that 'hedging' will be price insurance. If reasonably parallel, the 'hedging' practice might be justified as the nearest available equivalent to insurance. If not reasonably parallel, it might be condemned as having no reasonable relation to the business. 

But directors and officers of textile and milling corporations would probably be shocked if they were told that doubt may exist concerning a practice so long established." 92 This question has not as yet been decided by the Texas Supreme Court.

§ 131. In General 

The effect of ultra vires transactions in Texas has been confused somewhat by the loose terminology of the courts with respect to the words "capacity," "void," and "illegal" particularly.

Though a comparatively recent doctrine, the law, at least as far as results go, is now beginning to be fairly well settled, because of the many cases involving this question. 

There are three principal situations where the doctrine is concerned. They are: (1) actions by the state to forfeit the char- 339

§ 

Ch. 4

ter of a corporation, (2) suits by stockholders to prevent ultra vires acts by a corporation, and (3) actions on contracts or torts between a corporation and third parties where the defense of ultra vires is interposed. It is with the third of these that we are most concerned.

In Gaston & Ayres v. J. I. Campbell Co.¹ the basis of the doctrine is stated to be "(1) the fact that everyone is charged with constructive notice of the powers of a corporation, (2) the interest of the stockholders not to be subject to risks they have not undertaken, (3) and above all the interest of the public that the corporation shall not transcend the powers conferred on it by law." This statement has been adopted and approved many times.2 It is clear, however, that the first is not a reason for the defense but simply a means of upholding it. 

The defense often has little or no merit, and as a result, the courts have hedged it around closely with exceptions and limitations which we shall later examine, and have placed the burden of proof on the defendant or the party who claims that the transaction is ultra vires to prove that it is beyond the powers of the corporation.3 The general rule is "that strangers cannot question the lack of power of a corporation.'

Ch. § 132  § 132. A Corporation has Capacity to Exceed Its Powers 

Although some recent decisions give to a corporation general capacity to contract within the sphere of its chartered powers, the vast majority are in harmony with the general view that a corporation has only such powers as are given it expressly or impliedly by law. For instance, in the case Sealy Oil Mill & 

Manufacturing Company v. Bishop Manufacturing Company the court said: "It is our opinion that a corporation in the transaction of its business, the business for which it was organized, has the same latitude as the individual in the same character of business in those things that are essential to the successful operation of that particular business." This statement has been repeated several times in Texas cases. The English courts have always held that a company established by the king through royal grant has the same capacity to enter into contracts as an individual. In Palmer's Company Law, page 3, Fifteenth Edition, it is said: "There is a difference of a fundamental character between a chartered company and a company formed under a special act or registered under the Companies Acts, and it is this: 

At common law a corporation created by the king's charter has power, as was determined in the Sutton's Hospital case (1612) (10 Co.Rep. 30b), to deal with its property, to bind itself by contracts, and to do all such acts as ordinary persons can do, and so complete is this corporate autonomy that it is unaffected even by a direction contained in the creating charter in limitation of

For the common law has always held that such a direction of the Crown-though it may give the Crown a right to annul the charter if the direction is disregarded -cannot derogate from that plenary capacity with which the common law endows the company, even though the limitation is an essential part of the so-called bargain between the Crown and the corporation." It should be noted from the quotation from the Texas case that the court did not say that a Texas corporation has the same capacity as an individual. In other words, the court did not decide that a Texas corporation has general capacity to enter into any contract. The court limited the authority of a Texas corporation to those things that are usually and customarily done by an individual in carrying on the same or a similar business to that specified in the charter of the company. In determining the implied powers of a Texas corporation, we must always keep in mind the difference between "capacity" and "authority." The directors of any corporation have the physical power or capacity to enter into any contract for and on behalf of the corporation. But unless that transaction is expressly or impliedly granted to the corporation by its charter, the corporation has not the "authority" of the State of Texas to do the act. Whether it has the authority is largely a question of fact since what is reasonably necessary to do in carrying on such a business or what is customary in carrying on such a business is always a question of fact which should be established upon the trial of the case rather than left to the guess of the trial or appellate judges as was done in some of the Texas cases.³ 

If the doctrine that a corporation has the capacity or power to do only what it is expressly or impliedly authorized to do were taken literally, it would follow that any act done outside those powers is a complete nullity. The phraseology of some of the 

Texas courts might lead to the idea that such is the law. In

For this reason the above quotation is clearly dictum, and most assuredly does not state the present Texas law, as is shown throughout this and other chapters. 

The opinion from which the above quotation was copied is out of harmony with the Texas cases in saying that an ultra vires contract is "void". The court in writing the above dictum followed some of the recent Federal holdings and not the Texas cases.10 The conclusion of the court is correct, but if the dictum had been followed, the note would still be void even in the hands of an innocent purchaser. The true rule, and the one that is in fact followed in Texas, is that "there is nothing in the nature of a corporation which would prevent it from acquiring rights and incurring liabilities through an ultra vires act." 11

§ 134. Unauthorized Acts of Directors 

Some acts prohibited to the directors may yet be intra vires of the corporation.24 In dealing with a corporation the ordinary rules of agency apply, since a corporation can act only vicariously. Therefore, the corporation is not liable where the directors exceed their express or implied authority. If the officers of the corporation assume to make a contract outside the scope of the business, the stockholders should be able to restrain it, and the third party will not be able to enforce the contract against the corporation any more than any principal could be held on a contract beyond the scope of the agent's authority. For example, in Denton Milling Co. v. Blewett 25 the directors employed a manager for five years, which according to the by-laws was not within their power. It was held that the manager could not recover for his discharge within the time stated in the agreement, although there was clearly no question of public policy involved. The directors had simply exceeded their authority, and

§ 135. Effect of Ultra Vires Contracts Executed on Both Sides 

When an ultra vires contract has been executed on both sides, neither party can maintain an action to set it aside.2 26 Thus if a corporation purchased land it did not have the authority to own, neither the vendor nor anyone else except the state could question its title.27 The same is true if it purchased and paid for personal property, or where both promises in a bilateral contract are fully performed. If the contract was unilateral in its inception, and the act has been done or the forbearance suffered and the promisor has fully performed his promise, the courts will not disturb the vested rights of either party.28

 § 136. Contracts Executory on Both Sides 

Where the contract is executory on both sides; in other words, where neither party has partly or wholly performed his promise, there is no estoppel, and either party may deny the authority of the corporation to make it.29 For example, if a corporation agreed to lend money and that was not within its charter powers, it could recover the money if it made the loan,30 but the borrower could not get damages for failure to make it.³¹ And where a corporation with the power to manufacture building material contracted to construct improvements on a lot, the plaintiff could not recover damages for failure to do so where he had not yet paid for them.32

In Harris v. Independence Gas Co.33 the Supreme Court of 

Kansas held that an executory ultra vires contract is binding on both parties, even though it is executory on both sides. In that state the courts will grant specific performance of an ultra vires contract to purchase land. In a dictum in Staacke v. Rout-

ledge 34 the Supreme Court of Texas stated that "An inquiry into the abuse of its corporate power by the company can only be made by the State." From this quotation, and other parts of the opinion, one is lead to believe that Texas would follow the holding of Kansas announced in the Harris case. That the Kansas holding is the better of the two rules will scarcely be denied by any unbiased mind. When the court charges the third party dealing with a corporation with notice of its charter, the court bases its conclusion on a pure fiction. Business men simply cannot take time to acquaint themselves with the charter powers of corporation with which they have business dealings. The writer is firmly convinced that our courts should refrain from basing our rules of law on fiction and should assume that the directors are the persons above all who should know the powers of their own corporation; and, therefore, when they purport to deal with an innocent third party, he should be allowed to assume that they know the powers of the corporation and are not exceeding them. In fact, if the courts should hold that the directors warrant the authority and power of the corporation in all of their dealings with innocent third parties, justice would result more often than is now the case. When the Supreme 

Court published the above dictum in 1922, the writer was very hopeful that Texas would thereafter follow the Kansas holding.

But that hope was too sanguine, since every case that has arisen since the Staacke-Routledge case was decided discusses whether the contract is executed on both sides, on one side, or executory on both sides, and the earlier Texas cases are followed even though the suit is between the corporation and the third party.

§ 137. 

Contracts Executed on One Side 

A few cases hold that if the contract is ultra vires, it is of no effect, and there can be no recovery on it even though the consideration has been given on one side.37 This is clearly wrong, and it is now well settled in Texas that the contract is enforceable if executed on one side. The basis of the doctrine of ultra vires is grounded upon public policy, and when the contract has been fully performed on one side, the public policy against the enforcement of the contract is overbalanced by the hardship which such refusal would cause. The disability, being imposed for reasons of public welfare, is removed by the same considerations. If the corporation has received money or property directly from the transaction, it will be held "estopped" to assert its ultra vires character.38 The same is true where the corpora-

It is difficult to determine from the Texas cases whether the Bond-Terrell doctrine applies only where the corporation has received a direct benefit from the ultra vires contract.41 It seems fairly certain from the Texas decisions that the doctrine does not apply unless the defendant corporation has received a direct benefit from the ultra vires contract. Worthington,42 the obligation was executed on one side, since the two corporations had issued jointly $150,000 of bonds and nothing remained to be done except for the two defendants to pay the bonds that had been sold to the plaintiff, and, although each corporation received an incidental benefit from the success of the other corporation, still the Supreme Court held that each corporation was liable only for the amount of money received by it from the sale of the bonds.

the Deaton Grocery Company, the latter corporation would not be estopped to plead ultra vires since the corporation received no direct benefit from the sale of the goods by the International Harvester Company to Mr. Turner. In its opinion the court said: "We have reached the conclusion that if it be conceded that Turner was insolvent at the time the contract of guaranty was made, and that by reason of appellant's extension of time on its debt appeallant collected more from Turner than it otherwise would, still the contract of guaranty was ultra vires and is not binding upon appellant." In this case if the plaintiff had shown that the goods sold by the International Harvester Company to Turner had been sold by him and the proceeds of the sale used for the payment of Turner's debt to the Deaton Grocery Company, very probably the court would have held the defendant estopped to plead ultra vires, at least to the extent of the payment. The same question was involved in Brand, Banking Comm. v. Eastland County Lumber Co.45 In this case the lumber company indorsed the note of Rawlins to the plaintiff bank for accommodation. The question under consideration was not directly involved in the case because no estoppel was pleaded against the lumber company based upon the benefit it received through its sales of lumber to the maker of the note. However, in its opinion the Court said: "It is true that a corporation may be estopped to plead ultra vires, where corporate funds or assets have been augmented by money or other property received in the transaction. But a party may enforce such estoppel only when he shows that the benefit derived from the transaction with such corporation was direct and material. It is not sufficient to show an indirect or merely incidental or negligible benefit." From these and the other cases cited above it seems fairly evident that in Texas the corporation will be held liable for the contract price when the contract is executed on one side where the corporation received the entire consideration of the contract, as in the case of the sale of property to the corporation even though the

If the transaction is illegal and not merely ultra vires, the rules of illegal contracts will apply, In such cases, aside from a few exceptions, the courts will leave the parties where they find them. If the parties are not in pari delicto, the less guilty party will be given relief.52 But if a negotiable note evidences the illegal transaction, the court will enforce the same in favor of a bona fide purchaser.53 In Washer v. Smyer 54 the corporation issued stock in return for a note. As is shown in other chapters in this text such transactions are expressly forbidden by statute and the Texas Constitution. The court held that a bona fide purchaser of the note could collect despite the illegality of the transaction. Justice Phillips said, however, that the statute must expressly declare the note void before the court will refuse to give relief to an innocent purchaser; simply making the transaction illegal is not enough to preclude recovery by a bona fide purchaser of the note.

§ 138. Partial Performance on Either or Both Sides 

Whether part performance on one side or both sides renders the contract enforceable is a question on which there is little authority by our Texas Supreme Court. Distinction between Want and Abuse of Power 

When the contract is one which is apparently authorized, that is, of a class which the corporation may make and the ultra vires factor is not discoverable, the contract is valid,79 whether executory on one or both sides. For example, where a corporation with power to execute or endorse a note does so for accommodation merely and a bona fide purchaser obtains the note, it is enforceable.80

This is what the Texas courts really mean when they speak of "abuse of power," as distinguished from "want of power." A good example is the case of Taylor Feed Pen Company v. Taylor

National Bank.81 The Court of Civil Appeals in its opinion mentioned this supposed distinction and said that since a corporation had the power to borrow money and give a mortgage to secure it, a mortgage executed to secure the debt of another corporation was simply an abuse of power and the corporation having ratified it, was bound. The Court made this statement in spite of the fact that the bank not only knew of the transaction but

§ 142. Effect of Limitations in Charter of Corporations 

Charters of corporations are placed on record and are considered notice to the world of the limitations on the powers of the corporation contained therein.83 Thus where a national bank forwarded a note to another bank to be executed and endorsed by third parties, such action on the part of the second bank being ultra vires, the first bank was held charged with notice of that fact by reason of its charter powers and could not hold the bank at which the endorsement was found to be forged. So also, when a corporation increases its stock beyond the limit allowed by law, creditors are presumed to know that limit and cannot recover unpaid assessments from the subscribers to this excess stock.85 84 This doctrine is a technical one and if carried to its logical extent, would frequently result in great hardship. The courts have adopted a rule of reason and hold that third parties must take notice of the charter of the corporation with which they deal only as to the general powers of the corporation.86 If all

§ 143. 

Result of Known Ultra Vires Transactions 

If the principle on which ultra vires contracts are upheld is really estoppel, it would seem that the effect of knowledge would be to prevent the contract from being upheld, because the most important element of estoppel is detrimental action against himself on the part of the party who has been misled. If the third party knows the contract is ultra vires, there can be no estoppel.88 However, if the other party has performed and the corporation received the benefits, most authorities hold the corporation bound in spite of knowledge by the other party.89 This is forcibly brought out where the corporation has performed and is trying to hold the other party to the bargain. In most cases the officers of the corporation probably know they are exceeding their authority, and it is certain that the third party has done no holding out. Yet the cases, without even considering the question, say he is bound by estoppel; 90 an equitable result but not a good reason.

This same distinction was made by the Commission of Appeals, but that court realized that there is only one real meaning of ultra vires acts. "Accurately, the term 'ultra vires' applies only to those acts which are wholly beyond the power of the corporation acts which it has not the power to perform under any circumstances. It is believed that the two dicta, set out above, will not be followed by the Supreme Court of Texas. They are opposed to the 

Texas rule and to the best reasoned authorities which hold that, in the last analysis, the stockholders own the corporation—in fact are the corporation. In the Harvard Law Review Professor 

Warren said: "If, however, all the incorporated associates have consented that the funds of the corporation should be employed in a venture outside the scope of corporate action, as defined in the certificate of incorporation and a contract has been made in the course of such venture in the name of the corporation, the corporation cannot be allowed to escape liability on such contract, for the sake of affording protection to the incorporated associates. "The consent of the shareholders need not be expressed by any formal vote of authorization or ratification. Where the funds of

If shareholders are to be protected, to the detriment of outsiders, against the unauthorized acts of the directors and officers, it is not improper to impose a duty upon shareholders to inquire as to the conduct of the directors and officers, and to restrain such conduct, if improper." 94

The reason given by the New York Court in the last cited case is upheld by our Supreme Court in the case of Aransas Pass Harbor Co. v. Manning 96 though the exact point under consideration was not involved. In that case the Court said: "A stockholder, merely as such, has no direct agency in the control of the business of the corporation. He has no direct interest in the property. His right to such property is collateral. But in its last analysis, the stockholders are the beneficial owners of the assets of the corporation. This proceeding is instituted upon the theory, which we think a correct one, that the shareholders are the ultimate owners of the corporate property, and, when the corporation is dissolved and its creditors are satisfied, they hold the title to the assets in proportion to their respective shares.

In the chapter on Corporate Liability for Torts it is shown that the corporation is liable for torts committed in an ultra vires business or undertaking, where the stockholders either authorize or ratify the unauthorized business.97 Surely if the real owners of the property of the corporation can by ratification make the corporation liable for torts committed in conducting an ultra vires business, they can ratify an ultra vires contract and thereby make the corporation liable for its breach, especially where the corporation has received a benefit from the transaction.98

Whether the directors can "ratify" an ultra vires contract is discussed in the chapter entitled "Authority of Directors and Agents." According to the weight of authority, if the state does not complain and the rights of creditors are not involved, the stockholders can ratify an ultra vires contract. If a corporation is merely a collection of human beings, this rule should govern.

Rex, (1916) 1 A.C. 566, the court said: "In the case of a company created by charter the doctrine of ultra vires has no real application in the absence of statutory restriction added to what is written in the charter. Such a company has the capacity of a natural person to acquire powers and rights. If by the terms of the charter it is prohibited from doing so, a violation of this prohibition is an act not beyond its capacity, and is therefore not ultra vires, although such a violation may well give ground for proceedings by way of scire facias for the forfeiture of the charter. the case of a company the legal existence of which is wholly derived In from the words of a statute, the company does not possess the general capacity of a natural person and the doctrine of ultra vires applies."

corporations. The courts say that the shareholders are the ultimate and equitable owners of the property belonging to the corporation, and, if all the shareholders consent, they can do anything they wish with the corporate property so long as the rights of creditors are not involved. Of course, the corporation is a collection of human beings.

In determining whether a corporation can buy its own stock, and in many other cases discussed in the chapter on the "Rights and Remedies of Creditors," the same problem of solvency arises. 

Of course, in solving these questions the courts should realize that a corporation is a collection of human beings, but is also a legal entity. They should be more conscious of the fact that the shareholders do not individually own the property of the corporation, but such property belongs to them collectively, or as a legal unit; and, as a consideration for being permitted to carry on a business without personal liability for the debts of the legal unit, they have agreed to dedicate the corporate property to the creditors of the legal personality. The courts have too often lost sight of this principle in saying that the shareholders can dispose of the corporate property as though it belonged to them individually, so long as the rights of the creditors of the "legal unit" are not violated.

When our judges become better acquainted with the rules of accounting, and the above question is squarely presented to them in the many instances that arise in the law of private corporations, they will realize more clearly the importance of a correct and uniform solution of this question in all of its ramifications, and will, most assuredly, compel the shareholders of corporations to keep intact for corporate creditors that safety fund-

§ 145. Disregard of Indoor Regulations 

Where the ultra vires factor is simply in the method of doing an act that is clearly within the apparent power of the corporation, under many circumstances the corporation is estopped from pleading lack of authority.5 These are indoor affairs analogous to secret instructions to an agent in the law of Agency." 

In Texas Western Railway Company v. Gentry," it was held that even though a Texas statute provided that no mortgage by a railroad company would be valid unless authorized by a resolution adopted by a vote of two-thirds of all the stock, a mortgage without this resolution was valid. The mortgage would be binding on the corporation where the innocent third party does not know that the resolution was not adopted by the stockholders, even though the provision appears in a statute, in a by-law, or even in the charter of the corporation, since the third party has a right to assume that indoor affairs have been complied with where he has no notice or knowledge to the contrary. On this point the Supreme Court said: "In the case before us the railroad company had power to make a mortgage, but the statute provides it must be authorized by a vote in meeting of two-thirds in value of the stockholders. This provision is evidently for the protection of the latter. It seems from the evidence in this case

Of Personalty 

The same rule is true of personalty. Baker v. Farmers Welfare Union 10 was a case where a corporation was suing to recover personal property from a former employee. To his plea that the corporation had no power to own it, the court said that no one but the state could question the corporation's right to the property. And in Bishop Mfg. Co. v. Sealy Oil Mill & Refining

Co.20 the court said, by way of dictum, that if the purchase of cottonseed by a gin company was ultra vires, the corporation had a right to sell the seed it had already acquired by means of such a purchase.

Even though personal property is acquired by the exercise of an authority not granted by law, it is nevertheless the absolute property of the corporation.21 And any contract which the corporation may see fit to make with reference to its insurance, storage, or sale, if otherwise legal, would not be invalidated because the corporation acquired it by exceeding its corporate powers.22 $148.

Mercy v. Davidson 24 the court held that the doctrine applied in conveyances does not apply to devises of real estate. In the above case the court said: "The corporation claiming under the will asks the aid of the law to give the property to it and in so doing, it must show it has the authority to take." This reason is not convincing, as usually the executor, and not the devisee, files the will for probate, and the only issue before the Court is the validity of the will, and, therefore, the question of the capacity of the corporation to take title is not involved. 

Here, as in many other questions discussed in this chapter, the courts should not base their conclusions on estoppel. In fact, no question of estoppel is involved. Even in the case of a conveyance based on a valuable consideration the grantor has made no false representation that the corporation relied upon to its detriment. § 150. Remedy of Stockholder and Creditors 

The shareholder, too, has the right to insist that his money be devoted to the proper objects of the corporation, and even though the other shareholders assent, he may have his remedy by injunction to prevent the performance of an executory ultra vires act.35

As we have already shown, if damages have resulted from the ultra vires act, the stockholder's loss would be indirect, and, therefore, the corporation, and not the stockholder, should sue for the damages. If the directors refuse to sue in the name of the corporation, the shareholder's only remedy would be a shareholder's bill.36

As to whether creditors could enjoin the ultra vires act, the authorities have not fully determined. Mr. Ballantine is of the opinion that a creditor of a corporation should have more control over the operations of the company than he has over the business of an individual debtor.37 At least one case holds that intra vires creditors are given precedence over ultra vires creditors.38

Extreme cases will arise where even this rule will work great injustice. Suppose a bank by way of speculation buys a grocery store, and the manager of a flour mill sells to the bank

When the bank becomes insolvent, the flour is still on the shelves of the store worth more than when sold to the bank; and the store, as such, is able to pay all store creditors and have a surplus, but the bank—including the store assets and liabilities—is able to pay only five cents on the dollar. Under such circumstances it seems very unjust not to permit the store creditors to share pari passu with the strictly bank creditors. Would it not be better for the courts to permit all creditors of the same class, whether intra vires or ultra vires, to share pari passu except stockholder creditors under circumstances as extreme as those in the above supposititious case? There are not many cases that discuss this question.

Creditors of individuals would like very much to control the business affairs of their debtors, but, as a general rule, aside from conveyances to hinder creditors, a creditor has no right to interfere with his debtor's business. Mr. Ballantine says: "The bondholder is not merely a lender, but to a certain extent an investor in a business financed through bonds. § 171. Requisites of a De Facto Corporation 

The highest form of corporate existence known to the law is a de jure corporation. It can only exist where there is a valid law for incorporation and a substantial performance of all mandatory conditions precedent.¹ However, it is not within the scope of this chapter to deal with de jure corporations. There are two other classifications of corporate existence named in the opinions, which are de facto corporations and corporations by estoppel. It is with these two latter classifications that this chapter deals.

I. Finnegan v. Noerenberg, 53 N.W. 

1150, 52 Minn. 239, 18 L.R.A. 778, 38 Am.St.Rep. 552. 

Bank of De Soto v. Reed, 109 S.W. 

256, 50 Tex.Civ.App. 102.

Roaring Springs Townsite Co. V. 

Paducah Tel. Co., Tex.Civ.App., 164 S.W. 50, affirmed 212 S.W. 

147, 109 Tex. 452. 387

§ 

Ch. 5 

A de facto corporation is a corporation which though not a de jure corporation has a certain corporate existence recognized by the courts. In order to form a de facto corporation certain requirements must be met. These requirements are ably stated in the case of Roaring Springs Townsite Co. v. Paducah Telephone Co.,2 as follows: "From the decisions and text-books on corporations, we gather that the requisites of a de facto corporation, where the charter is not specifically granted by the legislature, and the same is constituted by articles of association under some general law, are: "First, the existence of some law under which a corporation with the powers assumed might lawfully be created; "Second, an effort in good faith to incorporate thereunder; "Third, an actual user under the franchise granted of the rights claimed to be conferred by such law." 

This quotation reflects the universal test used to determine the existence or non-existence of the de facto corporation. Let us deal with these requisites separately.

§ 173. Valid Law and Bona Fide Attempt at Compliance 

The second element named in the quotation from the Roaring Spring's Townsite Co. case is that there must be a bona fide attempt to comply with a valid law in existence in the jurisdiction where the corporation is chartered. 

From the cases it is impossible to state in a general rule what is necessary to constitute a good faith attempt or how far the organization must have progressed to fulfill this requisite of a de facto corporation. It seems clear that no bona fide attempt is made where the parties are so negligent as to fail in the filing of a charter with the Secretary of State as required by our general incorporation statutes.10 The statute on which this decision

Performance of all the prerequisites short of filing the charter with the Secretary of State is not sufficient to bring the company into existence as a corporation de jure. Are such acts sufficient to create the association a corporation de facto? We think not. Where the governing statute points out the manner in which the corporation shall be organized, and the statute is followed, the corporation is brought into existence, so that it may enter upon the objects of its creation. Thus the corporation is generally deemed to exist from the time when the certificate of incorporation prescribed by the governing statute is filed in accordance with the statute. In several jurisdictions it has been held that a compliance with the requirement that the charter shall be filed in the office of the Secretary of State is a condition precedent to the establishment of a corporation de jure; and without such compliance the association cannot be treated as a corporation de facto.

The filing of the charter is as essential to one as to the other." Where persons prepared what they considered were the necessary instruments, but the Secretary of State returned them for irregularities, there was no de facto corporation formed, although the business was conducted in the corporate name.¹¹ In a recent case the Commission of Appeals held that the company is not a de facto corporation during the period between the preparation of the charter and its approval by the Secretary of State.12 The court gave the following reason for its position: "One of the essential tests as to the existence of a de facto corporation is a 'colorable' attempt to form a corporation in accordance with the statutory requirements. This necessarily means that notwithstanding the attempt to follow the law, such attempt falls short of the formation of a de jure corporation. In the present instance there was not a colorable attempt, but a successful attempt, which

However, where the only defect is failure to select a board of directors, a de facto corporation has been formed.13 The Texas statute provides that at least two of the three persons who apply for the charter must be citizens of the State of Texas.14 

In American Salt Co. v. Heidenheimer 15 a charter was approved by the Secretary of State, but no one of those who applied for the charter was a citizen of Texas. The company bought goods on credit from the plaintiff company. The court held that the stockholders who bought stock of the defendant company without knowledge of any defect in the organization of the defendant company were not liable individually for the debts of the company. As these stockholders were innocent of any wrong, and the plaintiff dealt with them on a corporate basis, the creditor should be limited to the assets of the association for the satisfaction of his debt in accordance with the rules discussed later in this chapter in connection with the so-called "corporation by estoppel." However, the court said that the innocent shareholders were not liable because The Texas Salt Company was a "corporation de facto." Did the court mean to hold that the defendant company was "a de facto corporation"? If it did, we would be compelled to revise our three essentials of such a corporation. The second essential is a "bona fide attempt" to organize the company. No one would contend that a bona fide attempt is made where those who apply for the charter deliberately mislead the Secretary of State. There can be only one attempt to organize the corporation, and in the very nature of

As under the rules of estoppel the innocent stockholders should be relieved from personal liability where a creditor dealt with the company as a corporation. That part of the opinion dealing with the "corporation de facto" is pure dictum. As the original incorporators acted in bad faith even under the rules of estoppel they should have been held personally liable as partners, since so far as they were concerned, neither a de facto nor de jure corporation was formed. One of the original incorporators was made a party to the suit and held individually liable. The Supreme Court held that "The amended petition he was cited to answer shows a cause of action, and judgment should have been rendered against him by default." For this reason what the court said applied only to the liability of the innocent stockholders, and not to that of the guilty parties. The exact question involved in the dictum of the court has not been discussed by the authorities, and surely if the court meant that the company actually became a de facto corporation so far as the innocent stockholders are concerned, our requisites of such a corporation must be revised. 

In such a case, under the rules of estoppel, the contractual creditor should not be permitted to recover against the innocent shareholder.

But what is the position of a tort creditor? No questions of estoppel arise in his case. If logic alone is followed the stockholders should be held personally liable on all tort claims since they are members of a joint stock company as by hypothesis neither a de facto nor a de jure corporation was formed. Payment of fifty per cent of the capital stock is not essential to the creation of a corporation de facto 17 where the failure so to do was not fraudulent as where notes of the subscribers were taken as payment for shares of stock. 

It will be seen from these cases that no exact test is possible as to what will constitute a bona fide atttempt to comply with a valid law of the jurisdiction involved. However, an approximation may be deduced. It is clear that where the parties seek to evade the law fraudulently, no bona fide attempt is made.18 

It would seem also that if the parties are grossly negligent in disregarding fundamental requisites of incorporation such attempt will not be regarded as bona fide. 

From the above cases we may deduce that the lack of mere formalities in the attempted organization will not prevent the attempt being in good faith; while it does seem to follow logically that fraud or negligence will prevent the attempt being bona fide.

This view is well stated, and its soundness is clearly demonstrated both logically, and as a matter of policy, by the language

§ 174. User 

The last essential of a de facto corporation is that there must be a user of the corporate powers by the purported corporation. 

This requirement is generally present and is not a very stringent one. This condition is attributable to the fact that normally there will be a user before a legal problem arises. No Texas case, regarding a de facto corporation, has been found that turned on the question of user. In fact no case has yet arisen in Texas where the existence of this element has been challenged, but the cases by way of dictum express its importance as an essential element of a de facto corporation.23

Article 1387 26 says that a corporation is dissolved by the expiration of the time limited in its charter. In Clark v. Brown 27 this provision was said to be self-executing. Thus, it would seem to follow that in Texas there could be no de facto corporation after the expiration of the time limit fixed in the charter of the corporation. But according to the better holding the company is a joint-stock company only, and not a de facto corporation, if its business is carried on after the time specified in its charter expires without any renewal of the charter. If the stockholders make no attempt to renew the charter it is the same as if they had never attempted to incorporate in the first place. Certainly under those circumstances they could not claim to be even a de facto corporation, even though there was a valid law under which they could have incorporated. § 176. Powers and Liabilities 

A de facto corporation in a large measure enjoys the same powers and liabilities as a de jure corporation.34 In Roaring

Springs Townsite Co. v. Paducah Tel. Co.,35 a Court of Civil Ap peals said: "If an association is a de facto corporation, it has ordinarily in its relationship with all persons, except as against the state, the same powers, and is subject to the imposition of the same obligations, as a corporation de jure; it enjoys that status until the state questions its existence." The Texas decisions bear out the statement quoted above when we note some of the many and varied powers and obligations attributed to the de facto corporation. According to the above section a de facto corporation can recover on a pre-incorporation subscription although there is a direct conflict in the authorities on this point. That discussion applies here as well as to our discussion of the preincorporation subscriptions as the same reason applies to the right of the de facto corporation to exercise the right of eminent domain as to its right to recover on a pre-incorporation subscription.

In the Medlin case the defendant subscribed before the company was incorporated. The case of Stringfellow v. 

Panhandle Packing Co., a later case, held the subscriber liable; though it really turns upon a point of estoppel, because there the subscriber later actually took an active part in the organization of the company. In this case the corporation could not have been a de jure corporation if fifty per cent of the stock had not been paid in, as under the Texas statute that is definitely a condition precedent to de jure existence. Though the court does not say that the company was a de facto corporation, it could not have been a de jure one. The court may have meant to hold that the defendant was estopped to deny the corporate existence of the plaintiff.51 It is believed that the Texas court, when the question is squarely presented, will adopt the majority view and require as a condition precedent to recovery that the corporation show that a de jure corporation was formed. If the purported corporation is neither de jure nor de facto, it cannot recover against the subscriber.52

In other words, those two questions have not directly been decided by the Supreme Court, and the Court will probably hold that they are exceptions to the broad rule stated by Justice Critz in the Miller-Davis case.

§ 178. Corporations by Estoppel 

We now proceed to discuss "corporations by estoppel." It should be noticed at the outset that the question of estoppel arises only when the alleged corporation is neither de jure nor de facto.75 

The basis and requisites for the existence of corporations de jure and de facto as previously discussed are entirely different from those involved in the so-called corporation by estoppel. While the two first named corporations involve the recognition of a legal corporate status, the latter considers only

With this in mind it is clear that on principle at least there can be no objection to applying the equitable doctrine of estoppel just because a corporation or corporate usurpation is involved, for the sole object of equitable estoppel is to prevent injustice and to protect those who have been misled by promises or representations fair on their face which in the interest of justice and equity the party making them should not be permitted to deny.76 

But it seems that merely because it happens to be a corporation involved, there is no reason completely to disregard the requirements of estoppel which are (1) a false representation or concealment of a material fact to one ignorant of the truth of the matter with intent that he should act upon it; (2) action on the basis of that misrepresentation to his detriment." 

It seems, then, that strictly and correctly speaking there could be no corporation by estoppel unless there be (1) a misrepresentation of a material fact and (2) action in reliance on that fact to the damage of the party so acting. This being true, there would seem to be a few situations in which the doctrine should be applied.78

It is evident that the doctrine of estoppel is not necessary to a decision where a de facto corporation exists, as generally its corporate existence or liability cannot be collaterally questioned.80 But the courts even where a de facto corporation is involved use language implying estoppel.81 Some courts have, however, erroneously held the doctrine applies only in case of a de facto corporation,82 but this view is the decided minority and cannot be sustained on principle. The decided weight of authority is that there may be a corporation by estoppel or what amounts to the same, since under certain circumstances the third party cannot hold the stockholders liable individually as partners even though neither a de facto nor a de jure corporation was formed.83

§ 179. 

As Against the Association or the Associates

As a general rule one who holds an association out as a corporate body and thereby induces persons to deal with it as such is estopped to deny his representation to the prejudice of the other party. Such estoppel arises against the individuals or the corporation as a body since as to them all the elements of estoppel are established.84 It seems that this situation is the only one in which the doctrine of estoppel can be applied with any degree of precision. In these cases it seems clear that, in keeping with the doctrine of estoppel, there must be a misrepresentation and a change of position in reliance on the misrepresentation.85

As to the second category, that is, where the defendant seeks to escape liability to a corporation plaintiff by setting up irregularities in its organization, it is illogical to apply the doctrine of estoppel. It is clear in such cases that the corporation is in no position to assert that the defendant is estopped when he has made no representation whatsoever, nor has the corporation in any wise been misled. In such cases there is no semblance of reason for the application of the principles of estoppel, yet many courts hold that the defendant is estopped.91 The defendant has made no representation about the existence of the plaintiff as a corporation even though he has contracted with the corporation as such. The officers of the association represent to the defendant that it is a corporation and he merely assumes the truth of their statements. So on principle he should not be estopped. But where the plaintiff is entitled to recover it should be immaterial in what capacity the suit is instituted. Article 1317 93 provides: "No person who assumes an obligation to an ostensible corporation as such, shall resist the enforcement of such obligation, on the ground that there was in fact no such corporation, until that fact shall have been adjudged in a direct proceeding had for that purpose." Ch. § 180 

The Texas courts have never decided whether the above statutory provision would apply to a case where the stockholders acted mala fides in claiming to be a corporation. Suppose three persons agree to carry on their business under a fictitious name as a corporation without even attempting to comply with the statute providing for the organization of corporations. Will our courts permit such an "ostensible corporation" to sue on contractual obligations made to it as such? As the defendant owes the obligation to someone possibly the Legislature intended to provide for every case where the defendant contracted with an "ostensible corporation" regardless of whether the owners of the business acted in good faith or not in claiming to be a corporation. As stated above, this question has not as yet been settled in Texas. In the case of Davis, Rec. v. Allison,96 the Texas

Legislature by special act offered certain parties a charter to operate a bank. The offer, however, was not accepted before the present State Constitution went into effect. The Constitution prohibited the organization of banking corporations and this prohibition remained until 1904. After that time the promoters attempted to carry on the banking business under the original offer. The receiver of the purported corporation sued the defendant on a subscription contract. The Supreme Court of Texas held that the receiver of the company who represented the creditors of the company could not recover. The actual decision was based on the ground that "any contract to purchase it (stock) was without legal consideration and without legal force." As to the application of the above article to this case 

Chief Justice Phillips said: "Article 1138 [Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1317] does not, in our opinion, prevent the assertion of the defense that this purported corporation was, under the Constitution, wholly without any power to issue stock. The statute is designed to prevent a collateral attack upon corporations in respect to the class of transactions with which it deals. But the fact that one is denied the right to level such an attack upon a corporation does not prevent his asserting its entire want of cor- 

96. 211 S.W. 980, 109 Tex. 440, affirming, Civ.App., 189 S.W. 968. 419

§ 

Ch. 5

porate power. Parks v. West, 102 Tex. 19, 111 S.W. 726. It would be a mockery of justice to enforce these subscriptions if the purported corporation could not at any time have issued the stock upon their payment. The Constitution made the company powerless to issue stock by its prohibition against the company's existence as a corporation. A statute could not in effect legalize the stock by denying the right to assert the invalidity which the Constitution visited upon it. It was not intended, in our opinion, to have application to such cases, and can have none."

Since Judge Phillips based his decision on the grounds of lack of power in the purported corporation to sell stock and failure of consideration, and especially as he said, "The statute is designed to prevent a collateral attack upon corporations in respect to the class of transactions with which it deals," he surely meant to say that if the defendant's only defense is that the plaintiff sued in the wrong capacity his contention is of no avail where the defendant contracted with the plaintiff as an "ostensible corporation." But Judge Phillips held that all other defenses which bear upon the right of the plaintiff to recover are open to the defendant, such as failure of consideration or want of power on the part of the purported corporation to enter into the contract involved in the litigation.97 In a dictum in Empire Mills v.  § 181. Are the Associates Liable as Partners? 

Where the associates have not formed either a de jure or a de facto corporation and there have been no dealings between the parties on a corporate basis, the members of the association are liable as partners. The company is a joint-stock company, and unless a clause limiting the liability of the shareholders is inserted in the contract, the members are personally liable for all obligations of the company. However, it is now well settled in Texas that the liability of the members of a joint-stock company or partnership may be limited by a special provision in the contract to that effect and that even though the contract is in writing the defendants may show by parol that it was agreed that the liability of the defendants was limited." 

§ 182. Doctrine of Estoppel is Based on Equitable Grounds 

An examination of the cases in which the doctrine of estoppel to deny corporate existence has been applied will show that most of them rest on some basis of conduct, or of benefit obtained, or other cause rendering it inequitable to allow such denial. The doctrine is an equitable one, and should be applied only where there are equitable grounds for applying it. It

should never be applied where it would be inequitable to do so.⁹ 

Nor should it be applied unless it would be inequitable not to do so. To say, therefore, without qualification, that a person who deals with an association as a corporation is estopped to deny its existence as a corporation, is too broad. It is perfectly right that a person who deals with an association as a corporation, knowing that it is not, should be left in the position that he has thus assumed, and be precluded from denying that the body is a corporation in actions growing out of the transaction.10 

When, however, a person deals with a body as a corporation, which the members hold out as a corporation, and which he believes to be a corporation, there should be something more than the mere fact of his dealings to estop him.11 If, in such a case, he derives a benefit from the association, and assumes an obligation to pay therefor, as where a person borrows money or purchases goods from a pretended corporation, it is equitable that he should be estopped to deny its corporate existence in order to escape liability on his obligation. On the other hand, if a person deals with a pretended corporation, believing it to be a corporation, and, instead of receiving a benefit himself, confers a benefit upon the associates, he ought not, from the mere fact that he dealt with them as a corporation, to be estopped to deny their corporate existence, and hold them individually liable. 

Though there are cases to the contrary,12 there are many cases which hold that there is no estoppel under such circumstances,13

§ 183. Unlawful Assumption of Corporate Powers 

It has been said that the doctrine of estoppel does not apply, so as to prevent one who recognizes a pretended corporation by contracting with it from afterwards denying its corporate character, where the assumption of corporate powers by the body was unlawful, as being in violation of a prohibitory law, or as being for an illegal purpose. Under these circumstances the defendants should be held personally liable as they have no equitable grounds for claiming to be a corporation.15

Alston Grocery Co.27 the court held the stockholders liable as partners even though the plaintiff contracted with the defendants as a corporation where they had no equitable grounds for claiming to be a corporation. The correct line of demarcation is thus drawn by the Texas courts. As to contractual creditors, the stockholders are not subjected to partnership liability even though the company is neither de jure nor de facto, where the plaintiff has dealt with the defendants as a corporation and the stockholders have equitable grounds for claiming to be a corporation. If A deposits his money with the Western Bank & Trust Company as a corporation, or if he lends money to such company and accepts its note in which the company is represented as a corporation, has he not agreed to look only to the assets of such association and not to the stockholders personally for the satisfaction of his debt? That is clearly the intention of both parties since the plaintiff dealt with the defendants as a legal corporate unit. If the defendants have equitable grounds for claiming to be a corporation, the court should not set aside the understanding of the parties. § 186. Tort Liability 

According to the prevailing view in America, the stockholders of a company which is neither a de jure nor a de facto corporation are individually liable for all torts committed by its agents in furtherance of its business.31 The promoters may have acted in good faith, such as attempting to incorporate under an unconstitutional law, but as the company is merely a joint stock company and as in tort actions there can be no question of estoppel nor implied contract, it necessarily follows that the stockholders are individually liable for all torts of the company.32 This rule should be followed in Texas, but one Court of Civil Appeals held that the plaintiff in a tort action against a hotel corporation could not hold the shareholders individually liable by proving that two of the incorporators were not citizens of Texas when the charter was obtained. The only reason that the court gave for its decision was that "the alleged irregularities did not appear upon the face of the articles of incorporation." If at least two of the incorporators were not citizens of Texas and they had knowledge

 § 211. Form of the Subscription 

There is no particular form for subscription agreements. They are usually written documents, signed by those who subscribe, with the amount of the subscription set opposite each name, and the name, nature, purpose and terms of the proposed corporation to some extent indicated.19 The contract must be sufficiently definite to enable the court to ascertain the intention of the parties and to enforce it.20 If the agreement is considered as a contract between the subscribers for the benefit of a third party, no consideration is required by the corporation. 

In other words, if there is a valid consideration between the subscribers, the contract is valid so far as consideration is concerned, as no consideration need be furnished by the beneficiary.21 The Texas courts have said that consideration is satisfied by the mutual promises of the subscribers to contribute to the common object.22 There is some authority that a subscription can be either in writing or by parol; 23 but as yet it has not been necessary for the Texas courts to decide this question, as the Texas Legislature has never seen fit to adopt the 17th sec-

§ 212. When a Subscriber Becomes Bound-Subscription after Incorporation 

When a corporation is already organized, a subscription to its capital stock is like any other contract with the corporation. 

It is a contract between the corporation and the subscriber, and is subject to the principles governing the formation of other contracts. There must be an offer by one party and an acceptance by the other, resulting in mutual agreement. If the corporation opens subscription books or solicits subscriptions, and a person subscribes for shares, he makes an offer to the corporation; 24 and when the subscription or offer is accepted by the corporation, a contract is formed. On the other hand, the solicitation of subscriptions may be a general offer by the corporation, and a manifestation of willingness on the part of the offeree to take a definite number of the shares of the company would be an acceptance, and result in a contract without further assent on the part of the corporation.25 In these cases there is a contract between the subscriber and the corporation, which in most jurisdictions ipso facto makes the subscriber a shareholder, and binds him to pay the amount of the subscription.⁹6 

24. Kennebec Housing Co. v. Bar ton, 122 A. 852, 123 Me. 293. 25. 

Greer v. Chartiers Ry. Co., 96 

Pa. 391, 42 Am. Rep. 548. In this case plaintiff opened books for subscriptions, placing one of them in the defendant's hands for solicitation of subscriptions. Defendant entered his own name on the book as a subscriber, and kept the book for six months without attempting to withdraw his name. He then cut his name out and returned the book to plaintiff. He claimed that he had a right to withdraw at any time before he returned the book, but it was held that the contract of subscription was binding upon him, because the company, in soliciting subscriptions, "made a continuing offer which became an agreement with each acceptant for the number of shares for which he subscribed."

There must also be a consideration for the promise of the subscriber and for the undertaking of the corporation to recognize him as a stockholder. The consideration for the latter is the subscriber's promise to pay for his stock, and the consideration for the former is the acquisition by the subscriber of an interest in the franchises and property of the corporation and the right to share in its profits. It follows that the obligation must be mutual. "A stock subscription is a transaction between the subscriber and the company, and the obligation of one can only be sustained by the corresponding obligation of the other. If both are not bound, neither is bound, and the transaction is a nullity." 27 If the corporation evidences an intention to repudiate the subscription contract the subscriber may refuse to carry out his part of the agreement.28 If the corporation refuses to issue the stock to the subscriber after he has paid for the stock the consideration for the plaintiff's payment has failed, and he may sue the corporation for the value of the property transferred to the company in payment of his subscription agreement.29 If the company wrongfully refuses to issue the certificates to those who are entitled to the stock the company is guilty of conversion, and, therefore, the company and the directors or agents who instigate, aid or abet the conversion are jointly and severally liable for the damages

§ 213. Distinguished from a Sale of Shares 

A subscription to the capital stock of a corporation after its organization must be distinguished from a sale of shares by it.31 A purchase of shares, if fully performed, will make the purchaser a stockholder, but it does not make him a subscriber; and the rules governing subscriptions and sales of shares are different. In the case of subscription, failure of the corporation to issue or tender a certificate of stock, which is merely evidence of the ownership of shares, does not prevent the subscriber from becoming a shareholder, with all the rights and subject to all the liabilities of shareholders, unless there is a stipulation to that effect in the subscription.32 When stock is originally is-

Professor Stevens gives the following test to determine whether the contract is one of "purchase" or "subscription": "It would seem that the distinction should be made to turn upon the questions: first, whether the contract has been made by the acceptance of the subscriber's offer; and, second, whether the terms of the contract gave the subscriber the rights of a shareholder before payment or before the issue of the certificate." 42

As has been shown at length in the chapter on Payment for Stock the Supreme Court of Texas has held several times that the Texas Constitution prohibits the issue of stock before it is fully paid for, and that stock has been issued when one becomes the owner of the stock. The usual evidence of ownership stressed by the Supreme Court is that dividends have been paid to the stockholder, that he has been requested to attend stockholder's meetings and permitted to vote, and that a certificate has been made out in the owner's name and pledged by him to secure the amount still due for the stock.43

185 S.W. 619, affirmed 230 S.W. 141, 111 Tex. 170, rehearing denied Civ.

In this latter case the Supreme Court said: "In our opinion, under the facts recited in the certificate which we have summarized as above, there was plainly an issuance of the stock. The promoters stood originally in the place of the corporation, and Gahagan in the transaction of the note stood in their place. There being no agreement that the stock was not to be delivered until the appellant's note was paid, there can be no reason for denying the clear effect of the pledging by appellant of the stock as security for the note and of the understanding expressed in the collateral agreement that the stock should be sold if the note were not paid. In pledging the stock as security for the note, the intention must have been to pledge it as appellant's property. It could hardly have been the purpose that Gahagan should accept for the security of the note a pledge of his own property as agent or property belonging to the corporation. The provision in the collateral agreement was that the stock might be sold if the note were not paid. This could have contemplated nothing else than a sale of the stock as appellant's property. The whole transaction with respect to the note treated the stock as belonging to appellant in virtue of an effectuated sale and delivery. It is difficult to place any other construction upon it than as fully recognizing appellant's property right in the stock as stock duly issued." In the Turner case the court said: "This brings us to a consideration of the facts bearing upon the question of whether or not the stock involved in this litigation was issued. "It has been very earnestly insisted that the inhibition of the Constitution has in contemplation the issuance of the certificate evidencing the recognition of ownership of stock.

We are inclined to the view that the 'constitutional prohibition is broad enough to cover, not only the certificate, but the actual recognition or the origin of the rights of a stockholder which accrue to the subscriber. Were we to hold that the Constitution in its prohibition is limited alone to the ministerial act of writing up and delivering the certificate of stock, the evident purpose of the Constitution would be destroyed. Its evasion would be rendered easy. It would be necessary only for a subscriber to allow the stock to remain in the possession of the corporation without the issuance of a certificate evidencing, in his possession, ownership. All the rights which could possibly accrue to him as the possessor of the written certificate already exist without it. The certificate is not a necessary prerequisite to the exercise by him of all the powers of the stockholder, nor to the recognition by the corporation of an existence of these privileges in him and a permission to their exercise by him. 

As we construe the Constitution, it covers not only the certificate which may be put into circulation, but its ultimate and most effective force is to prohibit the exercise by the subscriber of the rights of a stockholder 444
