Again, under the present incorporation statute all the stock must be subscribed, but only fifty per cent must be paid in before the charter will be approved by the Secretary of State.40 

It is held that this statute is complied with if fifty per cent of the entire amount of the capital stock is paid in, regardless of the amount paid by each stockholder. If fifty per cent of the entire amount subscribed is paid in, the Secretary of State must file the charter. 47 

But suppose no "subscriber" has fully paid for his stock before the first annual stockholders' meeting is held. Who can vote at this meeting? If a "subscriber" is permitted to vote before he fully pays for his stock, he is recognized as the owner of the stock. If he becomes the owner, the stock is issued. If the stock is issued before it is fully paid for, the contract of subscription is "illegal," and the corporation cannot recover the balance due,48 but the creditors may recover the unpaid balance.49 The courts hold that the stock must be issued before it can be voted, and many hold it cannot be voted until fully paid for.50 There is no general custom in Texas as to what is done hold that the contract is illegal if the "subscriber" becomes the owner before he fully pays for his stock.

The Texas statutes do not differentiate between "stockholders" and "subscribers" to the stock of the corporation. For instance, in Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1308 it is provided that before the charter can be filed by the Secretary of State, the full amount of its capital stock must be subscribed by its stockholders. In article 1313 it is the stockholders that furnish evidence to the Secretary of State that the law has been complied with. 

According to article 1326 the by-laws may be altered, changed or amended by a majority vote of the stockholders. Article 

1328 provides that the books and records of the corporation shall be open to the inspection of any stockholder. Article 1336 authorizes the forfeiture of the stock if any stockholder neglects to pay any installment as required by the board of directors, and article 1345 authorizes an execution "against any of the stockholders to an extent equal to the amount of the stock unpaid." On the other hand, article 1335 provides that the board of directors may require "the subscribers" to the capital stock to pay the amount subscribed as is provided in the by-laws. In other words, in most instances, a party who has subscribed for stock in a corporation on credit is designated as "a stockholder" even though he has not fully paid for his stock. Therefore, the statutes do not furnish a solution or much assistance in deciding the above problems. However, the Supreme Court has decided that a negotiable note given in payment for stock, though it is illegal, is not void, and is valid in the hands of an innocent purchaser.51 And that if the stock is wrongfully issued before it is paid for, the stock is valid in the hands of an innocent pur-

In the Washer-Smyer case Chief Justice Phillips stated that the corporation has the right to cancel the stock that was issued in violation of the constitutional provision "to the extent of the default." The objection to this intimation is that the court makes a divisible contract for the parties where in most cases they intended an indivisible one.53 One Court of Civil Appeals has held that the stock subscription agreement is indivisible and a subscriber is not entitled to certificates of stock equal to his partial payments. 

In Cisco & N. E. R. Co. v. Ricks,54 the Court of Civil Appeals said: "Such a theory of recovery would be that one who had subscribed to the capital stock of a corporation and had paid only a part of same could, without offering to pay the balance due, make demand for the issue of stock to him in the amount that his partial payment would equal, and then put the corporation in default if it refused to do so. We think clearly the law imposes no such duty on the corporation, and therefore gives no such right to a subscriber to stock. It would be wholly inconsistent with the right of the corporation to forfeit stock subscriptions for failure to pay the unpaid part of the subscription price."

In some states the courts hold that persons who agree to take stock in a corporation before it is chartered are "subscribers", but that those who agree to take stock after the company is incorporated "even though it is unissued stock" are "purchasers" of the stock.62 These courts apply the rules discussed above as to purchasers of stock to the case where stock is bought after the company is chartered whether the stock is treasury stock or unissued stock. For instance, where the defendant is a "purchaser" rather than a "subscriber" the stock must be tendered to the purchaser before the company can recover the purchase price.63

So far, no Texas case has made the above distinction. In other words, before the act was passed in 1907 providing that all of the stock in most of the private corporations organized under our general incorporation statutes must be subscribed and 50% paid in before the charter will be approved by the Secretary of State, our Courts made no distinction between a preincorporation subscription and a subscription for the unissued stock which was created by the company after it was chartered.

Some courts have said that the subscriber is bound at the time of signing; others say that he becomes bound on delivery of the subscription to the corporation, or at the time the corporation comes into existence or when the corporation accepts the subscriber's offer.69

It is clear that there could be no binding contract with the corporation before it is formed, for there must be two parties for the existence of a valid contract, and no consideration can move from the corporation before its birth.70 It is also apparent that there is no contract between the parties, for whether there is such a contract depends upon the intention of the parties, and ordinarily the parties signing a subscription paper do not intend to contract with each other individually, but intend to contract with the corporation when formed. It is, of course, possible for persons to enter into a contract with each other individually to form a corporation and take stock therein; and if such an intention appears the courts should construe the contract accordingly. But is this the intention of the parties to a "subscription list" when the first subscribers do not even know who the later subscribers are?" If the parties to the

Therefore, in the absence of promissory estoppel the purported agreement would be uninforceable.72

If several members of a church, in response to the request of the minister, state that each will give the amount set opposite his name to build a new church or pay off a mortgage on the church, there is no manifested intention on the part of the members of the congregation to make promises to each other. Therefore, the members do not enter into bilateral contracts with each other and there is no consideration for the promises. However, if one member said to another, "I will promise to give to the church $100.00 in consideration of your promise to me to give $200.00 to the church", if this offer is accepted there would be consideration for the bilateral promise, as each promise is the agreed exchange for the other promise and each promise is detrimental to the promissor.73 The church as the beneficiary of the bilateral agreement could recover against each promissor.74 

But where promoters of a corporation sign a subscription list, even though it recites that the subscribers "promise by and with each other", there is no consideration for the "purported agreement" as the recited consideration is fictitious.75 By the weight of authority a subscriber may revoke his subscription and thus prevent a contract with the corporation at any time before the corporation is formed and the offer accepted.76

"In determining this question it becomes important to consider the nature of the subscription to the stock of a proposed corporation, and the relation of the different parties to each other. 

A subscription by a number of persons to the stock of a corporation to be thereafter formed by them has in law a double character: First. It is a contract between the subscribers themselves to become stockholders without further act on their part immediately upon formation of the corporation. As such a contract it is binding and irrevocable from the date of subscription, (at least in the absence of fraud or mistake,) unless canceled by consent of all the subscribers before acceptance by the corporation. Second. It is also in the nature of a continuing offer to the proposed corporation, which, upon acceptance by it after its formation, becomes as to each subscriber a contract between him and the corporation. the pro- moter, who solicited and obtained the subscriptions, occupied the position of agent for the subscribers as a body, to hold the subscriptions until the corporation was formed and then turn them over to the company without any further act of delivery on the part of the subscribers.

subscription agreements, appearing in Galveston Hotel Co. v. 

Bolton,⁹ has often been quoted. He said: "A subscription of stock in an incorporated company, or in anticipation of a company expected to be incorporated, is usually in the shape of a mutual agreement, written and signed by those desiring to be corporators, or of a mutual undertaking in writing, to be bound to take a share or shares in an incorporation already created, in which the nature, object, and terms of the association are to some extent indicated. Whether in one shape or in the other, the mutual agreement, or undertaking of all of the subscribers, may constitute the consideration for the agreement, or undertaking, of each one of them, so as to make it a valid contract in favor of and against each, to be carried out or enforced by the company when organized, if not already recognized. The company becomes a party to the contract, either expressly or by implication, from the terms of the subscription." 

The better authorities hold that in cases of preincorporation subscriptions there is no intent on the part of the subscribers to contract with each other. Therefore, the subscription papers evidence nothing but offers on the part of the subscribers to the future corporation. As there is no intent to contract with each other, the promise of one subscriber is not the consideration for the promise of the other.91 It would seem that if a subscription paper were considered as constituting both a contract between the subscribers as individuals and a continuing offer to the proposed corporation, a breach by one of the signers by withdrawing before formation of the corporation would merely give the other subscribers an action against him for breaching his contract with them, and would in no way make the withdrawing member liable to the corporation. Under this view in order to hold the withdrawing member liable to the corporation

Apparently the Texas courts have taken a false step with reference to this question. The elementary principles of contract law require a result in line with the majority rule.93 In view of the Texas statute 94 requiring all of the capital stock to be subscribed and fifty per cent paid in before a charter can be filed, it would seem that the logical time for the subscriber to become bound would be at the time of such filing.95 

If it is considered desirable, as a matter of policy, that a subscriber should not be permitted to revoke his offer to take shares in the proposed corporation, the desirable route to take in reaching this result is through the legislative bodies. It is undoubtedly within the power of the legislature to make subscriptions binding and irrevocable before the corporation is formed or accepts them. And it has been held, in several states, that the rule that a subscription to the stock of a corporation to be formed is not binding, and may be revoked by the subscriber at any time before the corporation is formed and accepts the same, does not apply to subscriptions made as a step authorized or required by a general law in the formation of a corporation as where one signs the affidavit or charter. § 215. Subscriptions Irrevocable by Force of Statute 

Since practically all modern corporations derive their existence from statutes, if the legislature by enactment, expressly or by implication, provides that promises to take shares of stock in a corporation to be formed subsequently, should be incapable of revocation by the subscriber, effect must of course be given to that legislative intent." In cases where corporations were formed by special act, it is not difficult to imply such a provision. It is not so readily discernible where incorporation is under a general law. Since the adoption of the present Texas constitution, all private corporations in this state must be organized under our general law.98 In the McCord-Southwestern Sundries Co. case,99 Mr. Justice Rasbury quoted from Cook on Corporations as follows: "A preliminary agreement to form a corporation and take stock therein is not a contract by the subscribers with each other.

This view has been adopted in some states but was not adopted by the Commission of Appeals 2 in holding that a subscriber could not withdraw before incorporation. The only instrument under the general incorporation statutes of Texas that must be signed by some of the shareholders, "made as a step authorized by statute in the process of forming a corporation," is the charter of the company. The statutes do not provide that the so-called subscription agreement must be signed. However, they do provide that all the stock of a 

Texas corporation must be subscribed before the "charter can be filed" by the Secretary of State.³ The charter "must be subscribed by three or more persons." 4 It would, therefore, seem evident that the quotation from Cook applies in Texas only to the charter of the corporation. § 216. Conditional Subscriptions 

By the weight of authority where general laws, under which it is proposed to organize a corporation, require that a certain amount of stock be subscribed before corporate powers can be exercised, persons subscribing for stock prior to the organization of the corporation, and for the purpose of organization, cannot attach conditions, but their subscriptions must be absolute and unconditional. In Burke v. Smith, it was said by Mr. Justice 

Strong, speaking of the invalidity of conditional subscriptions prior to organization of a railroad corporation: "When a company is incorporated under general laws, and the law prescribes that a certain amount of stock shall be subscribed before corporate powers shall be exercised, if subscriptions, obtained before the organization was effected, may be subsequently rendered unavailable by conditions attached to them, the substantial requirements of the laws are defeated. The purpose of such a requisition is, that the state may be assured of the successful prosecution of the work and that creditors of the company may have, to the extent at least of the required subscription, the means of obtaining satisfaction of their claims. 

The grant of the franchise is, therefore, made dependent upon securing a specified amount of capital. If the subscriptions to the stock can be clogged with such conditions as to render it impossible to collect the fund which the state required to be pro- 

6. Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1308. 

7. 16 Wall 390, 83 U.S. 390, 21 L.Ed. 361. 462

Ch. § 216  

vided before it would assent to the grant of corporate powers, a charter might be obtained without any available capital. Conditions attached to subscriptions, which, if valid, lessen the capital of the company, thus depriving the state of the security it exacted that the railroad would be built, and diminishing the means intended for the protection of creditors, are therefore a fraud upon the grantor of the franchise and upon those who may become creditors of the corporation. They are also a fraud upon unconditional stockholders, who subscribed to the stock in the faith that capital sufficient would be obtained to complete the projected work, and who may be compelled to pay their subscriptions, though the enterprise has failed, and their whole investment has been lost. It is for these reasons that such conditions are denied any effect."

In New York it is held that a conditional subscription prior to such an incorporation is a nullity, and that no rights or liabilities at all can arise out of it. In Pennsylvania and North 

Carolina it is held that the condition only is void, and that the subscription is to be treated as absolute, binding, and unconditional, especially where the rights of creditors have intervened. 

However, Texas at an early date 10 recognized the validity of conditions in such subscription contracts. § 217. Subscription of the Full Amount of Capital Stock

This is no arbitrary rule. It is founded on a plain dictate of justice and the strict principles regulating the obligation of contracts. When a man subscribes a share to a stock, to consist of one thousand shares, in order to carry on some designated enterprise, he binds himself to pay a thousandth part of the cost of the enterprise. If only five hundred are subscribed for, and he can have no assurance which he is bound to accept, that the remainder will be taken, he would be held, if liable to assessment, to pay a five hundredth part of the cost of the enterprise, besides incurring the risk of the entire failure of the enterprise itself and the loss of the amount advanced toward it. Thus when there is no provision to the contrary, the man who takes the first share of stock takes it on condition that all of the shares will be taken, until the amount fixed as the capital stock of the company shall be taken by persons who will be equally bound with himself to bear the expense of the enterprise, share and share alike. In principle, it is the same as if one would say, 'I will be one of five hundred persons who will bind themselves to contribute equal amounts, not exceeding five hundred dollars each, in building a first class hotel. # 25 In Belton Compress Company v. § 218. Incorporation of the Company 

The law imports the condition that the corporation will in fact come into existence as a de jure corporation before the subscriber to stock in a corporation to be formed will become liable.39 But where stock is sold in a corporation already in existence, there is no implied condition that the corporation is de jure and the stockholder can be held if in fact a corporation de facto exists. The stockholder in the latter instance was placed on inquiry to determine the status of the corporation at the time he subscribed.40

Where there is no material addition to the purposes of the corporation as contemplated in the subscription agreement, the fact that the company has embarked on an ultra vires business or one not contemplated in the subscription contract does not release the subscriber from liability on his subscription. The reason for this rule is that the stockholder has an inherent right to enjoin the performance of executory ultra vires transactions. 

Since this is true, and as it is very often difficult to determine whether the transaction is ultra vires, the courts will not imply a condition in the subscription agreement that the company will not enter into ultra vires contracts.58 Where the company exercises temporarily only part of the purpose or purposes for which it was incorporated the subscriber is not released.59 Even permanent abandonment of a part of the express or implied powers of the corporation will not release a subscriber unless the part abandoned is so material that it constitutes a material change in the business undertaken. There may be an express condition in the subscription contract that an abandonment of part of the undertaking will release the subscriber.60 But where the charter includes independent purposes other than those contemplated by the subscription agreement, the fact that the corporation when formed actively engaged only in the purpose set out in the subscription agreement will not cure the situation and the subscriber is not bound to take stock in the corporation formed. § 220. Subscriptions upon Special Terms 

67 A distinction is made between subscriptions to corporate stock on conditions precedent, or "conditional subscriptions in the proper sense," discussed in the foregoing sections, and subscriptions upon special terms, sometimes differentiated from the former by the designation, "subscriptions upon conditions subsequent.' 

In true conditional subscriptions the subscriber is not liable on his subscription until fulfillment of a stipulated condition precedent; whereas, in a subscription upon special terms, his contractual obligation as a shareholder attaches absolutely and unconditionally upon acceptance by the corporation, and the additional stipulations in the agreement represent collateral engagements on the part of the corporation, for breach of which his remedy is an action for damages, or where it represents a material breach of the subscription agreement, rescission of the previously consummated contract, where the rights of creditors are not involved. The Texas authorities do not always make this distinction and refer to "conditional subscriptions" without sharp differentiation between conditions precedent on the one hand, and mere covenants or promises, on the other hand. For instance, where, according to the subscription agreement, the corporation undertook to erect and operate a slaughterhouse and the subscribers agreed to pay less than par for their stock, the suspension of the business due to financial embarrassment does not relieve the subscribers from contractual liability nor authorize withdrawal from the agreement and

Did the court mean that liability never attached because of nonperformance of a condition precedent, or did it hold that the subscriber is entitled to rescission, because of the corporation's breach of a material obligation, constituting a "special term", in the previously consummated contract?

According to the above statement of the Court the subscriber may rescind the contract for a material breach of a "special term or condition subsequent." In an ordinary bilateral contract the promise of one party is the consideration for the promise of the other party. It follows that if one party breaches his promise in a material respect the other party can ordinarily rescind on the ground of the breach of an implied condition,-failure of consideration. These "special terms" are promises on the part of the corporation, and may be very material parts of the corporation's promise. Their breach therefore, should enable the subscriber to rescind the contract. In Bryan v. St. Andrews Bay

Community Hotel Corporation 71 the special term of the subscription contract provided that the hotel would be built at a cost not to exceed a certain amount. The defendant alleged that the cost greatly exceeded that amount, and for that reason tried to rescind the contract. In holding that the defendant could not rescind for breach of a "special term" the court said: "The failure to perform the conditions prescribed does not, therefore, give to the subscriber the right to maintain an action for the can- 

71. 126 So. 142, 99 Fla. 132. 

See other above. cases cited in notes 482 

1 HILDEBRAND TEX.CORP.

§ 220 

cellation of his subscription, nor where an action is brought for the enforcement of his subscription, may he set up as a defense the failure of the corporation to perform.

The sub scriber's remedy would be an action for the recovery from the corporation of the damages he suffered by reason of the nonperformance." This decision can be upheld only on the assumption that the breach was not material. 

The quotation from the Texas case cited above seems to apply the ordinary rules of contracts to "special terms" in subscription agreements. One way to uphold many of the cases cited in this section is to say that the important promise of the corporation is to transfer the title of the stock to the subscriber and that as that is such a material part of the corporation's promise all other promises of the corporation are of minor importance and, therefore, their breach cannot be material. But, in some of the cases cited in this section, the facts show that the breach of "the special terms" may make the stock almost worthless. Therefore, it would seem that the "special term" formed a material part of the consideration for the subscriber's promise. In such cases a breach of "a special term" would be a material breach and if the rules of contracts are followed the subscriber could rescind."2 The Supreme Court of Texas has not directly decided this question, but it refused a writ of error in the Meeks Case cited above in note 70. When the question is fairly presented to the Supreme Court it will very probably follow the weight of authority. 

If the authorities which discuss the law applicable to "special terms" in subscription contracts are not carefully weighed, one is apt to reach an erroneous conclusion. For instance, in 

Muir v. Schultz,73 the subscription agreement provided that his note for the purchase price of the stock "was to be paid" by his putting in the heating and plumbing work in the corporation's building. The breach of this promise on the part of the

In its opinion the court quotes from many text books which seem to say the stockholder's only remedy is "for damages".74 A more accurate statement of what the law should be, if not what it actually is today, is found in Professor Ballantine's treatise on private corporation. After stating that the usual remedy for breach of a "special term" is damages, he says: "If the special term, however, or undertaking on the part of the corporation, forms substantially the whole consideration for the subscription, a breach thereof by the corporation before the subscription is paid will discharge the subscriber, except as against creditors, on the ground that there is a failure of consideration." 75 This statement of the law is repeated by Fletcher in his permanent edition. In the opinion the court said: "In the case at the bar the oral evidence conclusively establishes the fact that the maintenance of a machinery warehouse at the town of Trent, where subscribers to the stock might exercise their right to purchase machinery at certain discounts, was essential to the validity of the note sued on, was one of the inducements to the signing of the subscription contract and note, and was an essential element which gave value to both." It is evident that the court realized that the promise of the Harvester Company to sell machinery to the defendant farmer at a discount was as important, if not more so, as its promise to transfer its title to one share of stock to him. The court, therefore, held that as the plaintiff had broken its promise in a material respect, the defendant could rescind the subscription agreement on the ground that the consideration for defendant's promise had failed "in whole or in part." 

The other cases cited in the preceding note go no further than the two cases discussed somewhat in detail above. It is, therefore, believed that they follow the ordinary rules of contract law to the effect that one party to a bilateral contract may rescind where the other party has broken his promise in a material respect. It seems to follow that these contracts form no exception to the ordinary rules of contract law, and that Ballantine and Fletcher state the rule too strictly when they say that the subscriber can rescind when the "undertaking on the part of the corporation, forms substantially the whole consideration for the subscription." Very seldom will the undertaking of the collateral promise of the corporation "form substantially the whole consideration" for the subscriber's agreement, as in most of these cases the agreement of the corporation to transfer title to the stock to the subscriber is certainly a material part of its agree- 485

§ 

Ch. 6

ment. A breach of a material promise should enable the subscriber to rescind. The writer believes that this idea is substantiated in a fairly recent case by the Court of Appeals of 

New York.78 In fact the New York case cited in the last note shows that the subscriber should be allowed to recover the consideration paid for the stock when the breach of the "special term" of the subscription contract goes "to the root of the contract." 79 That holding is in accordance with the ordinary rules of contract law.80 Most lawyers realize how difficult it is to determine when the breach of a promise is material; 81 and, if that is the idea that Ballantine and Fletcher meant to convey, no criticism of their statement of the law is justified. The above suggestion should be followed by the courts if their effort is to clarify the law. 

In the Cator 82 case cancellation of the subscription contract on the ground of failure of the corporation to make a stipulated loan was denied because of the subscriber's non-performance of a condition precedent to the corporation's obligation to do so; namely, payment in full. It was therefore not necessary for the court to discuss whether the agreement to lend money to the plaintiff was a condition precedent to liability on the part of the corporation or a "special term" of the subscription agreement. In American Home Life Ins. Co. v. Compere,83 the plaintiff subscribed for fifty shares of stock of the defendant company, attached to the subscription contract was this statement: "Subject to loan of $2500.00". The court did not discuss whether that provision of the contract was a condition precedent to plaintiff's liability to take and pay for the stock, but assumed it was a promise on the part of the company to make plaintiff a loan of the specified amount. In the opinion the court said: "The failure, therefore, to make the loan under the circumstances alleged constituted but a breach of the contract on the part of the insurance company. Such breach, if any, would en title the plaintiff, to damages or to a rescission of the subscription contract with a recovery of the money advanced thereon."

The meaning of the phrase "subject to a loan of $2500.00” is not definite. Did it mean that the plaintiff subscribed for fifty shares of stock "if the insurance company made the loan"? 

Surely that is not a reasonable construction of the phrase in view of its setting. The loan could not be made until after the stock was paid for and the insurance business launched. Therefore, it is evident that the above phrase was not an express condition precedent to plaintiff's liability to pay for the stock. For this reason the court was correct in holding that it was a promise on the part of the insurance company to make the plaintiff a loan; in other words a "special term" of the subscription agreement. Therefore, the court erred in stating that plaintiff was entitled to a judgment of rescission unless that agreement formed a material part of the subscription contract, and its breach, therefore, was a material one.84

A collateral agreement in a stock subscription contract to make payment in cash or securities is valid.85 And a written. subscription agreement is not subject to variation by the engrafting of contemporaneous parol agreements respecting the character of acceptable securities, modifying or limiting its interpretation in such a manner as to bring the agreement in conflict with constitutional or statutory requirements.86 No agreement collateral to a valid stock subscription contract will be enforced which contravenes the provisions of the Constitution or the laws of the State controlling such transactions, e. g., a stipulation that the subscriber will not be required to pay the full amount of his subscription.87 Such an agreement is illegal as a matter of law, and as to creditors the subscriber is fully liable on his contract shorn of the obnoxious element.88

Prerequisite to recovery of pecuniary redress for the corporation's breach of a collateral stipulation, or special term, in the contract is proof of resulting damages; 94 and rescission of the contract for the breach is contingent upon a showing with reasonable certainty that in the absence of such equitable relief irreparable injury will result to the complainant stockholder.95

If the courts would cease talking about "collateral stipulations or special terms" on the one hand, and conditions on the other hand, and merely apply the rule of contract law relating to covenants and conditions, the confusion in the authorities would disappear. What the courts generally call "collateral stipulations or special terms" are nothing but covenants and are not conditions, either precedent or subsequent, and the courts should treat these provisions as "covenants or promises" and not attempt to apply the rules of "conditions" to a mere promise.97

In the opinion of the writer the courts made the first mistake when they held that a corporation has "power and authority" to repurchase its own stock. This holding has caused endless confusion. The writer seriously doubts that the Legislatures would have enacted general laws providing for the organization of corporations had they realized that it is so easy for the directors of the corporation to tamper with the safety fund of the corporation which should always be kept in tack for the benefit of creditors, under the rule which permits a corporation to repurchase its own stock.99 But, if this mistake is continued by the courts, there is no inherent reason why stock cannot be sold, with a valid condition subsequent "to the passage of the title" inserted in the contract of sale, as well as in the case of the sale of a horse or real estate.¹

Termination of the Subscription Contract—Withdrawal 

According to the majority view, adhered to by the earlier Texas authorities, a subscription to shares in a proposed corporation is in the nature of a continuing offer and the legal creation of the corporation and its acceptance of the subscription are prerequisite to the formation of a binding contract. Prior thereto the subscriber may revoke the offer without liability to the subsequently organized corporation. The Coleman Hotel 

Co.-Crawford decision by the Commission of Appeals, how ever, represents a repudiation of the earlier authority and the definite establishment of the rule that the subscriber is powerless to withdraw from the transaction and revoke his offer, even before incorporation unless he obtains the consent of all other

This view is grounded upon the theory that an agreement between several parties to subscribe to the stock of a proposed corporation "constitutes a contract between the subscribers themselves to become stockholders when the corporation is formed on the condition expressed in the agreement, and, as such, is binding and irrevocable from the date of subscription." The corporation is a third party beneficiary in such contract to which the benefit of the mutual promises enures, and is empowered to insist upon performance from the first moment of its legal existence without the formality of an acceptance. 

An examination of the Texas decisions cited in the opinion reveals that the court's reliance upon them as authority was somewhat misplaced. J., discerned an element of estoppel in the stockholder-creditor relation: "The stockholder who has permitted himself to be held out as such, who has received and appropriated benefits from the corporate enterprise, but has not paid for his stock, rests under the duty to pay for it. With the debts of the corporation unpaid, it is a fraud upon innocent creditors, as well as a fraud upon the law, to release him from that duty."

This rule is stated as follows by the author of the best single volume text book on Corporations: 17 

"The doctrine invalidating the release of a subscriber by the corporation as against dissenting stockholders and creditors does not prevent a bona fide compromise between a corporation and a subscriber. If a stockholder is unable to pay for his shares, and the transaction is in good faith, the corporation may accept a surrender of his shares and release him from any further liability.18 Nor does the general rule apply when there is a bona fide dispute as to liability on a subscription. In such a case, the corporation, if the transaction is in good faith, may compromise the dispute, accepting a surrender of his shares from the subscriber, and releasing him from further liability." 19 

In other words, according to these authorities, if a dispute arises between a subscriber and the corporation and by a bona fide compromise the subscriber is released from liability, even a creditor cannot complain and have the release set aside. Of course, so long as the corporation is a going concern and not insolvent, just as an individual, it must have power and authority to enter into bona fide compromises with all claimants, otherwise its business career would be seriously hampered. But as is shown in the last part of this chapter even the right of a subscriber to rescind his contract of subscription on the ground of fraud is subordinate to the rights of, at least, subsequent

In the event of the insolvency of the corporation, the shareholder who is indebted on his subscription contract is not discharged to the extent of such credits as he has against the corporation; i. e., he is denied the advantage of a set-off generally allowed parties who stand in the relation of both debtor and creditor to a bankrupt, inasmuch as he would thus obtain a preference over corporate creditors.37 The denial is based on the theory that the one debt is due to an individual by the corporation, whereas the other runs from the individual to trust funds for corporate creditors, on the faith of which they have extended credit to the corporation. An exception appears in the allowance for cash advances, made with the knowledge of directors and all other stockholders, which became part of the corporate assets.38 

Rendition of services, pursuant to a valid agreement that the same shall be accepted in satisfaction of the liability on the subscription contract, is equivalent to cash advances in discharging pro tanto the subscriber's liability to the corporation thereon.39 

Where the subscriber fraudulently obtains money, or other property from the corporation, and transfers it to the company in payment of his stock, the court will indulge the presumption

§ 226. Statute of Limitations 

The proper statutes of limitation apply both to the claims of the corporation and its creditors against the subscribers on stock agreement contracts. But the claims of corporate creditors against stockholders who have not fully paid for the shares subscribed for do not accrue until they have exhausted their remedy against the corporation, in the application of all the corporate assets to the satisfaction of their claims; and until that time the limitation period does not commence to run as against the creditors or other persons representing them.41 The burden of proof is on the creditor to prove that the subscriber has not fully paid for his stock.42 227.

There are not wanting authorities declaring him an agent of the proposed corporation. Thus in Dickerman v. Northern 

Trust Co., 20 S.Ct. 311, 176 U.S. 181, 44 L.Ed. 423, it is said: ""The promoter is the agent of the corporation and subject to the disabilities of an ordinary agent."" "This language is quoted with approval in Fred Macey Co. v. 

Macey, 143 Mich. 138, 106 N.W. 722, 5 L.R.A.,N.S., 1036. "This is hardly an accurate statement. An agency implies the existence of a principal, and a delegation of authority from the principal to the agent. A non-existent corporation can have no agent. [Weatherford, M. W. & N. W.] Ry. Co. v. Granger, 86 

Tex. 350, 24 S.W. 795, 40 Am.St.Rep. 837. It follows, therefore, that a contract by a promoter in which he undertakes to bind the future corporation and create a liability against it cannot be enforced against the corporation unless and until adopted by it. [Weatherford, M. W. & N. W.] Ry. Co. v. Granger, supra;

Weathersby v. [Texas & Ohio] Lumber Co., 107 Tex. 474, 180 

"Though the promoter cannot, strictly speaking, be regarded as an agent, his relation to the future corporation and to the subscribers is of a fiduciary character. He is an intermediary between the corporation and the subscribers, future members, who in the aggregate will form the corporation. His relation to the corporation is analogous to that of an agent to his principal, and the rules governing the relation of principal and agent have been extended to apply to that of the promoter to the corporation. Under all the authorities, he is held accountable to the corporation in like manner as though the relation of principal and agent, in fact, existed." 45 

45. Cator v. Commonwealth B. & C. 

Ins. Co., Tex.Com.App., 216 S.W. 140. 

Acc. Harlan v. Acme S. F. Co., Tex. 

Civ.App., 240 S.W. 623; Trinity-Universal Ins. Co. v. Maxwell, Tex.Civ. 

App., 101 S.W.2d 606, writ dismissed. 504

The decision in Bivins v. Panhandle Packing Co.46 was based on the proposition that a promoter cannot be an agent of the future corporation, and, therefore, the subscription contract cannot be rescinded for the fraud of the promoter or his agent. 

But in the Cator case the Commission of Appeals held that the promoter was the quasi agent of the future corporation and the subscription contract can be rescinded if induced by the fraudulent representations of the promoter or his agent. 

Therefore, it is evident that the Bivins case will no longer be followed. In the Cator case it was held that even though the subscribers contract with each other the corporation cannot enforce the subscription contracts where they were induced by fraud as they were made for the benefit of the corporation and, under the rules of contract law, the beneficiary takes the contract subject to all defenses between the promisor and promisee. 

On this point Judge Sonfield said: "If the subscription be regarded as a present, binding contract, made for the benefit of the future corporation and enforceable by it upon organization, the rule that the rights of the person for whose benefit a contract is made are subject to the equities growing out of the contract between the original parties applies. 13 C.J. p. 610. As between the Organization 

Company and plaintiff in error, parties to the contract, there can be no question that the fraudulent representations by the agent of the Organization Company inducing the contract would be available as a ground for rescission. The corporation for whose benefit the contract was made, through its acceptance or adoption, acquired no higher or better right than the Organization Company."

After creation of the corporation, employment of an agent to sell stock carries with it apparent authority to make pertinent representations to prospective subscribers.47 Even a stipulation

"But a party may become liable for false representations made in the form of promises for future returns. If the representations relied on by plaintiff and found by the jury to have been made for that purpose were merely opinions, or promises, yet if they were known to be false by the agents when they made them, and were made for the purpose of deceiving plaintiff and inducing him to make the contract, they were nevertheless actionable, having been relied upon by plaintiff. This proposition has been often stated and approved in the opinions of this court, but we cite only the following authorities: "The Supreme Court, speaking through Justice Greenwood, in the case of Edward Thompson Co. v. Sawyers, 111 Tex. 374, 378, 234 S.W. 873, 874, say: 'Promises made without intention of fulfillment, in order to induce others to make contracts, are as culpable and as harmful as are willful misrepresentations of existing facts. Hence contracts may be avoided alike for such fraudulent promises and for such misrepresentations.'"

What purports to be a promise as to what will happen in the future may actually be a present misrepresentation of a fact if the promisor never intends performance; that is, a state of mind is subject to misrepresentation as well as any other fact, and rescission may be sought of a contract where such misrepresentation was an inducing cause.59 

To justify rescission for false representations, distinct from any consideration of damages in a tortious action for deceit, the test is materiality and not bad faith. Whether the representations were made with fraudulent design and a consciousness of their falsity seems beside the point; a subscriber who has justifiably relied on the representations of one who may reasonably be supposed to have access to a special means of knowledge of the subject of the representations may rescind if the latter are adjudged material and prove false without establishing bad faith on the part of the representing party, provided the injured party is damaged. Rescission for false representations of the stock subscription contract may be effected by notice to the corporation and an offer to return such shares as have been delivered to the subscriber.65 Cancellation of the contract may be had in a proceeding for the purpose and the money or other property delivered in consideration of the subscription contract may be recovered.66

The right of rescission of a single stockholder is not affected by an election of the other stockholders, similarly defrauded, to waive their right to rescind,67 however much their shares will depreciate in market value by reason of the restoration of the money or property to the rescinding member paid by him for the shares allotted to him.68 But the rights of the creditors of the corporation, who were ignorant of the fraud and whose claims arose after the defrauded stockholder subscribed for the stock, are paramount to those of the subscribers seeking to avoid their contracts because of fraud perpetrated when the shares were purchased or subscribed for.69 The insolvency of

In Park v. Kribs 72 it was held that the defrauded stockholder could rescind even after the corporation became insolvent where no claims of creditors arose subsequent to the subscription. In

It appears to be a well-established rule in Texas that a subscriber to the capital stock of a corporation cannot, as against subsequent creditors, defeat his liability as a stockholder on account of fraud in inducing his contract of subscrip tion. This rule is based on the theory that a subscriber to the corporate stock of a corporation, by his own act, has induced subsequent creditors of such corporation to believe that the capital stock subscribed by him has been, or will be, paid in and will remain a trust fund to which subsequent creditors may look for security. 

It is said that 'where a party has trusted and been deceived, he ought to bear the loss occasioned by his own credulity, rather than that the same should be borne by another who was not a party to such trans action'. Davis v. Burns, Tex.Civ.

If this balance amounted to a sizeable sum, the shareholder would naturally ratify the subscription contract where his share as a stockholder will exceed the amount that would be paid to him as a creditor upon rescission of the subscription contract. In those states in which the stockholder's right to rescind is subordinate to the rights of subsequent innocent creditors, should the courts place arbitrary limitations on such right? In other words, should the courts follow Georgia holding and refuse to let the stockholder rescind where the subsequent debts equal or exceed the stockholder's claim against the corporation? If the claim of the stockholder is always subordinated to the claim of such creditors should he not always share equally with the other unsecured creditors after his claim is subordinated to the rights of the subsequent innocent creditors.

For instance, suppose that the corporation owes A $5,000, B $5,000, C $500, and D $500. The stockholder X subscribed for ten shares of stock for which he actually paid $1,000.00. D's claim arose after X subscribed and paid for his stock. If X is considered a creditor of the company after he has rescinded the contract on the ground of fraud, for the return of $1,000 that he paid for his stock, the debts of the corporation amount to $12,- 000. Suppose the assets are sold for $10,000. Each creditor, if all are on the same basis, would be entitled to ten-twelfths of his claim. However, under the Texas law and the law in many other states D's claim has preference over X's claim. 

Therefore, if each of the above parties is given ten-twelfths of his claim and X is then compelled to pay D the difference between ten-elevenths of D's five hundred dollar claim and tentwelfths of the same claim, justice is meeted out to all parties according to the opinions of most courts.83 As X can always

Eleven thousand dollars would be given to A, B, C, and D, one thousand of the remaining two thousand dollars would be given to X, and the other one thousand dollars would be returned to the stockholders other than X.84 

A distinction between the case where the stockholder has fully paid for his stock and where he has paid only a part of what he agreed to pay for the stock is not made in all cases. In the latter case, where he has no right to rescind under the above rules, he is forced to pay the balance that he owes the corporation. Whether he is given the right of a creditor only against the company or is subordinated to the rights of creditors whose claims arose after he subscribes, depends upon the foregoing rules. Suppose, however, he has paid only a small amount of the agreed partial payments for his stock when the company became insolvent, and the court permits him to rescind the contract, in most cases he is in a better position than if he is permitted to rescind the contract and claim the rights of a creditor for the amount that he paid for the stock after rescission. Should the court make a distinction between these two cases? In many cases where he rescinds the contract after he has fully paid for his stock he may not receive more than 5% of his claim as a creditor of the company. Whereas, if he is permitted to rescind the contract where he has paid only a small amount, he will receive practically 100% of his claim against the company. In this latter case, should the court not hold that he must pay the balance that is due for his stock and then share as a creditor under the rules discussed in the foregoing paragraphs?

The court said even if he can rescind "such relief cannot be had to the loss of creditors of the corporation." Suppose the stockholder paid $10,000.00 for his stock or gave a tract of land worth that amount to the corporation for his stock and the property is still owned by the company and only $10,000.00 of debts were created after the shareholder was defrauded even though an equal amount of debts were paid by the corporation, did the court mean to say the defrauded shareholder would not share equally with the old creditors whose rights arose long before the fraud was perpetrated? As we have seen most of the Texas cases say that the reason he cannot rescind is because of the equity of subsequent creditors, and if there are no subsequent creditors he can rescind even though he is guilty of laches.88 Whether the prior or subsequent creditor should prevail over the defrauded stockholder is a question of balancing hardships as between those two parties. The facts in each case will determine in whose favor the scales are weighted. 

The general rule that all contracts induced by fraud are voidable at the instance of the injured party should be followed except where the equities of the subsequent creditors outweigh those of the defrauded shareholder. Too much stress should not be put on the fact that the business really belongs to all the shareholders and includes the defrauded person in that category since it could be contended with some show of reason that as the defrauded shareholder has a right to rescind the contract he was really never "a shareholder." Therefore, it would seem that the most equitable solution of the problem would be to say that the defrauded person can rescind "subject to the claims of subsequent innocent creditors," and work out the rights of the parties on the basis discussed in the foregoing sections. Let us suppose a case where the assets of the corporation would pay the prior creditors fifty per cent of their claims without reference to the property or money given to the company by the defrauded person. Is it equitable to take forty per cent of that property from the injured party and give it to the prior creditors even though they placed no reliance on that property when they gave credit to the company? Should he not be permitted to take back his property rather than only sixty per cent of it as a general creditor of the corporation? 

Some courts have worked out the rights of the defrauded shareholder on that basis, and to the writer such solution seems eminently equitable. In Morrisey v. Williams,89 the court said: "We cannot see that the liabilities increased one cent, or that a single new creditor came in, while the stock was in Morrisey's hands under the fraudulent sale. * ** Plainly Morrisey's right to a rescission is superior to the rights of creditors to whom debts were due from the bank before he became a stockholder. They lent no credit on the strength of his having stock, either theoretically or actually. They are in no worse position than if he had never purchased the stock. A rescission can do them no harm." 90

 § 228. Specific Performance of the Subscription Agreement 

When the stock of the corporation cannot readily be purchased in the open market a court of equity will give specific performance of the subscription agreement where the plaintiff has complied with all the provisions of the contract.* 

§ 229. Measure of Damages where Contract was Induced by 

Fraud

As a general rule where the contract of subscription was induced by fraud, the measure of damages is the difference between the value of the stock when the contract of subscription was made and what it would have been worth if the fraudulent representations had been true.5 In Oregon the measure of damages is the difference between the cost of the stock and its value at the time of purchase."

§ 251. In General 

When the ordinary layman speaks of "the capital" of a corporation, he has in mind the assets of the corporation, regardless of their source, that have come into the possession of the corporation and are being utilized by the corporation as a means of making profits.¹ But in the law of private corporations, the term "capital" is often used to mean the amount of the "capital stock" of the corporation as fixed by its charter. The caption of Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1330 speaks of "Increase of Capital", when obviously the meaning is as to the increase of the "capital stock". The same thing is true with reference to the caption 

1. Waco National Bank v. Rogers, 51 Tex. 606. 

Turner V. Cattleman's Trust Co.,

Tex.Com.App., 215 S.W. 831. 

Harrison v. Vines, 46 Tex. 15.

Ind. 252.

Tex.Civ.App., 250 S.W. 293. 530 

1 HILDEBRAND TEX.CORP.

Ch. § 251 

of Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 365, relating to impairment of the "capital" of a bank. In the case of Waco National Bank v. Rogers it is said: 3 "It has been established as the law * that the property or interest of a stockholder in a corporation, which are commonly called shares, the shares in their aggregate totality being called sometimes the capital stock of the corporation is a different thing from the moneyed capital of the corporation, held and owned by the corporation. The latter is owned by the bank as a corporate entity and not by the stockholders." 

There are of course general laws providing for the creation of corporations, and those general laws contemplate that the capital stock of the corporation will be divided into shares.¹

Very often the courts mean by the term "capital" the money or other property paid to the corporation for its stock. Some courts estimate the value of such property and if the assets exceed that amount the difference is considered profits. This is the reason why some courts will permit the payment of dividends even though the assets of the corporation do not exceed the liabilities of the company where the amount of the "capital stock" is put on the liability side of the balance sheet.5 These courts say that if the so-called "capital" is not impaired a dividend may be paid. "The capital stock" of a corporation is a book-keeping item and represents the amount of stock the corporation is authorized by its charter to issue. It should always be put on the liability side of the balance sheet in determining the "net worth" or "the surplus" of the company.

The careless use and interchange of the phrases "the capital” and "the capital stock" of a corporation has led to much confusion in both legislative enactments and court opinions. The di-

"A share of stock" is the interest of the shareholder in the company. A "certificate of stock" is the paper evidence of the shareholder's interest. 

§ 252. Classes of Stock 

Corporation stock at one time was issued in shares all of the same class, having the same rights, powers, privileges and immunities and subject to the same limitations, duties and liabilities. 

Today, shares of corporation stock are issued in different classes. 

There is the familiar classification, "preferred" and "common" shares. Shares differ in voting rights. A corporation may also classify its stock so some shares have par value and the residue without nominal or par value.8 "Preferred stock" or "preference stock" is so called because the holders are given a preference of some sort over the ordinary stockholders. The ordinary stock is called "common stock." Generally, the preference consists in the right to receive dividends from the earnings of the company before the holders of the common stock can share in such earnings. § 253. Power to Create Preferred Stock 

The original subscribers of the stock of a corporation to be formed may by agreement attach different rights to different classes of stock.15 In Texas, express statutory authority to issued preferred stock is given corporations issuing non-par stock 10 and to corporations organized for the purpose of dealing in oil, gas, salt brine and other mineral solutions.17 After the charter is granted, all corporations are authorized to amend the charter so as to issue preferred stock as an increase or to convert common stock, issued or unissued, into preferred stock.18 As a corporation may issue different classes of stock, and as no statute in Texas prohibits the issuance of preferred stock, a corporation organized under the general law may issue preferred stock.19

Pennsylvania case, it was held that, in the absence of a contrary stipulation, preferred stockholders share with common stockholders in all profits distributed, after the latter have received an amount equal to the stipulated dividend on the preferred stock.21 The Pennsylvania rule is not the weight of authority at this time, since most courts now understand that preferred stock, especially cumulative preferred, is considered more in the nature of a bond. The business understanding is that the preferred shareholder is limited to the preferences stated in his certificate. And as the common shareholders get nothing until after the preferred shareholders are given their preferences, it is fair and just that the common shareholders get the balance even though in some years the latter shareholders get more dividends than the preferred shareholders. It shall have preference both as to dividends and assets." 34 If the words "if earned" had been omitted, the certificate clearly evidenced an agreement to make the dividends cumulative, since they were to be paid "quarterly”, and that meant every year. But the phrase "if earned" seems to indicate clearly that the dividends were payable only during the years that profits were made. The court, therefore, could have held that the dividends were not strictly cumulative. As stated above, whether dividends are cumulative or not is a question of construction of the language of the stock-certificate.

Ordinarily, preferred stock is entitled to no preference over other stock in relation to capital on dissolution; but where there is an express agreement giving such a preference, not prohibited by local law or by the charter, it is binding upon the common stockholders.35 

If the payment of dividends on preferred stock is made dependent upon the profits of each particular year, "as declared by the board of directors," the holders of such stock are not entitled of right to dividends payable out of the net profits accruing in any particular year, unless the directors formally declare, or ought to declare, a dividend payable out of such profits; and whether a dividend should be declared in any year is a matter that comes within the sound discretion of the directors, determined by the condition of the company's property and its affairs as a whole.

§ 255. Voting Rights 

The ownership of preferred stock, as a general rule, carries with it the right to vote upon the same at any meeting of the stockholders. To this rule there are exceptions. It is competent for a corporation in issuing certificates of preferred stock to stipulate therein that the holders shall not be entitled to vote the same at the stockholders' meetings, and the stipulation will be binding upon them.38 Such a provision affects only the two classes of stockholders, and does not concern the public or violate any rule of public policy.39 The preferred stockholder may be given the right to vote upon the happening of certain conditions, as in Langben v. Goodman,40 where the preferred stockholders were given equal voting rights after the corporation had failed to pay dividends for one year, until the past due dividends were paid.

It is evident from this statement that the court did not fully comprehend the meaning of the word "issue," in saying that the stock had to be paid for before it was issued, and in holding that manual delivery of the certificate is the most important fact in determining whether the stock has been "issued." The very constitutional provision which condemns the sale of stock on credit recognizes that stock may be “issued" before it is paid for, and for this reason provides against it. Little notice is merited by the case, however, for it is believed that more recent and better reasoned cases have served to clarify the meaning of the word "issued" and have overruled the Zapp case. In Turner v. Cattlemen's Trust Company," the court recognizes that the consideration of major importance is the ownership of the stock. It was there stated that the ultimate purpose of the constitution was to prevent any person from becoming the owner of corporate shares without the payment of money, or its lawful equivalent, for them. The certificate of stock, made out to the purchaser, and an entry on the books of the corporation to the effect that the purchaser is the owner, are merely evidences of the ownership of the stock. Acts of the parties determine the essential question of ownership. A stock certificate may be delivered without the stock becoming issued, or it may be issued, in the sense that the subscriber becomes the owner, without a certificate of stock ever being made out.

"There are certain rights, powers, and privileges that accrue to a stockholder in a corporation, the exercise of which are but manifestations of the intention on the part of the shareholder in reference to his attitude towards ownership of the stock, such as the right to attend stockholders' meetings and vote on matters under consideration by shareholders; the right to hold official position of trust in the corporation; and the right to receive dividends from the profits and gains made by the common fund. To "issue" stock signifies that the person to whom it is issued has become the owner of the stock. When the stock certificate is filled out and pledged to secure the stockholders note the evidence of ownership is the fact that the stockholder has pledged the stock. Judge Phillips in the last case cited stated: "In pledging the stock as security for the note, the intention must have been to pledge it as appellant's property. It could hardly have been the purpose that Gahagan should accept for the security of the note a pledge of his own property as agent or property belonging to the corporation. The provision in the collateral agreement was that the stock might be sold if the note were not paid. This could have contemplated nothing else than a sale of the stock as appellant's property." However, in the Kanaman-Gahagan case, in affirming the case of Farmers' & Merchants' State Bank v. Falvey," the court stated that, even though the stock is pledged to secure the stockholder's note, if the stock is not to be delivered until the note is paid, the stock is not issued.73 Isn't this a distinction without a difference? The reason for the Kanaman-Gahagan holding, as is shown by the above quotation from that case, is that the stockholder became the owner of the stock as he was permitted to exercise ownership over it by pledging the stock to secure his note. The same evidence of ownership was adduced in the Falvey case. But in the latter case there was an agreement that the stock was not to be delivered until the note was paid. To say the least, the distinction made in the Kanaman-Gahagan case in attempting to sustain the holding in the Falvey case, is very doubtful. The distinction between the case where a note is given as evidence of an indebtedness upon a stock subscription contract and where it is given as a payment for the stock itself, is clearly shown in Sturdevant v. Falvey. The reason for such a distinction is that the stock when subscribed for, but not issued, does not represent an outstanding liability of the corporation, and it does not mislead the public, whereas stock issued, but not paid for, does represent an outstanding liability as stock, and is calculated to mislead the public, in making them think that the stock has been fully paid for.75 It might appear, as a first impression, that the statute 70 which requires all the stock of a corporation to be subscribed, but only 50% paid in, before the charter will be approved and filed by the Secretary of State, would affect the result in cases of sales of corporate stock partly for cash and partly for credit. That statute, however, has nothing to do with sales on credit. In the first place, it could not nullify the plain provisions of the constitution; secondly, it relates only to the prerequisites of incorporation and in no wise undertakes to regulate the "issuance" of stock.”

Shares of stock are in the nature of a chose in action.80 If the subscriber fully pays for his stock and the company refuses "to issue" the stock to him he may recover what he paid for the stock for the reason that the consideration has failed.81 Shares of stock are usually represented by a certificate issued by the corporation to the stockholders, stating that the holder is the owner of a certain number of shares. But a certificate is merely the paper representative of an incorporeal right in the stockholder. It stands on a footing similar to other muniments of title.82 As expressed in Turner v. Ch. 7  § 259. Conversion of Shares of Stock 

A share of stock in a corporation is presumably a thing of value, and when represented by a certificate of stock may be converted so that the guilty party may be held liable for conversion of the certificate.91 For instance, if the pledgee makes claims that are inconsistent with the owner's rights, such conduct on the part of the pledgee will give rise to an action for the conversion of the certificate of stock, and limitation will not begin the run until the owner learns of such wrongful conduct on the part of the pledgee.92

The reason for this rule is that the pledgee holds the stock as trustee for the pledgor. But if the defendant does not sustain a fiduciary relation to the plaintiff, in other words, is a stranger converter, limitation begins to run when the certificate is converted although the owner is not aware of the conversion.93

Where the corporation denies that plaintiff is the owner of some of its stock, the four years' statute of limitations applies to

It has been held that by registering a forged or unauthorized transfer and issuing a new certificate to the transferee, the corporation is estopped to deny the validity of the transfer, even as against the person who induced the secretary to make the transfer.12 This seems unsound, and, by the better opinion, the estoppel does not operate in favor of the party who presented the certificate with the forged indorsement to the secretary of the company and to whom the new certificate was issued; for he did not take the certificate on the faith of the corporation's conduct in issuing it and recognizing the transfer as valid, but on the faith of the forged or unauthorized assignment and power of attorney.13 And the corporation in such case may maintain an action against him for the damages it may have sustained. This is based on the ground that the party demanding the transfer impliedly warrants the genuineness of the indorsement to the corporation. Where the true owner's name is forged to the stolen certificate and the stock is sold to an innocent purchaser the latter gets no title.16 If the purchaser induces the corporation to issue a new certificate to him he has committed a wrong, as he at last impliedly represented that he was the true owner of the certificate. Therefore, the true owner could make him surrender the certificate. However, if the new certificate is sold to an innocent purchaser for value, the corporation cannot refuse to recognize his rights." If the innocent purchaser is forced to surrender the new certificate to the true owner, the former may recover his damages against the corporation, which in turn can recover from the party who induced the company to recognize the forged indorsement and issue the new certificate such damages as it was forced to pay the innocent purchaser. This party from whom the corporation recovers could recover against his vendor, as the vendor of personal property impliedly warrants his title.18 Where the new certificate is sold to an innocent purchaser the real owner of the original certificate may compel the corporation to issue to him the number of shares represented by the old certificate if the company has on hand either unissued or treasury stock or can purchase a sufficient number of shares in the market to satisfy the demand of the real owner. If the thief, or a purchaser from the thief, induces the corporation to issue a new certificate the title of the stock or share remains in the original owner. When the corporation wrongfully recognizes the purchaser from the thief and issues a new certificate the real title of the true owner has not been affected any more than where the thief of a stolen horse, or a purchaser from the thief, has blotted out the old brand on the horse and burnt some other brand over the mutilated one. on the books of the corporation on the indorsement and surrender of the certificate, is a continuing affirmation as to the ownership of the stock, and is notice that the corporation will not transfer the stock upon its books unless the certificate is first surrendered. It is an assurance to the commercial world that the shares of stock are the property of the person designated, and that he has the power and right to transfer and sell the stock, until this power and right has been lawfully terminated.29 

It is therefore not only the right, but the duty, of a corporation not to register a transfer on its books and issue a new certificate to the transferee without production and surrender of the original certificate. This is generally expressly required by the terms of the certificates, or by the charter or by-laws of the corporation, but the duty is the same where there is no such express requirement.30 If a corporation does register a transfer and issue a new certificate without surrender of the outstanding certificate, a bona fide purchaser of the new certificate or the old may hold the corporation liable thereon, because an entry of the transfer on the books of the corporation is not necessary to vest title to the stock.31 If the corporation had the power to increase its stock, he will be entitled to the shares. If it had no such power, the purchaser may maintain an action for damages. Purchasers of the outstanding certificates in such cases have a right to assume that no transfer has been made by the corporation, and cannot be affected by a transfer on its books. of which they had no notice.32 Where the owner has indorsed the certificate in blank and this certificate is stolen, a bona fide purchaser from the thief gains no better title than his vendor had.33 But where the purchaser takes the stolen certificate, 29. § 261. Amount of Capital Stock 

"The authorized capital stock of a corporation, chartered under the laws of this, or under laws of any state having similar requirement, is the number of shares authorized to be subscribed, and which have actually been subscribed, multiplied by the face or par value of each of such shares." 36 This amount is fixed by the charter or articles of incorporation and remains unchanged, except where increased or diminished by charter amendment under legal sanction.37 The legislature in accord with the public policy of the state has provided that the charter of most corporations organized for profit must set forth the amount of the capital stock and the number of shares into which it is divided.38 "Before the charter of a private corporation created for profit can be filed by the Secretary of State, the full amount of its authorized capital stock must be in good faith subscribed by its stockholders and fifty per cent thereof paid in cash, or its equivalent in other property or labor done, the product of which shall be worth to the company the actual value at which it was taken or at which the property was received. § 262. Increase of Capital Stock 

Though generally a corporation starts out with a definite amount of capital stock subscribed, or possible of issuance upon subscription, in most jurisdictions and in Texas, there may be under certain circumstances an increase in the capital stock. In 

Texas, if authorized by a two thirds vote of all its outstanding stock with voting privileges, the board of directors of a corporation may increase its authorized capital stock by filing with the Secretary of State an affidavit stating the names of the subscribers, and the consideration for and the classes of the additional stock to be issued.43 Where the capital stock is to be increased by an issue of stock without nominal or par value, the corporation must file an amendment authenticated by a majority of the

Quite a number of courts have based their decision on the purpose to be served by issuing such shares.59 The Court of Appeals of New York held that if the issue of such original shares, authorized but unissued, is reasonably necessary to raise money to be used in the business of the corporation, or to pay its debts, the original shareholders have no right to count on obtaining and keeping their proportionate part of the original stock. It would seem that the company could "raise money to be used in the business" by selling the unissued stock to the existing shareholders as well as to outside parties. The courts have also denied the pre-emptive right to holders of convertible bonds or non-voting stock which under certain circumstances may be converted into voting shares, until the convertible bonds or non-voting stock have been converted into voting stock.66

By the better holding the owners of voting stock have the pre-emptive right to purchase their pro rata share of bonds that may be converted into voting stock.67 Nor is the general rule applied where stock that has been issued is later retransferred to the corporation.68 In this latter case the stockholder's voting strength is not impaired by a resale of this stock, as would be the case if denied the right to invest in new issues of stock, since the stock was originally owned by other subscribers. Such stock is designated as "treasury stock." In Wisconsin the shareholders have the pre-emptive right in treasury shares if when they were purchased there was no intent to resell them.69 Treasury stock is acquired either by donation, purchase or forfeiture for nonpayment of calls for the balance due on the stock. The reason for this rule is that the directors are the fiduciary agents of the shareholders and must act fairly towards the real owners of the business.”71 The basis for the existence in a shareholder of a right to have offered to him a proportion of additional shares about to be created is that he may thereby be enabled to maintain his proportionate interest in the voting control of the corporation, and his interest in its net assets and net earnings, and especially his pro rata share of the assets upon dissolution. The pre-emptive right doctrine was announced 72 at a time when corporations issued only one class of stock; i. e., common stock, and therefore the question was fairly simple. The present corporate structure may contain as many classifications of stock as the ingenuity of the attorney drawing the incorporation articles can devise.73 It has been pointed out that "in the light of modern complex share structures, the orthodox preemptive right rule that 'every shareholder has a right to subscribe proportionately to any increase in the capital stock of his corporation' is either unjustifiably arbitrary or impossible of rational application."74
