Where the corporate set-up is very complicated by the issuance of many different kinds of stock, and especially where bondholders have the privilege of converting their bonds into stock, it often becomes almost impossible to determine how the new stock should be distributed among the old shareholders.

After reading all the cases on the pre-emptive rights of shareholders one is forced to the conclusion that the cases are not entirely satisfactory. From the cases it is clearly manifest that the directors are fiduciary agents and in disposing of new stock must act fairly and honestly towards the shareholders. For instance, they cannot sell the new stock to themselves in order to further their own personal interests, nor for less than the stock is worth to non-members of the corporation. Some of the cases cited in the above notes seem to indicate that this rule is the basis of the pre-emptive right of the shareholders and should be the guide in determining the shareholders rights.84 Professor

Stevens thinks that the so-called exceptions to the general rule, stated above, "should be regarded merely as certain illustrative instances in which group interests may sometimes, but will not always, be found to preponderate over the claims of individual shareholders, and in which, the preponderance being found to be in favor of the group, the pre-emptive right is denied." 85 In stating this test surely Professor Stevens does not mean to differentiate "group interests" on the one hand and the claims of separated "individual shareholders" on the other hand. If not, then according to his test when the corporate "group interests" preponderate over the claims of group "individual shareholders" the latter lose their pre-emptive rights. If the latter statement is what Professor Stevens meant his test becomes difficult to apply, and, in fact, meaningless, for the claims of the corporate group will never preponderate over the claims of the individual group of shareholders.

Where the corporate structure is so complicated that it is impossible, as a practical matter, to work out the pre-emptive rights of the different classes of stockholders and convertible bondholders, should the courts not say that this is tantamount to a provision in the charter by which the pre-emptive right is surrendered? In other words, the stockholders knew what they were doing when they authorized the creation of this complicated structure; they knew it was impossible to determine the preemptive rights of each class of stock, and, therefore, they impliedly agreed to surrender the pre-emptive right.86 This is the method adopted by the courts to solve such questions in contract law and no reason occurs to the writer why such method is not applicable under the above circumstances. In an excellent article in the Harvard Law Review, it is suggested that in the case of large corporations everyone's interests are sufficiently protected if the courts should hold the pre-emptive right is waived where it is virtually impossible to determine the equities of all the stockholders, as the fiduciary obligation of the directors is a sufficient guaranty that all stockholders will be treated justly and fairly. This article contends that if the courts adopt this suggestion all interested parties except the "corporate pirate" are sufficiently protected, and, as a general rule, are benefited by the sale of the increased stock as a whole to the investment banker and thereby compensated for the loss due to the surrender of the pre-emptive right. If the courts will read carefully every case cited in this section they will be convinced that the 87 

86. In Yoakam v. It had its origin in the days of simple corporate structures; that is, during the period when it was usual for a corporation to have but one class of stock.

The doctrine is one developed by judicial decisions to the end of protecting stockholders in their relative voice or proportionate interest in the assets and control of the enterprise involved. § 264. Reduction of Capital Stock 

Courts look upon the reduction of capital stock in much the same way that they do the increase of the capital stock, and, therefore, if the rights of the creditors of the corporation are not affected by the reduction, the stockholders may vote a reduction in the same manner as an increase is voted.91 By Vernon's

De crease of capital.—A corporation may decrease its capital stock by such amount as its stockholders may decide, by a two-thirds vote of all its outstanding stock, in like manner as is required for an increase. § 265. Change in Number, Classification or Par Value of Shares of 

Stock Corporations often times find it desirable to change the number, classification or par value of their shares of stock. Statutes have been enacted authorizing such changes independent of the right to increase or decrease the capital stock of the corporation." The corporation may by vote of the majority of its outstanding stock entitled to vote, convert its par value stock, issued or unissued, into preferred stock.98 A corporation having stock with par value may, under the same conditions, change its shares, or any classes thereof, into the same number or into a larger or smaller number of shares without nominal or par value.⁹⁹ But under Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1538d, subd. (d) before a par value corporation can change to a non-par value corporation its capital stock must amount to at least $25,000. If a corporation has more than one class of stock to be affected by the change, all shares in any one class must be changed on the same basis.¹ 

A stockholder, who does not consent to such change, is protected by the provision that "the preferences, rights, limitations, privileges and restrictions granted or imposed with respect to any shares of outstanding stock shall not be impaired, diminished or changed without the consent of the holder thereof." * as amended by Acts 1931, 42nd
